01-001.json.summary: The Purana opens with a bow to Narayana, Nara, the goddess Sarasvati and Vyasa, and to Vishnu who, taking the false form of a dwarf (Vamana), took the three worlds from Bali and gave them to Indra. Narada asks the sage Pulastya, sitting in his hermitage, to tell the Purana about Vamana: how Vishnu became the dwarf, how the demon Prahlada, though a devotee of Vishnu, fought the gods, why Sati, Daksha's daughter and Shankara's dear wife, gave up her body, was born in the house of Himavan and became Shiva's wife again, and also the greatness of holy places, gifts and vows. Pulastya begins. Long ago, when summer came, the goddess said to Shiva on Mount Mandara that they had no house to shelter them from wind and heat. Shiva replied that he had no home and always wandered in the forest, so Sati spent the summer with him in the shade of trees. Then the rainy season came, with roaring clouds, lightning, dancing peacocks, flooding rivers and flowering kadamba trees, and Sati lovingly asked Shiva to build a house. Shiva said he had no wealth to build one: his clothing was a lion's skin, his sacred thread the king of snakes, and his earrings, armlets, bracelets and girdle were all serpents. Hearing this, Sati, ashamed and angry, looked at the ground and asked how she would pass the rains sitting under a tree. Shiva said she would live with her body resting on the clouds, so no rain would fall on her. He then climbed onto a high bank of cloud with Daksha's daughter and stayed there, and from this he became known in heaven as Jimutaketu, 'he whose banner is the cloud'.

01-002.json.summary: Pulastya tells Narada that the rainy season passed while Shiva lived on the cloud, and the pleasant autumn came, with clear skies, open lotuses and moonlight. Shiva took Sati to Mount Mandara and enjoyed himself with her there. When autumn ended and Vishnu woke from his sleep, Daksha, the chief of the Prajapatis, began a great sacrifice. He invited the twelve Adityas, Indra and the other gods, Kashyapa, and the sages with their wives (Vasishtha with Arundhati, Atri with Anasuya, Gautama with Ahalya and others) as members of the assembly; he made Dharma with his wife Ahimsa the gatekeeper, Arishtanemi the fetcher of firewood, Bhrigu the one in charge of the mantras, and the Moon with Rohini the keeper of wealth. He invited all his daughters, sons-in-law and grandsons, except Sati and Shankara. Narada asks why Shiva, the eldest and greatest, was not invited, and Pulastya says it was because Daksha knew him to be a skull-bearer (kapali). Narada asks how Shiva became a skull-bearer, and Pulastya tells an old story from the first Purana spoken by Brahma. At the start of creation, when all was one ocean in darkness, Brahma with five faces arose from the quality of passion, and the three-eyed Shiva arose from darkness. Both were filled with pride and argued about who had created whom; at that time Narada himself was born and flew into the sky with his vina. Shiva was defeated in the argument, and Brahma's fifth face mocked him as a naked, bull-riding destroyer of the world. Shiva grew five shining faces of his own, and Brahma's face sneered that they were mere bubbles on water. In anger Shiva cut off that harsh-speaking head with the tip of his nail, and it fell into his left palm and would not leave his hand. Brahma then created an armed, four-armed man like the sun, who told Shiva to go away as a sinner. Ashamed, Shiva went to Badarikashrama, the home of Nara and Narayana in the Himalaya, and asked Narayana for alms as a great skull-bearer. Narayana told him to strike his left arm with the trident. Three streams flowed from the wound: one went into the sky and became the starry path; the second fell on the earth and was caught by Atri, and from it Durvasas was born as a part of Shiva; the third fell into the skull, and from it a young warrior in armour with bow and arrows was born, shouting whom he should behead. Shiva told this Nara, born of Narayana's arm, to kill Brahma's man. Nara took up the ancient bow Ajagava and endless quivers, and the two fought for a thousand divine years. Shiva told Brahma that his man had been beaten; Brahma answered that the matter was not settled and both were great. Shiva then threw Brahma's man into the sun, and placed Nara into the body of Nara, son of Dharma.

01-003.json.summary: Pulastya continues. With the terrible skull fixed in his palm, Shiva was troubled. Then Brahmahatya, the sin of killing a Brahmin, came to him as a fearful dark woman with red hair, said she was the sin of Brahma's killing, and entered his body, burning him. Shiva went to Badarikashrama but did not find Nara and Narayana there. He went to bathe in the Yamuna, but its water dried up; the Sarasvati vanished when he came near. He bathed at Pushkara, the Magadha, Saindhava, Naimisha and Dharma forests and at many rivers, holy places, hermitages and temples, but the sin did not leave him. In despair he went to Kurujangala and saw Vishnu, holding conch, discus and mace, and with joined hands praised him as the lord of the gods, without qualities and endless, the form of Brahma in passion and of Vishnu in goodness, while Shiva himself was the form of darkness born from Vishnu's anger; Vishnu is the earth, water, sky, fire, wind, mind and night, and also dharma, sacrifice, penance, truth, non-violence, purity, forgiveness, giving, mercy and the Vedas. He begged Vishnu to destroy the sin of Brahmin-killing in his body. Vishnu answered that in Prayaga lives a part of himself known as Yogashayi; from his right foot flows the holy river Varana and from his left the river Asi, and the land between them is the best holy place in the three worlds, the city of Varanasi, where even pleasure-seekers merge into Shiva. Vishnu describes the beautiful city, its temples, flags and women, in playful poetic images, and says the sun god Lola, who removes all sins, lives there, and his own part Keshava lives at Dashashvamedha; going there, Shiva will be freed. Shiva bowed and hurried to Varanasi, saw Lola and Dashashvamedha, bathed in the holy places and was freed from the sin. He went to Keshava and said the sin was gone by his grace, but the skull still would not leave his hand. Keshava told him to bathe in the holy lake before him, full of lotuses; the skull would fall from his hand, he would be known in the world as Kapali, and the place would be called Kapalamochana. Shiva bathed there in the Vedic way, the skull fell from his hand, and the holy place was named Kapalamochana ('freeing from the skull') by the Lord's grace.

01-004.json.summary: Pulastya tells Narada that because Shiva had become a skull-bearer, Daksha did not invite him to the sacrifice, and he did not invite Sati either, though she was worthy, knowing her as the wife of a skull-bearer. Meanwhile Jaya, daughter of Gautama, came to Mount Mandara to see Sati. Sati asked why her sisters Vijaya, Jayanti and Aparajita had not come. Jaya said they had all gone, invited, to their grandfather's sacrifice with Gautama and Ahalya, along with all sages, their wives, the gods, the Moon and every creature of the fourteen worlds, and she asked whether Sati had not been invited. Hearing this, which struck her like a thunderbolt, Sati was overcome with grief and anger and died. Jaya wept loudly; Shiva came, saw Sati lying on the ground like a creeper cut by an axe, and Jaya told him that Sati had died of inner pain on hearing that her sisters and their husbands were at Daksha's sacrifice. Shiva blazed with anger, and from the hairs of his body were born lion-faced attendants (ganas) led by Virabhadra. With them he went from Mandara to Kanakhala, where Daksha was performing the sacrifice. Virabhadra took the north-west, Jaya with a mace the south-east, and Shiva with his trident stood in the middle. Dharma, the gatekeeper, attacked Virabhadra; both took many arms and weapons and fought until they were red with blood like flowering kimshuka trees, and Dharma was defeated and turned away. Virabhadra entered the sacrificial ground. The Vasus, the nine planets, the Adityas, the Rudras, the Vishvadevas, Sadhyas, Siddhas, Gandharvas, Yakshas, kings such as Dharmakirti and Bhojakirti, and the demons all attacked him, but he cut their weapons and drove them back. When he reached the middle of the sacrifice, the frightened sages left the fire and ran to Vishnu for shelter. Vishnu told them not to fear and shot fiery arrows, but they fell useless from Virabhadra's body; his divine weapons, mace, Balarama's pestle and plough were all blocked. Vishnu then threw his discus Sudarshana, and Virabhadra swallowed it. Vishnu in rage lifted him and crushed him on the ground, and the discus came out of his mouth with a stream of blood; Vishnu took it back and let Virabhadra go. Virabhadra went to Shiva and reported his defeat. Seeing him covered in blood and breathing like a snake, Shiva grew angry, set Virabhadra and Bhadrakali at their posts, and himself entered the sacrificial ground with his trident, and the sages were struck with fear.

01-005.json.summary: Pulastya continues. Seeing Shiva in anger, Vishnu left the place and hid at Kubjamra. The eight Vasus, seeing Shiva, melted away in fear and became the river Sita, a form of the Sarasvati. The eleven Rudras ran and merged into Shiva; the Vishvadevas, Ashvins, Sadhyas, Maruts, Fire and the Sun stayed eating the sacrificial cake; the Moon rose into the sky with the stars, and Kashyapa and the sages stood bowing with flowers in their hands, reciting the Shatarudriya hymn. Daksha's wife wept pitifully. Shiva struck down many gods with slaps, kicks, his trident and the fire of his eye. Pushan rushed at him with outstretched arms; Shiva caught his arms and swung him round like a lion with a fawn until the sinews broke and his arms became short, then threw him away. When Pushan laughed, showing his teeth, and mocked him as a skull-bearer, Shiva knocked out his teeth with his fist. When Bhaga glared at him, Shiva struck out his eyes with his palm. Indra, the Adityas, Maruts and Fires fled in all directions, while Prahlada and the demon lords stood bowing. Shiva looked with his three eyes at the three sacred fires and burned them to ashes. With the fire destroyed, the Sacrifice took the divine form of a deer and fled into the sky with his wife Dakshina; Shiva, taking the form of Time (Kala), drew his bow with the Pashupata arrow and chased him. Half of Shiva stayed at the sacrificial ground and is called Jatadhara; the other half in the sky is called Kalarupi. Narada asks about this form, and Pulastya describes the body of Time in the sky made of the twelve zodiac signs and their lunar mansions: Aries is the head, Taurus the face, Gemini the arms, Cancer the sides, Leo the heart, Virgo the belly, Libra the navel, Scorpio the genitals, Sagittarius the thighs, Capricorn the knees, Aquarius the shanks and Pisces the feet, naming the lunar mansions and ruling planets of each. In this form Shiva shot the Sacrifice with arrows, and the Sacrifice, freed of pain and awareness, stayed in the sky, his body set with stars. Narada then asks about the signs, and Pulastya gives the form and haunts of each: Aries looks like a ram and lives among sheep, grain and jewel stores and fresh grass; Taurus like a bull among cattle and farmers; Gemini as a man and woman with a vina among singers, dancers and craftsmen; Cancer like a crab in water and fields; Leo in mountains, forests, caves and hunters' villages; Virgo a maiden in a boat with grain and a lamp; Libra a man with scales in markets and streets; Scorpio in holes, anthills and stones; Sagittarius a bowman among horses, elephants and chariots; Capricorn with a deer's face in rivers and the ocean; Aquarius a man with an empty pot on his shoulder in gambling halls and liquor houses; Pisces two joined fish in holy waters, temples and Brahmins' houses. Pulastya tells Narada to keep this old secret, and ends by saying this holy, sin-removing story of how Shiva destroyed the sacrifice has been told.

01-006.json.summary: Pulastya tells Narada that Dharma, born from Brahma's heart, had four sons by his wife, Daksha's daughter: Hari, Krishna, Nara and Narayana. Hari and Krishna were devoted to yoga, and Nara and Narayana did penance for the good of the world at Badarikashrama on the bank of the Ganga in the Himalaya. Their penance heated the world, and Indra, disturbed, sent Rambha and other chief apsaras, with Kama (the god of love) and his friend Spring, to disturb them. Spring arrived at the hermitage, and the text describes it in rich images: flaming flame-of-the-forest trees, golden karnikara groves like princes, red ashoka groves like soldiers wet with blood, and the Beauty of Spring as a woman whose limbs are flowers, birds and bees. Narayana, looking around, saw Ananga (the bodiless one). Narada asks who Ananga is, and Pulastya says he is Kama, son of Harsha, who became bodiless after Shiva burned him; then he tells how. After Sati died and Shiva destroyed Daksha's sacrifice, Kama struck the wifeless Shiva with his arrow of madness. Maddened, Shiva wandered through forests and lakes thinking of Sati. He fell into the river Kalindi (Yamuna) and its water was burned black, and from then on its water has been dark as collyrium. He wandered everywhere without peace, singing, weeping, meditating on Sati and, in dreams, begging her to speak to him and embrace him. Kama struck him again with the arrows of burning and of yawning, and Shiva, tormented, saw Panchalika, son of Kubera, the lord of the Yakshas. He asked him, as his nephew, to take on the yawning, burning and madness, which no one else could bear, and the Yaksha accepted them. Pleased, Shiva gave him a boon: whoever sees, touches or worships him in the month of Chaitra, old or young, man or woman, will become full of madness, singing, dancing, playing music and joking before him; he will be worshipped as Panchalikesha in a holy land north of Kalanjara and south of the Himalaya. Shiva then went to the Vindhya mountain, where Kama found him again; Shiva fled into the dreadful Daruvana forest, where sages lived with their wives, and asked the sages for alms. They stayed silent while he walked through all the hermitages, and the wives of Bhrigu, Atri and the others, all except Arundhati and Anasuya, who were devoted to their husbands, were overcome by desire and followed him, leaving their hermitages empty. The angry sages cursed him: 'May his linga fall on the earth.' His linga fell, split the earth, entered the underworld and broke through the top of the cosmic egg, and Shiva vanished. The earth, mountains, rivers and lower worlds shook. Brahma went to Vishnu on the Ocean of Milk, learned the cause, and both came to see it. Vishnu went down through the seven underworlds on Garuda and Brahma rose upward on his lotus chariot, but neither found its end. They returned, joined hands and praised Shiva, the beginning, middle and end of the world. Shiva appeared and asked why they praised him, burning with desire as he was. They asked him to take back his linga; he said he would do so only if the gods would worship his linga, and Vishnu agreed. Brahma took up the golden linga and set up four orders for the worship of Shiva with their main scriptures: the Shaiva, the Pashupata, the Kalavadana and the Kapalika. He names their first teachers and pupils: Shakti, dear to Vasishtha, and his pupil Gopayana; Bharadvaja and his pupil, the king Rishabha Somakeshvara; Apastamba and his pupil Krathesvara, a Vaishya; and Dhanada with his pupil Karnodara, a Shudra by birth and a great ascetic. Brahma then went home, and Shiva drew the linga back and set it up in subtle form in Chitravana. When Kama again stood before him with bow drawn, Shiva looked at him in anger from head to foot, and Kama began to burn from the feet up like dry grass. As he burned, he threw away his bow, which broke into five parts and became flowering plants: the gold grip became the champaka tree, the diamond-set binding place the bakula, the sapphire-set tip the patala, the moonstone part the jati jasmine, and the coral-set part the many-petalled malli. The arrows he dropped became thousands of fruit trees such as the mango, sweet and fragrant, born by Shiva's grace. Having burned Kama, Shiva controlled himself and went to the Himalaya for penance, and from then on Kama has been praised by the gods as Ananga, the bodiless one.

01-007.json.summary: Pulastya continues. When the sage Narayana saw Kama at Badarikashrama, he smiled and invited him to sit; Kama was amazed that the sage was not disturbed, and Spring grew worried. Narayana welcomed the apsaras and Spring, then, smiling, took a flowering spray and from his thigh created a golden young woman. Kama, seeing her perfect beauty (described limb by limb), wondered whether she was his own beloved Rati and was himself overcome by desire, and Spring too was struck by her and stood still as if in meditation. Narayana told them that this woman born from his thigh (uru) was to be taken to heaven and given to Indra; trembling, they took Urvashi to Indra and told him what the two sons of Dharma had done, and this story became famous in all worlds. Later, after Hiranyakashipu was killed, the demon Prahlada was made king. Under him, as he honoured gods and Brahmins, kings performed sacrifices, Brahmins practised penance and pilgrimage, Vaishyas kept cattle, Shudras served, all four classes kept to their duties, and the gods were provided for. The great sage Chyavana, son of Bhrigu, went to bathe in the Narmada at the holy place of Nakulishvara; a red-eyed serpent seized him, but when he remembered Vishnu the serpent lost its poison, carried him to the underworld and let him go. Honoured by serpent maidens, he reached the demons' city, where Prahlada welcomed him. Prahlada asked which are the holy places on earth, in the sky and in the underworld, and Chyavana said Naimisha on earth, Pushkara in the sky and Chakratirtha in the underworld. Prahlada led the demons to Naimisha to bathe and to see Vishnu. While hunting there, he saw by the Sarasvati a great sal tree pierced with arrows, arrows stuck tip to tip, and two ascetics in black deerskin with matted hair, with the bows Sharnga and Ajagava and endless quivers beside them. Thinking them frauds, he asked what this pretence was, ascetics with weapons. Nara answered that whoever has the power may do as he likes, and that no one can defeat Nara and Narayana in battle. Angry, Prahlada vowed to defeat them, and he and Nara fought with countless arrows, the numbers growing each round, until the earth, sky and directions were covered. Prahlada's Brahma weapon and Narayana's Maheshvara weapon struck each other and fell. Then Prahlada jumped from his chariot with a mace, and Narayana put Nara behind him to fight Prahlada himself.

01-008.json.summary: Pulastya continues. Prahlada struck Narayana on the head with his mace; tears like a rain of fire fell from Narayana's eyes, but the mace broke into a hundred pieces. Prahlada returned to his chariot and they shot arrows at each other while the gods gathered in the sky to watch, beating drums and showering flowers. Narayana pierced Prahlada in every vital spot and cut bow after bow from his hand, then broke his iron club, his hammer, his lance and his spear, and finally struck him in the heart with an iron arrow, so that he fell senseless and his charioteer carried him away. When he recovered and came back, Narayana told him to go and do his daily rites and fight again in the morning. They fought in this way for a thousand divine years, and each night Prahlada wondered how to defeat this 'pretender', but he could not. Then he went to Vishnu, the yellow-robed one, and asked why he could not defeat Narayana. Vishnu said Narayana, the son of Dharma, cannot be defeated even by gods and demons together. Prahlada said a man like him could not live after breaking a vow, and he would purify his body before Vishnu; he bathed and stood reciting the eternal Brahman. Vishnu told him he would win over Narayana by devotion, not by battle, for it was Vishnu himself who had taken up penance to spread dharma for the good of the worlds; so he should serve and worship the son of Dharma. Pleased, Prahlada called Andhaka, gave him the kingdom and the care of the demons, and went to Badarikashrama, where he bowed at the feet of Nara and Narayana. Narayana asked why he bowed without having won, and Prahlada praised him: none can defeat him, the endless lord, Vishnu with the bow Sharnga, worshipped by yogis and sacrificers, who took the forms of the Fish, Hayagriva, the Tortoise, the Boar that killed Hiranyaksha, and the Man-Lion that killed Prahlada's own father, and who is Brahma, Shiva, Indra, Fire, Yama, Varuna, Wind, Sun, Moon and all the elements; he can be won only by devotion. Narayana said he was pleased and had been defeated by Prahlada's single-minded devotion, and as the loser must pay a penalty, he offered a boon. Prahlada asked that his sins of body, mind and speech from fighting with him and with Nara be destroyed; then that his mind always rest in Vishnu and his worship; and finally that he be known always by Vishnu's lotus feet. Narayana granted these and added that he would be imperishable, ageless and immortal, would not be bound by his actions while his mind was on Vishnu, and should go home, rule the demons and do the best duty suited to his kind. When Prahlada asked how he could take back a kingdom he had given up, Narayana told him to go home and be the teacher who gives good advice to the demons. Prahlada returned; Andhaka and the demons honoured him and offered him the throne, but he refused it, guiding the demon lords on the right path and staying absorbed in meditation on Keshava.

01-009.json.summary: Narada asks how Prahlada, knowing the eternal rules of kingship, could crown Andhaka, who was blind. Pulastya says Andhaka had regained his sight while Hiranyaksha was still alive, and so Prahlada placed him on his own throne. Narada asks what Andhaka did as king. Pulastya says Andhaka, son of Hiranyaksha, worshipped Shiva with penance and won boons: that gods, siddhas, sages and serpents could not defeat or kill him, fire could not burn him and water could not wet him. With Shukra as his priest he ruled, then set out against the gods: he conquered all the kings of the earth, made them his allies, and went with them to the peak of Meru. Indra mounted his great elephant, guarded Amaravati and marched out, followed by the world guardians and the gods: the twelve Adityas in front, the Rudras behind, the Vasus, Vishvadevas, Sadhyas, Ashvins, Maruts, Yakshas and Vidyadharas in the middle. At Narada's request, Pulastya lists their mounts: Indra's white elephant born from Rudra's palm; Yama's black buffalo Paundraka born from Rudra's thigh; Varuna's dolphin (shishumara) born from Rudra's sweat; Kubera's man-mount born from Ambika's foot; the Rudras ride Gandharvas, great serpents and white bulls; the Moon has a chariot drawn by five hundred swans; the Adityas have chariots drawn by horses; the Vasus ride elephants, the Yakshas men, the Kinnaras serpents, the Ashvins horses, the Maruts deer, the poets parrots, and the Gandharvas go on foot. He then lists the demons' mounts: Andhaka's thousand-spoked chariot with black horses, Prahlada's white-gold chariot with eight moon-white horses, Virochana's elephant, Kujambha's horse, Jambha's chariot with golden horses, Shankukarna's horse, Hayagriva's elephant, Maya's chariot, Dundubhi's great serpent, Shambara's aerial car and Ayahshanku's lion, while Bala and Vritra came on foot with mace and pestle. A terrible confused battle followed, dust hid the world, father did not know son, and chariot fought chariot, elephant elephant, horseman horseman and foot soldier foot soldier. A river of blood flowed, described as a river with chariots for whirlpools, elephants' heads for tortoises, arrows for fish, entrails for moss and banners for foam, which brave warriors crossed in their chariots. Rakshasas, Yakshas, Pishachas, jackals and vultures feasted, and the field looked like a cremation ground. Andhaka on his chariot faced Indra on his elephant; Prahlada faced Yama on his buffalo; Virochana faced Varuna, Jambha faced Kubera, Shambara faced Wind and Maya faced Fire, and other demons led by Hayagriva fought the Fire gods, Suns, Vasus and serpent lords in pairs, shouting challenges, while sages and siddhas watched from the sky and the chief apsaras carried off the brave who fell facing the enemy.

01-010.json.summary: Pulastya continues the battle. Indra and Andhaka shot arrows at each other; Indra hurled his thunderbolt, Andhaka's weapons could not stop it, so he jumped down from his chariot, and the thunderbolt burned his chariot, charioteer, horses and flag to ashes. When the thunderbolt came at him, Andhaka struck it to the ground with his fist and roared. He then attacked Indra's elephant with his palm, feet and knee, broke its tusk and felled it, and Indra leapt off, took his thunderbolt and fled into Amaravati, while Andhaka struck down the gods' army. Yama attacked Prahlada with his staff, knocked aside his rain of arrows and hurled the staff, which blazed like the fire of the world's end; the demons cried that Prahlada was lost, but Andhaka said 'Do not fear while I am here', caught the staff with his left hand, laughing, and whirled it roaring, and Yama, finding him unbearable, vanished. Prahlada then tore through the army of the gods. Varuna on his dolphin bound demons with his nooses and struck them with his mace; Virochana attacked him with many weapons, felled him and had his elephant toss and trample him, but the Moon shot the elephant. Varuna seized the elephant's feet, tied its tail with a serpent and flung Virochana with his elephant and driver into the sky, and he fell like the city of Sukeshi struck down by the sun. As Varuna ran to kill him, the demons cried out for help; Jambha and others rushed at Varuna like moths into fire, but Varuna struck down Jambha with his noose, Tara with his palm, Vritra and Kujambha with his foot and Bala with his fist, and the demons fled. Andhaka then came, was struck and bound by Varuna, but threw the noose and mace back at him, and Varuna fled into the ocean. Fire, fanned by Wind, burned the demon army; Maya and Shambara attacked, but Fire pierced Maya's armour with his spear so that he fell, and seized Shambara by the throat, burning him so that he screamed like an elephant caught by a lion. Andhaka, urged by the demons, ran at Fire with an iron club; Fire threw Shambara down and crushed him, but Andhaka struck Fire on the body and then on the head, and Fire fled from the field. Andhaka then drove back the Wind, Moon, Sun, Sadhyas, Rudras, Ashvins, Vasus and serpents with his arrows. Having defeated the gods with Indra, Rudra, Yama and Soma, and honoured by the demons, he came to earth, made the kings pay him tribute, brought the whole world under his control and entered his fine city Ashmaka in the underworld, where Gandharvas, Vidyadharas, Siddhas and apsaras came to live and serve him.

01-011.json.summary: Narada asks about the city of Sukeshi that the sun threw down from the sky: who Sukeshi was, who gave him the city and why it was thrown down. Pulastya tells the old story as Brahma told it to him. Vidyutkeshi was a lord of the night-wanderers (rakshasas), and his virtuous son was Sukeshi. Shiva, pleased with Sukeshi, gave him a city that moved through the sky, and made him unconquerable and unkillable by enemies; Sukeshi lived there happily with his rakshasas, always following dharma. Once he went to the Magadha forest, saw the hermitages of the sages, bowed to them, sat down and asked, not as a command but as a question, what is good in this world and the next, and how one is honoured by the good and lives happily. The sages said that dharma is the good in both worlds; whoever relies on it is honoured and happy. Asked what dharma is, they listed the dharma of each kind of being: for the gods, sacrifice, Vedic study and worship of Vishnu; for the Daityas, strength of arm, rivalry, war, knowledge of statecraft and devotion to Shiva; for the Siddhas, yoga, study, knowledge of Brahman and devotion to both gods; for the Gandharvas, music and dance and devotion to Sarasvati; for the Vidyadharas, their special knowledge, manly effort and devotion to Bhavani; for the Kimpurushas, the Gandharva arts, devotion to the Sun and skill in all crafts; for the ancestors, celibacy, humility, yoga and free movement; for sages, celibacy, restraint in food, prayer and knowledge; for human beings, study, celibacy, giving, sacrifice, generosity, non-violence, forgiveness, self-control, purity and devotion to Vishnu, Shiva, the Sun and the Goddess; for the Guhyakas, lordship over wealth, pleasures, study, worship of Shiva and pride; for the rakshasas, violating others' wives, greed for others' wealth, study and devotion to Shiva; and for the Pishachas, lack of judgement, ignorance, impurity, untruth and a craving for meat. These twelve kinds of birth and their twelve dharmas were taught by Brahma. Sukeshi asks about human dharma, and the sages describe the earth: it is fifty crore yojanas wide, floating on water like a boat, with Meru in its centre like the seed-pod of a lotus. Around Jambudvipa (one lakh yojanas) lie the seven continents and seven oceans, each double the one before: the salt ocean, Plaksha, the sugar-cane-juice ocean, Shalmali, the wine ocean, Kusha, the ghee ocean, Krauncha, the curd ocean, Shaka and the Ocean of Milk, where Vishnu lies on Shesha; beyond is Pushkara with the sweet-water ocean, and all is enclosed by the shell of the cosmic egg. In the continents from Plaksha to Shaka there are no ages (yugas); people live happily like gods and perish only at the end of the cosmic cycle. The people of the fearful Pushkara follow the dharma of the Pishachas. Asked why Pushkara is fearful, the sages say the dreadful hells such as Raurava are there. They then list the twenty-one hells with some sizes: Raurava of burning coals, two thousand yojanas; Maharaurava of hot copper; Tamisra; Andhatamisra; Kalachakra; Apratishtha; Ghatiyantra; Asipatravana (the sword-leaf forest); Taptakumbha; Kutashalmali; Karapatra (the saw); Shvabhojana; Sandamsha (the tongs); Lohapinda; Karambhasikata (hot sand); the river of caustic water; Krimibhojana; the dreadful river Vaitarani; and the hells of blood and pus, of razor edges and of the wheel, and Samshoshana.

01-012.json.summary: Sukeshi asks the sages which deeds lead to these hells. The sages list them. Those who constantly blame the Vedas, gods and Brahmins, who do not respect the Puranas and histories, who obstruct sacrifices or stop a giver, and who cause quarrels between friends, husband and wife, brothers, master and servant, father and son, or priest and patron, fall into the hells. Those who promise a daughter to one man and give her to another are sawn in two by Yama's servants. Those who cause others pain or steal sandal paste, fans and such go to the hot sand. A man who eats elsewhere after being invited to a ritual meal for gods or ancestors is torn in two by sharp-beaked birds; birds peck those who wound good people with words, and crows pull out the tongues of slanderers. Those who scorned mother, father and teacher sink head down in pus, dung and urine. Those who eat before gods, guests, servants, children, father, the sacred fire and mother have eaten must eat blood and pus and are born as needle-mouthed hungry beings with mountain-sized bodies. Those who serve unequal food to people sitting in one row go to the hell of excrement; those who eat without sharing with a needy fellow traveller go to the hell of phlegm. Those who touch a cow, Brahmin or fire while ritually impure have their hands thrust into the boiling pot, and those who look at the sun, moon and stars in that state have fire blown into their eyes. Those who touch a friend's wife, mother, elder brother, father, sister, teachers or elders with their feet are thrown in iron chains into Raurava. Those who eat milk-rice, khichdi or meat 'in vain' (without offering it) have hot iron balls put into their mouths, and those who listen to blame of teachers, gods, Brahmins and the Vedas have red-hot iron nails driven into their ears. Those who destroy water sheds, temples, gardens, Brahmins' houses, assembly halls, monasteries, wells and tanks are flayed; those who pass urine at cows, Brahmins, the sun or fire have their entrails pulled out by crows. A man who looks after only himself and abandons his children, servants, wife and relatives in famine or danger falls into the hell where dogs eat him; those who abandon those who seek shelter, or jailers, are crushed in the press; those who make Brahmins and others do wrong work are ground on millstones; those who steal deposits are chained, starving, among scorpions. Those who have intercourse on holy days or with others' wives must embrace the red-hot thorny silk-cotton tree. A Brahmin who studies after slighting his teacher, and the one who teaches him, must carry a stone on the head; those who put urine, phlegm or dung into water fall into a stinking pit of filth; those who ate at each other's ancestral rites eat their own flesh; those who abandon the Vedas, the fire, the teacher, wife or parents are thrown from mountain peaks; the husbands of remarried women, those who defile maidens and those who eat at the rites for such a child eat worms and ants; a priest or patron who takes gifts from a Chandala or outcaste becomes a large worm inside stone; backbiters and bribe-takers are thrown to the wolves. The stealer of gold, the killer of a Brahmin, the drinker of liquor, one who violates the teacher's bed, those who steal cows or land, those who kill cows, women or children, and twice-born men who sell cows, soma or the Veda, corrupt judges, the impure, those who neglect daily and occasional rites and false witnesses stay in Maharaurava, then ten thousand years each in Tamisra, Andhatamisra, the sword-leaf forest, Ghatiyantra and Taptakumbha. All these hells together are for the ungrateful man, who is condemned by the world. Then a long list of 'the best of each kind' follows: as Vishnu is first of the gods, the Himalaya of mountains, Sudarshana of weapons, Garuda of birds, the Ganga of rivers, Kurujangala of lands, Prithudaka of holy places, the Ashvamedha of sacrifices, the Matsya of Puranas, Manu of law books, the Brahmin among two-footed beings, the cow among animals, the householder among those in the stages of life, and Vaitarani among the hells, so the ungrateful man is the worst of sinners. There is atonement even for killing a Brahmin or a cow, but none for the ungrateful man who destroys the good done to him by a friend, not in crores of years.

01-013.json.summary: Sukeshi asks the sages to describe Jambudvipa. They say it has nine regions (varshas): Ilavrita in the middle, Bhadrashva in the east, Hiranya in the north-east, Kinnara in the south-east, Bharata in the south, Hari in the south-west, Ketumala in the west, Ramyaka in the north-west and Kuru in the north, full of wish-granting trees. In the eight regions other than Bharata there are no ages, no old age, death or fear, happiness comes naturally without effort, and there is no high, middle or low. Bharata has nine parts separated by sea and unreachable from each other: Indradvipa, Kaserumat, Tamravarna, Gabhastimat, Nagadvipa, Kataha, Simhala, Varuna, and the ninth, called Kumara, which runs from south to north; it has Kiratas at its eastern end, Yavanas in the west, Andhras in the south and Turushkas in the north. In between live Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas and Shudras, made pure by their own work of sacrifice, war, trade and so on; through these actions they gain heaven or liberation, merit or sin. Its seven chief mountain ranges are Mahendra, Malaya, Sahya, Shuktiman, Riksha, Vindhya and Pariyatra, and there are hundreds of thousands of other hills, of which many are named (Kolahala, Mandara, Mainaka, Govardhana, Arbuda, Raivata, Rishyamuka, Chitrakuta, Shriparvata and others). Among them live peoples, both Aryan and Mleccha. The sages then list the rivers by the mountains they flow from: from the Himalaya the five-fold Sarasvati, Yamuna, Shatadru, Vitasta, Iravati, Gomati, Drishadvati, Gandaki, Kaushiki, Sarayu, Lauhitya and others; from Pariyatra the Vedasmriti, Sindhu, Parnasha, Charmanvati, Vidisha, Vetravati, Sipra and others; from Riksha the Shona, Narmada, Mandakini, Dasharna, Tamasa, Vipasha and others; from the Vindhya the Payoshni, Nirvindhya, Tapi, Vaitarani and others; from Sahya the Godavari, Bhimarathi, Krishna, Vena, Tungabhadra, Kaveri and others; and from Shuktiman the Kritamala, Tamraparni and others. All are holy, remove sin, are mothers of the world and wives of the ocean, and there are thousands of smaller rivers, some flowing always and some only in the rains. Finally they list the peoples of the middle country (Matsya, Panchala, Kashi, Kosala and others), of the north (Bahlika, Abhira, Gandhara, Yavana, Sindhu-Sauvira, Madra, Kekaya, Kamboja, Darada, Barbara, China, Tushara, Kirata, Kuluta and others), of the east (Anga, Vanga, Pragjyotisha, Videha, Tamralipta, Magadha and others), of the south (Pundra, Kerala, Chola, Maharashtra, Kalinga, Vidarbha, Dandaka, Ashmaka, Andhra and others), of the west (Surparaka, Bharukaccha, Saurashtra, Avanti, Arbuda and others), of the Vindhya region (Karusha, Mekala, Utkala, Dasharna, Bhoja, Kosala, Naishadha, Avanti and others), and of the mountains (Tangana, Khasha, Trigarta, Kirata, Tomara and others). They say they will next describe the customs of these lands.

01-014.json.summary: The sages tell Sukeshi that non-violence, truth, not stealing, giving, forgiveness, self-control, calm, generosity, purity and penance are the ten-part dharma common to all classes, and that for Brahmins the four stages of life are also laid down. A student, after his sacred thread ceremony, lives with his teacher, studies, tends the fire, bathes, begs alms and eats them only after offering them to the teacher and with his leave, works for the teacher and studies when called. After learning one, two or all the Vedas and giving the teacher his fee, he may become a householder or a forest-dweller or take the fourth stage, or he may stay in his teacher's house for life, serving the teacher, or the teacher's son or pupil, without pride; such a Brahmin conquers death. To become a householder he should marry a girl not of the same sage lineage (gotra), earn wealth by his own work, and please ancestors, gods and guests while keeping good conduct. Asked what good conduct (sadachara) is, they say that without it no sacrifice, gift or penance brings good, here or hereafter. It is a tree whose root is dharma, branch wealth, flower desire and fruit liberation. One should wake at the Brahma hour before dawn and remember the gods and sages, reciting the morning blessing taught by Shiva; at Sukeshi's request they give it: 'May Brahma, Vishnu, Shiva, the Sun, Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus and Saturn, the sages Bhrigu, Vasishtha and others, Sanatkumara and his brothers, the seven notes and seven underworlds, the five elements, the seven oceans, mountains, sages, continents and worlds all make my morning good.' Reading, hearing or remembering it destroys bad dreams. Then one thinks of dharma and wealth, rises saying 'Hari', and goes to relieve oneself, not on the road to a temple, cowshed, Brahmin or fire, a royal road or crossroads; cleans the body with earth a set number of times (not from water, a rat's hole, a used place or an anthill); sips water facing north or east; touches the sense openings and head; performs the twilight worship; combs the hair, cleans the teeth and looks in a mirror; bathes, offers water to ancestors and gods, makes the fire offering, and before going out touches auspicious things such as durva grass, curd, ghee, a water pot, a cow with calf, a bull, gold, earth, cow dung, a svastika, unbroken rice, honey, a Brahmin girl, white flowers, fire, sandal, the sun and the peepal tree. One should then follow the duty of one's class, region, family and lineage, earn wealth by it, and avoid idle, untrue, harsh or unscriptural speech and bad company. Intercourse is to be avoided at twilight, by day, with other women, in empty houses, on the bare ground, in water and with a menstruating wife. A householder must not wander, give or kill animals 'in vain', or take a wife improperly, which brings loss of offspring and fear of mixing of classes. One must not set one's mind on others' wealth or wives, look at a naked woman, talk to thieves, or see, touch or talk to a menstruating woman, nor sit on one seat with a sister, another's wife, one's mother or daughter; one must not bathe or sleep naked or wander naked. The chapter gives rules on which lunar days, weekdays and lunar mansions to avoid oil massage, shaving, meat and women; one should not sleep with the head to the north or west, nor eat facing south or west; one should walk around temples, sacred trees, crossroads and teachers keeping them on the right, and not wear garlands or clothes worn by others. One should bathe daily but not at night without cause, except at eclipses, a relative's death, or when the moon is in one's birth star; and should live in lands with good kings, peaceful, just and generous people, farmers and medicinal plants, not where the king is weak and fond of punishment and the people are always quarrelling, feasting and seeking conquest.

01-015.json.summary: Pulastya tells Narada that Sukeshi returned to his city, called all the rakshasas and told them the dharma the sages had taught him: non-violence, truth, not stealing, purity, control of the senses, giving, kindness, forgiveness, celibacy, humility, kind and truthful speech, love of good deeds and good conduct, which lead to the higher world; he ordered them to follow it without question. The rakshasas gladly followed this thirteen-part dharma and grew greatly in children, grandchildren and wealth, and their brightness became so great that the sun, moon and stars could not pass; the rakshasa city shone like the moon by day and like the sun by night. The world was confused: lotuses opened at night, owls came out by day and were killed by crows, bathers stood in rivers all night thinking it was day, and the chakravaka birds, who part at night, did not part. People gave many explanations: some said the sun pitied a chakravaka who had died of separation and so would not set; some that the moon had defeated the sun because of vows such as the Ashunyashayana (the 'never-empty bed' vow) to Vishnu and Lakshmi, Rohini's penance to Shiva on Akshaya Ashtami, or the moon's own worship of Vishnu's feet; and lovers praised the moon for making every night moonlit. Hearing all this, the Sun meditated and saw that the three worlds were overrun by the rakshasas; he saw that they were pure, of good conduct and devoted to gods and Brahmins, and looked for a flaw by which to destroy them. He found it: they had fallen away from their own proper dharma (svadharma), which destroys all dharma. In anger he looked at the rakshasa city with his rays, and it fell from the sky like a planet whose merit is spent. As it fell, Sukeshi (also called Shalakatankata) cried 'Salutation to Bhava, to Sharva!', and the Charanas in the sky lamented that a devotee of Shiva was falling. Shiva learned that the Sun had thrown down the city and, angry, looked at the Sun, who at once fell from the sky, glowing like a flame-of-the-forest flower, surrounded by Kinnaras and Charanas like a half-ripe palm fruit surrounded by monkeys. Sages told him to fall in Vishnu's holy land if he wished for good, and said this land, which now belongs to Vasudeva and later will belong to Shankara, is the city of Varanasi, from Yogashayi up to Keshava. The Sun, burned by the fire of Shiva's eye, fell between the Varana and Asi rivers, plunged into the Asi and then the Varana, and kept rolling (lul) back and forth between them like a whirling firebrand. All the beings who live on the Sun's chariot went to tell Brahma, who with the gods went to Shiva on Mount Mandara, pleased him and brought him to Varanasi. Shiva lifted the Sun with his hand, named him Lola and set him back on his chariot, and Brahma lifted Sukeshi with his city and kin back into the sky, embraced Shiva, bowed to Keshava and went home. So the Sun threw Sukeshi's city to earth, and Shiva threw the Sun down by his gaze without burning him, then restored him to give light.

01-016.json.summary: Narada asks about the vows mentioned by the lovers for worshipping Vishnu and Shiva. Pulastya explains. When the sun turns after the full moon of Ashadha, Vishnu, lord of Shri, goes to sleep on the serpent's coils, and the gods, Gandharvas, Guhyakas and the mothers of the gods sleep in turn. On the eleventh day of the bright half when the sun is in Gemini, one should make a bed of Shesha for Keshava and worship him, give him a sacred thread and honour Brahmins, and on the twelfth, with their leave, put the yellow-robed god to sleep. On the thirteenth Kama sleeps on a bed of kadamba flowers, on the fourteenth the Yakshas on a golden lotus bed, and on the full moon Shiva on a tiger skin, binding up his matted hair. Then, with the sun in Cancer, the gods' night (the southern course) begins: from the first lunar day of the dark half, Brahma sleeps on a bed of blue lotuses, then Vishvakarma, Parvati, Vinayaka, Yama, Skanda, the Sun, Katyayani, Lakshmi, the serpents and the Sadhyas in turn up to the eleventh. Then the rains come, cranes climb the trees and crows build nests. The second lunar day, on which Vishvakarma sleeps, is the holy Ashunyashayana ('never-empty bed') day. On it one worships four-armed Vishnu on his couch with Lakshmi with scents and flowers, places fragrant fruits on the bed, and prays: 'As you, Trivikrama, are never parted from Lakshmi, so may our bed never be empty; by that truth may my household life not be destroyed.' One eats only at night, without oil or salt, and the next day gives fruits to a Brahmin, saying 'May the bearer of Lakshmi be pleased.' This four-month vow is kept until the sun is in Scorpio; the gods wake in turn, and with the sun in Libra Vishnu, Kama and Shiva wake. At the end an image of Vishnu with bed and bedding is given, as one can afford. This first vow keeps anyone from separation. Next is the Kalashtami: the dark eighth of Bhadrapada joined with the Mrigashira star, when Shiva sleeps in all lingas and worship there gives undying merit. One bathes with cow urine and water, worships Shiva with datura flowers, offers incense of saffron resin and honey and ghee, says 'May Virupaksha be pleased' and gives a Brahmin the offering with gold. The chapter then gives the rite for each month: fasting on the eighth and bathing on the ninth, with a different bath (cow dung, milk, curd, ghee, kusha water, the five products of the cow, udumbara fruits, scented water, amalaka, bilva, deer's food), flowers, incense, food offering, fee and name of Shiva for each month from Ashvina to Shravana, such as 'May Hiranyaksha be pleased', 'May Sthanu be pleased', 'Salutation to Tryambaka', 'May Uma's lord be pleased', 'Salutation to the lord of dance', 'Kalaghna', 'Salutation to the destroyer of Bhaga's eyes and Pushan's teeth', 'Salutation to the destroyer of Daksha's sacrifice', and 'Gangadhara'. After the first six months the vow is broken (parana) with a bath of Shiva and worship with gorochana and jaggery, praying for the end of sorrow; after the next six months the second parana is made with gifts such as a white bull, a tawny cow, gold and red cloth. One who worships Shiva in this way for a full year gains undying wishes, as Shiva himself declared.

01-017.json.summary: Pulastya continues with the vows. In the month of Ashvina, when the lotus comes out of Vishnu's navel, plants were born from the bodies of the gods, and each god takes delight in his own plant (the opening verses here are incomplete in the text; the second half mentions that someone's love grows with the kadamba): the banyan from Manibhadra, lord of the Yakshas; the datura from Shiva's heart; the emerald-green khadira from the middle of Brahma's body, dear to Vishvakarma; the kunda jasmine from Parvati's palm; the sinduvara on Ganesha's forehead; the palasha on Yama's right side; the black udumbara from Rudra; the bandhujiva for Skanda; the peepal for the Sun; the shami for Katyayani; the bilva in Lakshmi's hand; the reed for the lord of serpents; white durva grass on Vasuki's tail; and green sandal from the hearts of the Sadhyas. On the bright eleventh of that season one should worship Vishnu, which makes whole whatever is broken (akhanda). Until autumn one offers flowers, leaves, fruits and herbs of every scent, colour and taste, ghee, sesame, rice, barley, gold, jewels, pearls, coral, cloths and all six tastes, all unbroken, so that the whole year is unbroken in one's home. After a fast, the next day one bathes, rubs the body with white mustard or sesame, bathes Vishnu with ghee, offers fire offerings and gifts as one can, worships Keshava from the feet up with flowers, incense, gold, jewels and cloth, offers sweets and food, and prays: 'Salutation to you, Padmanabha; may dharma, wealth, desire and liberation be unbroken for me; as you are whole everywhere, by that truth may they be whole.' Keeping this Akhanda vow for a full year with fasting and self-control pleases the gods and makes the four aims of life undying. Pulastya then gives the 'cage of Vishnu' (Vaishnava panjara), a prayer for protection: Vishnu is asked to guard the east holding the discus Sudarshana, the south with the mace Kaumodaki, the west with the plough Saunanda, the north with the pestle, the north-east with the bow Sharnga and the Narayana weapon, the south-east as the sacrificial Boar with the conch Panchajanya and lotus, the south-west as the Man-Lion with shield and sword, the north-west as Hayagriva with the Vaijayanti garland and Shrivatsa, the sky riding Garuda, and the underworld riding the tortoise; and to form an eight-armed cage around the hands, head, feet and joints. Vishnu once gave this prayer to Katyayani for protection when she killed the demons Mahisha, Namara, Raktabija and others. Narada asks who Katyayani, Mahisha, Raktabija and Namara were. Pulastya tells the sin-destroying story of Durga Katyayani. Two mighty demon brothers, Rambha and Karambha, had no sons and did penance for many years in the waters of Panchanada, one standing in the water, the other amid five fires, facing the Yaksha Malavata. Indra, as a crocodile, seized Karambha by the feet in the water and killed him. In rage Rambha tried to cut off his own head with a sword and offer it into the fire, but Fire stopped him, saying that killing oneself is even harder to escape than killing another, and offered him a boon. Rambha asked for a son who would conquer the three worlds, be unconquerable by gods, men and demons, strong as the wind, able to take any form and skilled in weapons. Fire said he would have such a son by whatever female he set his mind on. Rambha went to the Yaksha Malavata, where the treasure Padma lived among elephants, buffaloes, horses, cows, goats and sheep, and there he desired a beautiful three-year-old female buffalo; she came to him willingly, and she conceived. He took her to the underworld, but his relatives cast him out for this wrong deed, and he returned to Malavata with her. There she gave birth to a white buffalo son, Mahisha, who could take any form. Another buffalo saw her in season and came at her; she ran to Rambha to protect her virtue, and when Rambha attacked the buffalo with his sword, it gored him through the heart and he died. She took refuge with the Yakshas, who drove off the lustful buffalo; it fell into a divine lake and died, and was reborn as the mighty demon Namara, who lived with the Yakshas hunting wild beasts. The Yakshas placed Rambha on a funeral pyre, and the female buffalo climbed onto it with her husband. From the middle of the fire rose a terrible man with a sword who drove off the Yakshas and killed all the buffaloes except Mahisha, son of Rambha; he was the demon Raktabija, who later defeated all the gods with Indra, Rudra, the Sun and the Wind. Mahisha, the 'enemy of horses', was the mightiest and was crowned king by the great demons Shambara, Taraka and others whom he had defeated; the gods with the world guardians, Fire and the Sun could not resist him, the Moon, Indra and Sun left their places, and Dharma was driven far away.

01-018.json.summary: Pulastya continues. Defeated by Mahisha, the gods left their places and, led by Brahma, went to Vishnu, whom they found with Shiva. They told them that Mahisha had taken over the offices of the Ashvins, Sun, Moon, Wind, Fire, Brahma, Varuna and Indra and driven them from heaven to live on earth, and asked for help, or else they would have to flee to the underworld. Hearing this, Vishnu became angry like the fire of the world's end, and from his face, and from the faces of Shiva, Brahma, Indra and the other gods, came a great blaze of energy. It joined into one mass like a mountain peak at the hermitage of the sage Katyayana, who added his own energy to it, and from that blaze, bright as a thousand suns, was born Katyayani, with long, shining eyes and a body pure through yoga. From Shiva's energy came her face, from Fire her three eyes, from Yama her hair, from Vishnu her eighteen arms, from the Moon her breasts, from Indra her waist, from Varuna her thighs, shanks and hips, from Brahma her lotus-like feet, from the Suns her toes, from the Vasus her fingers, from the Prajapatis her teeth, from the Yakshas her nose, from the Wind her ears and from the Sadhyas her eyebrows like Kama's bow. Because this energy came through the sage, she became famous as Katyayani. The gods gave her weapons and ornaments: Shiva a trident, Vishnu a discus, Varuna a conch, Fire a spear, Wind a bow, the Sun two quivers with endless arrows, Indra a thunderbolt and a bell, Yama a staff, Kubera a mace, Brahma a rosary and water pot, Time a sword and shield, the Moon a necklace and whisk, the Ocean a garland, Himavan a lion to ride, Vishvakarma a crest jewel, earrings, a half-moon and an axe, the king of the Gandharvas a silver drinking cup, the lord of serpents a snake necklace, and the Seasons a garland of unfading flowers. Pleased, the three-eyed goddess laughed loudly, and the gods praised her as the goddess who spreads over the earth as sleep, thirst, shame, hunger, fear, beauty, faith, memory, nourishment, patience, shadow, power, Lakshmi, livelihood, mercy, confusion and illusion. Then she rode her lion to the Vindhya mountain, whose high peaks Agastya had once made low. Narada asks why Agastya did this. Pulastya says that long ago the Vindhya blocked the path of the Sun in the sky. The Sun came to Agastya, the sage born from a jar, at the end of his fire offering, and asked him for a gift. Agastya said no one who asks of him goes away disappointed, and the Sun asked him to make the Vindhya low, since it blocked his path. Agastya promised it, praised and bowed to the Sun, and, as an old man, left the Dandaka forest and went to the Vindhya. He told the mountain he was going to a great holy place, was old and could not climb it, and asked it to become low at once. The mountain lowered its peaks, Agastya crossed over and told it not to grow again until he returned from his bath at the holy place, or he would curse it for disobeying. He then went south through the sky, built a beautiful hermitage with gates of pure gold, left his wife, the princess of Vidarbha, there, and returned to his own hermitage. He stays in the sky hermitage at every season and holy time, and spends the rest of the time doing penance in the Dandaka forest. Seeing the hermitage in the sky, the Vindhya does not grow for fear of the sage, thinking he has not returned, and stays low. On its high peak Durga, praised by the sages, took her place to destroy the demons, and the gods, siddhas, serpents, Vidyadharas, spirits and apsaras stayed there with Katyayani, free of sorrow.

01-019.json.summary: Pulastya tells Narada that the two demons Chanda and Munda saw Katyayani, the ascetic goddess, living on the peak of the Vindhya mountain. They hurried home and told the demon king Mahishasura that a girl more beautiful than the women of heaven lived there, and they praised her body at length, limb by limb: her hair beats the clouds, her face the moon, her three eyes the three sacred fires, her eighteen strong arms hold weapons; they did not know whose daughter she was, and urged him to go and see this jewel on earth for himself. Mahishasura made up his mind at once; Pulastya remarks that good and bad fortune are fixed for a person beforehand by the Creator, who leads him to it or makes him go. Mahishasura sent Munda, Namara, Chanda, Bidalanetra, Pishanga, Bashkala, Ugrayudha, Chikshura and Raktabija, who beat war drums, left heaven and camped at the foot of the mountain. He then sent Dundubhi, son of Maya, as his messenger. Katyayani invited him to speak without fear, and Dundubhi gave Mahisha's message: he has beaten the gods, rules heaven, earth, sky and the underworld, calls himself Indra, Rudra and the Sun, no one can face him in battle, all the jewels of the worlds have come to him, and since she is the jewel among women she should take him as her husband. Katyayani answered that this was true, but her family has a custom called the bride price (shulka). Dundubhi said Mahisha would give even his own head. Laughing, the goddess said the price set by her elders is this: whoever defeats a girl of her family in battle becomes her husband. Dundubhi reported this, and Mahisha came with all the demons to fight her. His general Chikshura put the demon Namara at the head of the army, and Namara rushed at Durga. The gods led by Brahma asked the goddess to put on armour, but she refused, saying no demon could stand before her. Since she wore no armour, Shiva spoke the Vishnu-panjara (the 'cage of Vishnu', a protective prayer) to protect her; guarded by it, Durga crushed Mahisha, who could not be killed by any of the gods, and killed him with blows of her feet. The Vishnu-panjara is called the best of all protections: who can humble in battle a man in whose mind Vishnu, holder of the discus, dwells?

01-020.json.summary: Narada asks Pulastya to tell in full how Katyayani killed Mahishasura with his followers and mounts, and why she crushed him with her feet when she had weapons. Pulastya tells the ancient story. Namara charged with elephants, horses and chariots and covered the mountain with arrows. The angry goddess drew her golden-backed bow and struck down demons with arrows, sword, mace, pestle and shield, while her lion, alone, killed many; demons fell to the thunderbolt, spear, plough, axe, staff and discus, and the rest fled, thinking her the Night of Death. Namara came on a mad elephant and hurled a spear at her and a trident at the lion; she burned both to ash with the sound 'hum'. The elephant seized the lion by the middle, but the lion leapt up, killed Namara with a slap, threw him from the elephant and gave him to the goddess. She swung him in her left hand and beat him like a drum, and laughed loudly; from her laughter came many strange beings with the faces of tigers, wolves, horses, buffaloes, boars, rats, cocks, cows, goats and sheep, who sang, danced, played music and praised her, and with them she cut down the demon army like hail cuts grain. Then the general Chikshura shot showers of arrows; Durga cut them, killed his four horses with four arrows, his charioteer with one, cut his banner and bow, then his sword and shield with four arrows, and when he ran at her with a trident she cut off his feet, hands and head with five arrows. Next Ugrasya, Karalasya, Bashkala, Uddhata, Udagra, Durdhara, Durmukha, Bidalanayana and others attacked. Durga playfully played a vina and a damaru drum while her beings danced and laughed; she seized the demons by the hair, leapt from the lion onto the mountain top, danced playing the vina and drank wine, and the demons lay broken and lifeless. Then Mahishasura scattered her beings with his hooves, mouth, tail, chest, breath, roar and horn tips, shook mountains and seas, and charged the lion. Durga bound him with a noose; he became an elephant, she cut off the tip of its trunk, and he became a buffalo again. Her trident, Agni's spear, Vishnu's discus, Kubera's mace, Varuna's noose, Yama's staff and Indra's thunderbolt all failed against him. So she left the lion, jumped onto his back and crushed him with her soft feet like a wet hide until his strength was gone. She pierced his throat with the trident; a man holding a sword came out of it, and she struck him on the chest with her foot, seized him by the hair and cut off his head with her sword. Chanda, Munda, Maya, Tara and Asiloman, beaten by her followers, fled in fear to the underworld. The gods praised her as Narayani, support of the world, Katyayani, fierce of face and beautiful. Saying 'I will appear again for the gods', Durga entered into them at Shiva's feet.

01-021.json.summary: Narada asks how the goddess was born again. Pulastya says that to kill the demon Shumbha she was born again: Uma, daughter of Himalaya and wife of Shiva, gave rise from her body-sheath (kosha) to Kaushiki, who will go to the Vindhya with her hosts of beings and kill Shumbha and Nishumbha. Narada asks how Sati, Daksha's daughter who had died, was reborn as Himalaya's daughter, how Kaushiki came from Parvati's sheath, how she killed the two demons, and whose sons they were. Pulastya promises to tell of Parvati's birth and of the birth of Skanda. After Sati died, Rudra kept the vow of a celibate student and, being without shelter, went off to do penance; he had been the general of the gods, and with him gone the gods were defeated by Mahisha. They went to Vishnu in Shvetadvipa. Vishnu told them: Mena is the mind-born daughter of the divine ancestors called Agnishvatta; worship them on the great lunar day and ask for Mena as wife for the Himalaya mountain. In her will be born the ascetic woman who gave up her life in anger at Daksha, and she will bear to Shankara a son from his own energy who will kill Mahisha and his followers. So they should go to Kurukshetra and worship the ancestors at the holy place Prithudaka on that great day. The gods asked what Kurukshetra is, how Prithudaka arose, and what this day is, and Vishnu began the story. Riksha was a king of the Moon dynasty at the start of the Krita age; his son Samvarana was crowned while still a boy, was devoted to dharma and to Vishnu, and was taught the Vedas by his priest Vasishtha, son of Varuna. Hunting alone, Samvarana reached the Vaibhraja forest, full of flowers and lotus pools where Apsaras played, and among them saw a lovely girl. At first sight both were struck by love and fainted; the king fell from his horse and was revived with water by Gandharvas, and the Apsaras carried the girl to her father's home. The king returned to his city Pratishthana, but from the day he saw Tapati he could neither eat nor sleep. Vasishtha learned of it by his power, flew to the Sun's disc, was honoured by the Sun and asked for his daughter for Samvarana; the Sun gave Tapati, and Vasishtha took her to his hermitage. Tapati told Vasishtha that she already loved the prince she had seen in the forest, and described his marks of a great man: feet marked with discus, mace and sword, thighs like an elephant's trunk, lion's waist, conch-shaped neck, long strong arms, umbrella-shaped head, dark curly hair and the classic groups of raised, deep, long, red, dark, bowed and white parts; she begged him not to give her, who loved another, to anyone else. Vasishtha meditated and told her joyfully that this same prince, Samvarana son of Riksha, was coming to the hermitage. Samvarana came, bowed to Vasishtha, recognised Tapati and asked who she was; Vasishtha told him she was the Sun's daughter, brought for him, and told him to take her hand. The king married her by the rite, and she delighted with him in fine palaces like a demon's daughter (Shachi) with Indra in heaven.

01-022.json.summary: Vishnu continues to the gods. Samvarana and Tapati had a son with royal marks who received the birth and other rites; Vasishtha performed his tonsure and, at nine, his sacred-thread rite, and by fourteen or so he knew all the Vedas and sciences. He became famous as Kuru, son of Samvarana. His father married him to Saudamini, beautiful daughter of Sudaman, made him crown prince and then king. Kuru ruled his people like his own children, guarding fields and cattle. He thought that fame in the world is the greatest thing, since one lives with the gods as long as one's fame lasts, and he travelled the whole earth for fame. In the holy Dvaitavana he saw the goddess Sarasvati, born of the plaksha tree, daughter of Brahma, mother of Sudarshana, forming a wide lake on whose bank stood countless holy places. He bathed there and then came to Brahma's northern altar, Samantapanchaka, a place of dharma five yojanas each way. (The gods ask how many altars Brahma has; Vishnu says five, where Shiva sacrificed: Prayaga the middle, Gayashiras the east, Viraja the south, Pushkara with its three pools the west, and Samantapanchaka the north.) Kuru thought this field would give great fruit and decided to plough it. He made a golden plough, yoked Shiva's bull and Yama's buffalo Paundraka, and began to plough himself. Indra came and asked what he was doing (this verse is printed twice). Kuru said he was ploughing for penance, truth, forgiveness, compassion, purity, giving, yoga and celibacy. Indra asked where he got the seed, laughed and left. Kuru kept ploughing seven kos each day around the field. Here the speaker, Vishnu, says in the first person that he himself went and asked Kuru what he was doing; Kuru named the eightfold dharma; Vishnu asked where the seed was; Kuru said it was in his body, and Vishnu said, 'Give it to me, I will sow it while you plough.' Kuru held out his right arm; Vishnu cut it into a thousand pieces with his discus and gave them (to the gods); then his left arm and his two thighs were given and cut; finally Kuru offered his head. Pleased, Vishnu granted a boon. Kuru asked that as much land as he had ploughed should be a field of dharma (dharmakshetra); that bathing or dying there, and fasting, giving, japa, fire offerings and sacrifices, good or bad, should bring endless fruit there by Vishnu's grace; and that Vishnu should live there with the gods and Shiva, in a place bearing Kuru's name. Vishnu agreed, gave him a divine body again, promised he would merge into Vishnu at death and that his fame would last, and that priests would perform thousands of sacrifices there. To guard the field Vishnu set the yaksha Chandra, the serpent Vasuki, the vidyadhara Shankukarna, the rakshasa lord Sukeshi, king Ajavana, Mahadeva and Agni, with their followers, including eight thousand bowmen who keep evil-doers from bathing there. In its middle is Prithudaka, very holy and sin-removing, where the river flows east; it shone there from the very beginning of creation, and all oceans, holy places, rivers and lakes were made here and their waters joined in it. The text then begins a section called the Greatness of the Lake (Saromahatmya), in prose-like lines without verse numbers. Between the Sarasvati and Drishadvati rivers, in Kurujangala, Brahmins ask the old sage Lomaharshana about the power and size of the lake, its holy places, its gods and the birth of Vamana. Bowing to Brahma, Vishnu and Rudra, he begins to describe the great holy lake Brahmasaras, called Sannihita, as given by Brahma and by Vyasa: it stretches from Vishveshvara to Asthipura, the virgin Jaradgavi and the Oghavati, half a yojana all round. Gods and sages live by it seeking liberation or heaven; Brahma served it wishing to create, Vishnu wishing to sustain, and Rudra entered the lake and gained the state of Sthanu. It was first Brahma's altar, then called Rama's lake, and since Kuru ploughed it, Kurukshetra; the land between Tarantuka and Arantuka and from Rama's lake to Chaturmukha is Kurukshetra-Samantapanchaka, Brahma's northern altar.

01-023.json.summary: In this part (the Greatness of the Lake section, though the closing line still names the Pulastya-Narada dialogue) the sages ask Lomaharshana to tell the greatness and birth of Vamana, and how Bali was held back and Indra's kingdom given back. Lomaharshana tells them of Vamana's birth, power and home in Kurujangala, and first of the demon line into which Bali, son of Virochana, was born. Hiranyakashipu was the first man of the demons; his son was Prahlada, Prahlada's son Virochana, and Virochana's son Bali. After Hiranyakashipu was killed, Bali drove out the gods everywhere and ruled the three worlds as he wished, with the mighty Maya and Shambara winning victories. Under the demons the world was in good order: all directions were clear, dharma was practised, dharma stood on all four feet and adharma on only one, kings protected their people, people of the life stages kept their own duties, and there was no sin. All the demons crowned Bali as king of the demons. Then Lakshmi, shining like a lotus and holding a lotus, came to Bali and said: 'Bali, best of the strong, I am pleased with you for defeating the king of the gods; seeing your great strength I have come of my own will. It is no wonder that one born in Hiranyakashipu's family does such deeds; you have even surpassed your great-grandfather, who enjoyed all the three worlds.' With these words she entered into Bali. The other goddesses were also pleased and came to him: Modesty, Fame, Splendour, Light, Firmness, Patience, Prosperity, Wealth, Intelligence, Scripture, Memory, Ida, Peace, Nourishment and Action, and all the heavenly Apsaras skilled in dance and song. So Bali, who spoke of Brahman, gained the three worlds and matchless lordship.

01-024.json.summary: The sages ask Lomaharshana what the defeated gods did and how Vishnu came to be Vamana. Lomaharshana says that when Indra saw the three worlds in Bali's hands, he went to his mother Aditi's home on a slope of Mount Meru and told her how the Adityas had been beaten by the demon. Aditi said that if Bali son of Virochana could not be killed in battle by Indra and all the Maruts, only the thousand-headed one (Vishnu) could kill him, and no one else; she would ask their father Kashyapa how Bali could be defeated. With Aditi the gods went to Kashyapa, son of Marichi, and saw him shining with penance like the sun or a flame, wearing black antelope skin and bark, smelling of ghee offerings, the teacher of gods and demons and a lord of creatures. Bowing, they told him that Bali could not be beaten by Indra and asked for what was good for them. Kashyapa decided to go to Brahma's world, and with Aditi and the gods he went there in a moment in divine chariots that go at will. They entered Brahma's great hall, sweet with the humming of bees and the chanting of Samaveda singers, where they heard the Rigveda verses recited in their word and step forms, and Brahmins learned in sacrifice, Vedas, phonetics, metres and every science, even the leading Lokayatikas (materialists), and saw Brahmins devoted to japa and fire offerings. There Brahma sat, attended by the lords of creatures Daksha, Pracetas, Pulaha, Marichi, Bhrigu, Atri, Vasishtha, Gautama and Narada; by the sciences, the elements, the sense objects, nature and its changes, the four Vedas with their limbs, the rules and rites, will and breath; by wealth, dharma, desire, anger and joy; by the planets Shukra, Brihaspati, Budha, Shani and Rahu with Samvarta; by the Maruts, Vishvakarma, the Vasus, sun and moon, day and night, fortnights, months and the six seasons. Kashyapa and the gods bowed their heads to Brahma on his high seat, and by bowing at his feet were freed from all sins and became calm. Seeing them come with Kashyapa, the mighty Brahma spoke to them (his words follow in the next chapter).

01-025.json.summary: Brahma tells the gods that he knows why they have come and that they will get all they want. The one who will conquer Bali is the maker of the universe, the refuge not only of the gods but of Brahma too, leader of the three worlds, the eternal first god whom even the gods do not truly know, though he knows them, the Veda and the world. By his grace Brahma tells them the way: on the northern shore of the Ocean of Milk, in the north, the maker of the world practises hard penance in yoga at a supreme place the wise call Amrita. They should go there and do hard penance with strict vows. Then they will hear a voice, deep and gentle like a cloud full of water at the end of summer, clear, sweet, fearless, pure and true, which destroys all sin: at the end of his vow the god will say, 'Welcome, best of gods; what boon shall I give to each of you?' Then Aditi and Kashyapa should bow at his feet and ask, 'Be pleased, Lord; be our son.' He will answer, 'So be it.' The gods, Kashyapa and Aditi agreed, bowed to Brahma and went north towards Shvetadvipa. They soon reached the Ocean of Milk, crossing all seas, mountains, forests and rivers, and saw a terrible darkness with no living beings, no sun and no boundary. Reaching the Amrita place, with Kashyapa they took up a thousand-year vow to please Narayana, the god of yoga: in celibacy, silence and the hero's sitting posture (virasana) they performed fierce penance in turn, and Kashyapa recited for the Lord's favour the supreme hymn taught in the Veda.

01-026.json.summary: Kashyapa's hymn to Vishnu, opening with 'Om, salutation to Lord Vasudeva'. It is a long string of names and titles addressed to him: the one-horned, Vrishakapi, bull among gods, without beginning, Rudra, Kapila, Vishvaksena, lord of all beings, Dharma and adharma, Vaikuntha, without beginning, middle or end, Dhananjaya, lotus-naveled, Brahma (Virinci), of many forms, imperishable, eater of offerings, Shiva with the axe, Indra, Hrishikesha, the subtle, without form, firstborn; the thousand-headed, thousand-footed, thousand-armed, thousand-faced Great Person and Supreme Person. He is called the cry vaushat and vashat, the first eater in sacrifices, the three worlds Bhuh, Bhuvah and Svah, the one known by the Vedas, dear to Brahmins, the sky, the wind, dharma, the priests and the cause of the fire offering; the sacrifice, the fuel, the mind, the goal and the giver; liberation and yoga; the creator, Soma, the one consecrated for sacrifice and the sacrificial fee; the whole universe and its protector. He is also hailed as Hiranyanabha, Narayana, three-eyed, sun-coloured, the first god, Shambhu, self-born, the source of the elements, lord of heaven and lord of speech, giver of boons to those who seek them. The hymn ends: 'Salutation to you, the soul of the offering, who are offered to with four, with four, with two, with five and again with two' (the syllable counts of the sacrificial calls).

01-027.json.summary: Lomaharshana continues. Pleased by Kashyapa's hymn, Narayana told the gods to choose a boon. Kashyapa said that since he was pleased, all had one wish: that the Lord be born as Aditi's son and Indra's younger brother, bringing joy to the family; Aditi too asked for him as her son. The gods asked him always to be their protector, supporter, giver and refuge. Vishnu promised that none of their enemies would stand before him even for a moment; he would kill the demons and make the gods again the first eaters of the sacrificial shares and the ancestors the eaters of the ancestral offerings, and he told them to go back the way they came. Joyful, the gods, Kashyapa and Aditi worshipped him and went east to Kashyapa's large hermitage in the great forest of Kurukshetra. There they persuaded Aditi to do penance, and she did fierce penance for ten thousand years, keeping silent and living on air, to worship Krishna; the forest named after her became holy and grants all wishes. Seeing her sons driven out by the demons and feeling she had borne sons in vain, out of grief and love she praised Vishnu, the refuge, with a hymn. In it she bows to him as the remover of pain, wearer of a lotus garland, lotus-eyed and lotus-naveled, source of Brahma, husband of Shri, holder of discus, lotus and sword, without qualities, the one in whom the world rests but who is not seen in the world, both gross and very subtle; the one people do not see though they see the whole world, but who is seen in the heart by those who look away from the world; the first lord of creatures, lord of the ancestors and gods; the giver of heaven and liberation who is untouched by actions; who removes all sin when merely thought of; whom those who see him are not born again; the person of sacrifice, known by all the Vedas, from whom the universe arises and into whom it dissolves, who fills all from Brahma to a blade of grass, who holds the world in the form of water, who as the sun destroys the darkness that is the demons, and whose eyes are the sun and moon watching all deeds. She ends: if all she has said is true, by that truth may all her wishes be fulfilled.

01-028.json.summary: Lomaharshana continues. Praised by Aditi, Vasudeva, unseen by all other beings but visible to her, said she would surely gain her wishes by his grace, since seeing him is never fruitless. Whoever stays three nights in her forest gains all he desires; whoever even remembers Aditi's forest from far away goes to the highest place, still more one who lives there; and whoever feeds five, three, two or even one Brahmin there with faith reaches the supreme goal. Aditi asked that her son Indra be lord of the three worlds again, since the demons had taken his kingdom and his share of sacrifice; the lost kingdom did not grieve her as much as the loss of what belonged to those who seek refuge. Vishnu said he had granted her wish: by a part of himself he would be born in her womb from Kashyapa and kill her enemies. Aditi said she could not carry in her womb the Lord in whom everything rests. Vishnu replied that he would carry both her and himself and would cause her no pain, and vanished. Aditi conceived. When Krishna was in the womb the whole earth shook, great mountains trembled and the oceans were stirred; wherever Aditi walked the earth bowed under her steps; and, as Brahma had said, all the demons lost their splendour.

01-029.json.summary: Lomaharshana continues. Seeing all the demons without splendour, Bali asked his grandfather Prahlada why they had suddenly lost their power, as if burned by fire or struck by a Brahmin's curse, and whether some evil rite had been made to destroy them. Prahlada thought for a long time and said that the mountains shake, the earth loses its steadiness, the seas are stirred, the planets do not move as before at sunrise, and the gods' great fortune can be inferred; this is a great cause and must not be taken lightly.
