Then Prahlada, a great devotee, turned his mind to Hari in meditation and saw in Aditi's womb the dwarf form (Vamana), and within it the Vasus, Rudras, Ashvins, Maruts, Sadhyas, Vishvedevas, Adityas, Gandharvas, serpents and Rakshasas, Virochana, Bali himself, Jambha, Kujambha, Naraka, Bana and other demons, himself, earth, sky, wind, water, fire, the seas, mountains, rivers and islands, animals, birds, men and reptiles, Brahma, Shiva, the planets and stars and Daksha and the other lords of creatures. Amazed, he came back to himself and told Bali the cause: Hari, the god of gods, without beginning, the source of the world, has entered a womb to keep the world in order; he has come down as Aditi's son, by a part of himself, to give the three worlds a protector. Prahlada then praises Vasudeva in verse: neither Rudra, Brahma, Indra nor the sun and moon know his true form; those freed of sin by knowledge enter him and are not born again; all beings rise from him like waves from the sea and dissolve in him; he has no senses yet is the self-shining lord to be known by reasoning; he lifted the earth on one tusk and sleeps having swallowed the world; by his partial descent in the womb he took away the splendour of the great demons; he is the axe that cuts the tree of worldly life. With a sixteenth part of himself he has entered the womb of Indra's mother and taken their strength and bodies. Bali asked who this Hari was, saying he had hundreds of demons stronger than Vasudeva, such as Viprachitti, Shibi, Shanku, Ayahshanku, Hayashiras, Ashvashiras, Bhangakara, Mahahanu, Pratapi, Praghasa, Shambhu, Kukkuraksha and Durjaya, each of whom Krishna does not equal even in half his strength. Angry, Prahlada said the demons will perish with such a foolish king; who but Bali would speak so of Vasudeva, of whom all the demons, gods with Brahma, the whole world, Bali and Prahlada himself are only a tiny part. He grieved that Bali's father, whose son insults the god of gods, was born in his house, and asked whether Bali did not at least respect his own devotion to Krishna, who is dearer to him than his own body or life. Virochana is Bali's teacher, Prahlada is Virochana's, and Narayana is the teacher of all; since Bali has insulted the teacher of his teacher's teacher, Prahlada cursed him: as Bali's insult to Achyuta is worse to him than having his head cut off, so Bali shall fall from his kingdom; and as there is no saviour from the sea of worldly life except Krishna, so may Prahlada soon see him lose his throne.

01-030.json.summary: Lomaharshana continues. Hearing this harsh curse, Bali bowed again and again to Prahlada and begged forgiveness, saying he had spoken out of pride in his strength and confusion; the curse on a wrongdoer was just, and he would lose his kingdom and fame; the rule of the three worlds is not hard to get, but teachers like Prahlada are rare, and he burns day and night with Prahlada's anger. Prahlada said his anger had clouded his judgement and made him curse; otherwise how could he, knowing Hari is everywhere, curse anyone. But what he has said must happen, so Bali should not grieve; from now on Bali should be devoted to Hari, who will protect him, and should remember the Lord now that he is cursed; Prahlada will advise him so that he gains what is good. Then Aditi's child grew in her womb, and in the tenth month Govinda was born in the form of a dwarf. With his descent the gods and Aditi were freed from sorrow, pleasant winds blew, the sky was free of dust, all beings turned their minds to dharma and men felt no distress. Brahma performed the birth rites and praised him with a hymn of victory: 'Victory to you, unconquered teacher of the world, beyond birth, death and old age, endless, the witness, maker and teacher of the world, present in all hearts, beginning, middle and end, subtler than the subtle and the gross world itself, who lies on Shesha, who raised the earth on one tusk, who as the man-lion tore the chest of the gods' enemy, and now the dwarf by your own illusion (maya).' Neither Brahma, Shiva, Indra, the sages like Sanaka nor yogis can know him; only one whom he favours knows him; Brahma asks him to grow for the good of the world. Smiling, the dwarf Hrishikesha said he had been praised before by Indra and Kashyapa and had promised the three worlds to Indra, and had heard Aditi's prayer; he would give Indra the three worlds free of enemies, and Indra would be lord of the world; this he said was true. Then Brahma gave him a black antelope skin, Brihaspati the sacred thread, Marichi a staff of palasha wood (ashadha), Vasishtha a water pot, Angiras a kusha-grass garment, Pulaha a seat and Pulastya two yellow cloths; the Vedas adorned with the syllable Om, all the scriptures and the teachings of Sankhya and Yoga attended him. With matted hair, staff, umbrella and water pot, the dwarf, made of all the gods, set out for Bali's sacrifice. Wherever he set his foot the earth, pressed down, opened a hole; walking slowly and heavily, in play, he shook the whole earth with its mountains, seas and islands, while Brihaspati gently showed him the way. Then the great serpent Shesha came out of the underworld to help him, and that hole, the famous Serpent's Hole (Aher bila), still exists; just by seeing it one has no fear of snakes.

01-031.json.summary: Lomaharshana continues. Seeing the earth with its mountains and forests shaken, Bali bowed and asked his teacher Shukra (Ushanas) why the earth trembled and why the sacred fires would not accept the demons' shares. After long thought Shukra said that Hari, source of the world, has been born in Kashyapa's house as a dwarf and is surely coming to Bali's sacrifice; the earth shakes under his steps because it cannot bear him, though it is he who holds up the earth and all beings; and because he is near, the three fires will not eat the demons' shares. Thrilled, Bali said he was blessed that the lord of sacrifice, whom yogis long to see, was coming to his sacrifice, and asked what he should do. Shukra said that by the Veda the gods are the eaters of the sacrificial shares, but Bali has made the demons eaters of them; Vishnu, who keeps the world in order, will surely make Bali a prisoner; so Bali should promise him nothing, not even something small, and should speak kindly but to no purpose, saying only, 'I can give you enough wealth,' since Krishna is working for the gods' welfare. Bali refused: how could he say 'there is not' to Hari, the remover of sin, when he has never said it to any other beggar? That Govinda, who is won by vows and fasts and for whom great sacrifices are made, should himself say 'give' to him is the fruit of all his good deeds and penance; he would rather give up his life than say 'no'. In his kingdom no one is unhappy, poor, sick or troubled; all are content. If his gift falls on Janardana, the best of receivers, what does he not gain? Giving brings a hundred times more joy than enjoying. If Hari comes in kindness, he comes to help; if he comes in anger over the gods' shares to kill him, death at Achyuta's hands is still more praiseworthy; so Shukra should not hinder his gift. As he spoke, Vishnu arrived in his magic dwarf form. The demons lost their splendour and were shaken; the sages present, Vasishtha, Vishvamitra (son of Gadhi), Garga and others, chanted; Bali felt his whole life fruitful, and no one spoke. The dwarf praised the sacrifice, the fire, the patron, the officiants and the wealth of offerings, and the members of the assembly praised him in return. With hair standing on end, Bali honoured Govinda with the guest water (arghya) and offered him gold, jewels, elephants, horses, women, clothes, ornaments, cows, villages or the whole earth, whatever he wished. Smiling, the dwarf asked for three steps of ground for his sacred fire, and told Bali to give gold and villages to others who ask. Bali asked why only three steps, not a hundred or a hundred thousand; Vamana said this was enough for him. Bali then formally declared the gift. As soon as the water fell on his hand, the dwarf was no longer a dwarf and showed his form made of all the gods: sun and moon his eyes, sky his head, earth his feet, Pishachas his toes, Guhyakas his fingers, Vishvedevas his knees, Sadhyas his shanks, Yakshas his nails, Apsaras the lines of his hands, the stars his sight, the sun's rays his hair, the stars his pores, the great sages his body hairs, the directions his arms and ears, the Ashvins his hearing, wind his nose, the moon his grace, dharma his mind, truth his speech, Sarasvati his tongue, Aditi his neck, Tvashta and Pushan his brows, Agni his mouth, Prajapati his testicles, Brahman his heart, Kashyapa his manhood, the Vasus his back, the Maruts his joints and belly, Rudra his chest, the ocean his courage, Gandharvas in his belly, Lakshmi, intelligence, firmness, beauty and the sciences his waist, the Vedas in his sides and the great sacrifices his knees. The demons rushed at him like moths to a flame. The great demon Chikshura seized his big toe with his teeth, and Hari struck his neck with the toe. Crushing all the demons with his feet and hands, Vishnu took a huge form and at once took the earth; as he strode over the earth the sun and moon were at his chest, as he strode the sky they were at his thighs, and as he took the highest step they were at his knees. Having won the three worlds and killed the leading demons, wide-striding Vishnu gave the three worlds to Indra and gave Bali the underworld called Sutala, below the earth. He told Bali that because Bali had given water that Vishnu took in his hand, Bali would live for a whole kalpa, and when the Vaivasvata Manu period is over, in the Savarni Manu period Bali will be Indra; for now the world was given to Indra for seventy-one and a bit cycles of four ages, and Vishnu must restrain all his enemies, since Indra had worshipped him earlier with great devotion. Bali should live in Sutala, among hundreds of palaces, lotus lakes and clear rivers, adorned and perfumed, enjoying dance, song and great pleasures with a hundred women, as long as he does not oppose the gods and Brahmins; if he does, Varuna's fearsome nooses will bind him. Bali asked what would provide his enjoyments there, so that, nourished by it, he might always remember Vishnu. Vishnu said: gifts given without the proper rite, ancestral offerings (shraddha) without a Veda-learned Brahmin, offerings made without faith, sacrifices without fees, rites done wrongly, study without vows, worship without water, rites without darbha grass and fire offerings without ghee will give their fruit to Bali. But whoever performs rites at this place will never have a share go to the demons; at the very holy Jyeshthashrama and the Vishnupada lake, ancestral offerings, vows and observances, done by rule or not, become endless. One who fasts on the eleventh day of the bright half of Jyeshtha, sees Vamana on the twelfth, bathes in the Vishnupada lake and gives gifts as he can reaches the highest state. Having given this boon to Bali and heaven to Indra, Hari vanished in his all-pervading form; Indra ruled the three worlds as before, and Bali stayed in the underworld. Whoever hears this greatness of Vamana is freed from all sins; those who remember the talk of Bali and Prahlada, the counsel of Bali and Shukra, and the deeds of Bali and Vishnu will have no mental or bodily illness and no confusion; one who has lost his kingdom regains it and one separated from what he loves gets it back; a Brahmin gains the Veda, a Kshatriya wins the earth, a Vaishya gains wealth and a Shudra gains happiness.

01-032.json.summary: The sages ask Lomaharshana how the Sarasvati, best of rivers, which flows through Kurukshetra, came into being, and how she reached the lake, made holy places along her banks and went west, sometimes seen and sometimes unseen. Lomaharshana says the eternal Sarasvati rose from a plaksha (fig) tree; just remembering her destroys all sins. Splitting thousands of mountains, she entered the forest called Dvaitavana. Seeing her standing at the plaksha tree, the great sage Markandeya bowed his head and praised her: she is the mother of all worlds and the fire-stick from which the gods arise; all that is real and unreal, whatever gives liberation, rests in her; the imperishable supreme Brahman and this perishable world are in her as fire is in wood and smell in earth. She is the syllable Om; its three measures are the three worlds, the three Vedas, the three fires, the three lights, the three aims of life beginning with dharma, the three qualities, the three classes, the three gods, the three bodily humours, the three states and the ancestors; the Soma, oblation and cooked-food sacrifices are done by speaking her. The half-measure beyond them is her highest form, which cannot be described and cannot be spoken with mouth, tongue, palate or lips; it is Vishnu, Shiva, Brahma, the light of moon and sun, the home and self of the universe, taught in Sankhya and the Vedas, without beginning, middle or end, one and many, both non-dual Brahman and the world of duality. All things, lasting or passing, gross or subtle, on earth or in the sky, with form or without, are known through her vowels and consonants. (Verse 21 is missing in the numbering.) Thus praised, Sarasvati, Vishnu's tongue, said to Markandeya, 'I will go tirelessly wherever you lead me.' Markandeya said: first is the holy Brahmasaras, then called Rama's lake, then Kurukshetra because the sage Kuru ploughed it; flow deep through its middle, holy one with holy water. (The chapter ends here.)

01-033.json.summary: Lomaharshana tells the sages that after hearing Markandeya, the river Sarasvati entered Kurukshetra, reached Rantuka, flooded Kurukshetra and flowed on to the west. Along her there are thousands of holy places (tirthas) visited by sages, which he will name by Brahma's grace. Remembering holy places is meritorious, seeing them destroys sin, and bathing in them gives liberation even to an evil-doer; those who remember them, please the gods and bathe with faith reach the highest goal. Whoever remembers Kurukshetra, pure or impure, in any state, becomes pure inside and out; just saying 'I will go to Kurukshetra, I will live in Kurukshetra' frees one from all sins, even if said constantly from far away. Four kinds of liberation are named: knowledge of Brahman, ancestral offerings at Gaya, death while saving cattle, and living in Kurukshetra. The land between the divine rivers Sarasvati and Drishadvati, made by the gods, is called Brahmavarta. One who bathes in the lake and lives on the Sarasvati's bank will surely gain knowledge of Brahman. Gods, sages and Siddhas live in Kurujangala; by serving it one sees Brahman in oneself, and even evil-doers who gain this fleeting human birth and serve it with self-control, seeking liberation, are freed from the stains of many births and see the pure eternal god in their heart. Those who live by Brahma's altar Kurukshetra and the holy Sannihita lake reach the highest state. Planets and stars may fall in time, but those who die in Kurukshetra never fall. Bathing with faith in the great lake of Sthanu (Shiva) gains whatever one wishes. The pilgrim should take a vow, walk around the lake keeping it on his right, go to Rantuka and ask pardon again and again, bathe in the Sarasvati, see and bow to the yaksha (Rantuka), offer flowers, incense and food, and say: 'By your grace, lord of yakshas, I will wander the forests, rivers and holy places; keep me always free of obstacles.'

01-034.json.summary: The sages ask Lomaharshana to name the seven forests, the nine rivers, all the holy places and the fruit of bathing in each by its rite. The seven forests in Kurukshetra are Kamyaka, Aditivana, Vyasavana, Phalakivana, Suryavana, Madhuvana and Shitavana. The rivers are Sarasvati, Vaitarani, Apaga, Ganga Mandakini, Madhusrava, Vasunadi, Kaushiki, Drishadvati and Hiranvati; all except the Sarasvati flow only in the rainy season, their water is holy then, and by the power of the place they are never counted as impure in that season (as rivers usually are). Then the pilgrimage: after greeting the mighty yaksha gatekeeper Rantuka, go to Aditivana, where Aditi did penance for a son; bathing there and seeing Aditi one gets a brave, faultless son and rides a chariot bright as a hundred suns. Then Savana, Vishnu's place, where Hari is always present. Bathing at Vimala and seeing Vimaleshvara one goes to heaven and Rudra's world; seeing Hari and Baladeva on one seat frees one from the sins of the Kali age. At Pariplava, seeing Brahma with the Vedas, one gains the fruit of the Veda and heaven; bathing at its meeting with the Kaushiki one reaches the highest state. At the Dharani (earth) tirtha a patient person who bathes is forgiven all wrongs done to the earth. At Daksha's hermitage, seeing Shiva as Daksheshvara gives the fruit of a horse sacrifice. At Shalukini, worshipping Hari joined with Hara leads to the worlds one desires. At Sarpirdadhi, the serpents' tirtha, bathing frees one from fear of snakes. Then go to the gatekeeper Rantuka, stay one night, bathe, worship the second gatekeeper with care, feed Brahmins, bow and ask pardon: 'By your grace, lord of yakshas, one is freed of sins; may I gain the success I seek.' Then go to Panchanada, the five streams made by Rudra to frighten the demons; Koti-tirtha, where Rudra gathered ten million holy places, where bathing and seeing Koteshvara gives the fruit of the five daily sacrifices; there also Vamana was installed by the gods, and bathing gives the fruit of an Agnishtoma sacrifice. At the Ashvins' tirtha a self-controlled person gains beauty and fame; at Varaha-tirtha, named by Vishnu, the highest state. Soma-tirtha, where the Moon was cured of disease by penance, gives the fruit of a Rajasuya sacrifice, freedom from disease and a long stay in the Moon's world; worshipping the two lingas Bhuteshvara and Jvalamaleshvara there ends rebirth. Bathing at Ekahamsa gives the fruit of a thousand cows; at Kritashaucha one gains the fruit of a Pundarika sacrifice and becomes pure. Fasting one night at Munjavata, Shiva's place, one becomes a leader of Shiva's hosts (ganapati); there is also the famous yakshini Mahagrahi, and bathing, pleasing her and fasting there destroys great sins. That is the gate of Kurukshetra; walk around it and feed Brahmins. Then go to Pushkara, brought there by Parashurama, and worship the ancestors and gods; a king gains his aims and the fruit of a horse sacrifice, and whoever gives a daughter in marriage there on the full moon of Kartika is granted his wishes by the pleased gods. The great yaksha Kapila himself stands there as gatekeeper, blocks sinners and gives them a bad end. His wife, the yakshi Udukhalamekhala, roams there always beating a drum. Once she saw a woman with her son, from a sinful land, and, beating her drum at night, said to her: 'You ate curd at Yugandhara, stayed at Achyutasthala and bathed at Bhutalaya, and now want to live here with your son; I told you by day, tonight I will surely eat you.' The woman bowed and begged for mercy, and the yakshi kindly said: 'When an eclipse of the sun comes in time, bathe in the Sannihati (lake); you will be purified and go to heaven.'

01-035.json.summary: Lomaharshana continues the pilgrimage. Next is Rama's lake (Ramahrada), where the Brahmin hero Parashurama, after destroying the Kshatriyas, made five lakes and filled them with their blood, as the sages have heard, and offered water to his fathers and grandfathers. Pleased with his devotion to his father and his valour, the ancestors offered him a boon. Parashurama asked, with joined palms, that his penance be restored by their grace, that he be freed by their power from the sin of destroying the Kshatriyas in anger, and that the lakes become famous holy places. The ancestors replied that his penance would grow, he was freed from that sin since the Kshatriyas had fallen by their own deeds, and the lakes would surely become holy; whoever bathes in them and offers water to his ancestors will be given the boons he desires, his wishes and lasting heaven. They then vanished. A celibate of pure vows who bathes in Rama's lakes and worships Rama with faith gains much gold. At Vamshamula, bathing brings success to one's family line. At the famous Kayashodhana bathing purifies the body, and with a purified body one reaches the place of no return; Siddhas wander the tirthas until they reach this one. Then Lokoddhara, where Vishnu raised up all the worlds; bathing there one sees the eternal worlds, and pleasing Vishnu and Shiva, who always live there, by bowing gives liberation. At Shri-tirtha (Shalagrama) the goddess (Lakshmi) is always near the bather. At Kapilahrada, bathing and worshipping gods and ancestors gives the fruit of a thousand brown cows, and seeing Shiva there in Kapila's form, worshipped by sages, gives liberation. At Surya-tirtha, bathing, worshipping ancestors and gods and fasting gives the fruit of an Agnishtoma and the Sun's world, and seeing the thousand-rayed Sun with knowledge gives liberation. At Bhavanivana bathing gives the fruit of a thousand cows. Story: once when Brahma drank nectar, the cow Surabhi was born from his belch and went to the underworld; her daughters, the mothers of the world, filled the underworld; when Brahma, sacrificing, called them to be his sacrificial fee, they came out confused through a hole, and Ganapati himself stands at that hole's mouth; seeing him a self-controlled person gains all wishes. At Sangini, the goddess's tirtha, bathing gives beauty, endless wealth, sons and grandsons, great pleasures and then the highest state. One who bathes in Brahmavarta gains knowledge of Brahman and dies when he chooses. Then go again to the gatekeeper Rantuka's tirtha on the Sarasvati; bathing and fasting there, by the yaksha's grace, gives the fruit one wishes. Then Brahmavarta, praised by sages, where bathing surely brings Brahman. Then Sutirthaka, where the ancestors and gods are always present; bathing and worshipping them gives the fruit of a horse sacrifice and pleases the ancestors for ever. At Ambuvana, Kameshvara's tirtha frees from all disease and gives Brahman; at the Mothers' tirtha (Matri-tirtha) there, bathing with devotion makes one's offspring increase and gives endless wealth. Then Shitavana, a tirtha rare elsewhere, which purifies even by sight; sprinkling one's hair there frees one from sin. There is also Svanulomayana, where wise Brahmins shed their body hair by breath control and, purified, reach the highest goal. Dashashvamedhika there gives the fruit of ten horse sacrifices. Then go to the famous Manusha tirtha, whose sight frees one from sin. Long ago black deer wounded by a hunter's arrows plunged into its lake and became human (Brahmins). The hunters asked these Brahmins where the wounded deer had gone; they said, 'We are those deer, made human by the power of this tirtha; bathe here with faith and without envy and you will be freed of all sins.' The hunters bathed, became pure and went to heaven. Those who hear this greatness of Manusha with faith also reach the highest goal.

01-036.json.summary: Lomaharshana continues the pilgrimage. One krosha east of Manusha is the river Apaga, visited by Brahmins. Those who give Brahmins shyamaka millet cooked in milk and soaked in ghee there have no sin; those who perform ancestral offerings (shraddha) there gain all wishes. The ancestors say they hope a son or grandson of their line will go to the Apaga and offer them water with sesame, which will satisfy them for a hundred kalpas; one who offers rice balls (pinda) there at midday on the fourteenth day of the dark half of Bhadrapada (Nabhasya) gains liberation. Next is Brahma's place Brahmodumbara; bathing in the pools of the Brahmin sages made there by the seven sages Bharadvaja, Gautama, Jamadagni, Kashyapa, Vishvamitra, Vasishtha and Atri gives the fruit of seven Soma sacrifices and Brahma's world; feeding a Brahmin there for the gods and ancestors pleases the ancestors, and bathing separately for each of the seven sages makes one lord of the seven worlds. Kapisthala, where the god called Vriddhakedara lives, destroys all sins; bathing and worshipping Rudra with Dindi gives the power to vanish and joy in Shiva's world; offering water, drinking three handfuls and bowing to Dindi gives the fruit of Kedara; a shraddha there for Shiva on the fourteenth of the bright half of Chaitra leads to the highest state. At Kalasi, where the goddess Durga, Katyayani, Bhadra, Nidra and eternal Maya lives, bathing and seeing Durga on the bank lets one cross the hard forest of worldly life. At Saraka, seeing Maheshvara on the fourteenth of the dark half grants all wishes and Shiva's world; there are thirty million tirthas there, and Rudrakoti in a well in the middle of the lake; one who bathes and remembers Rudrakoti has worshipped it and, by the Rudras' grace, gains Indra's knowledge and the highest state. Idaspada there removes sin and fear and gives liberation by sight; Kedara gives the fruit of all gifts; Kimrupa gives the fruit of all sacrifices. East of Saraka is Anyajanma. Story: after Vishnu took the man-lion form and killed the mighty demon, he stayed in the animal world, taking delight among lions. The gods and Gandharvas worshipped Shiva and asked him to recover Vishnu's body. Shiva took the form of a sharabha and fought him for a thousand divine years, and both fell into the lake. The divine sage Narada, meditating under a peepal tree on its bank, saw Vishnu come out with four arms and Shiva as a linga, and praised them: 'Salutation to Shiva and Vishnu, Hari and the husband of Uma, Hara of many forms, Vishnu of universal form, three-eyed Tryambaka and Krishna, cause of knowledge.' He said his hermitage was purified by them and would be known in the three worlds as Anyajanma (another birth); whoever bathes there and offers water to the ancestors with faith will gain Indra's knowledge, and Narada always lives at the root of the peepal; one who bows to the peepal will not see fierce Yama. Then the Naga's lake; bathing at Paundarika gives the fruit of a Pundarika sacrifice, and bathing, japa and shraddha on the tenth of the bright half of Chaitra open the path to liberation. At Trivishtapa is the holy river Vaitarani; bathing and worshipping Shiva with the trident and bull banner leads to the highest goal. Bathing at Rasavarta brings supreme success; bathing at Alepaka on the fourteenth of the bright half of Chaitra and worshipping Shiva leaves no stain of sin. Then Phalakivana, where gods, Gandharvas, Sadhyas and sages do penance for a thousand divine years; bathing in the Drishadvati and offering water to the gods gives the fruit of Agnishtoma and Atiratra sacrifices; a shraddha there at the new moon or on a Monday pleases the ancestors as one at Gaya does, and even remembering Phalakivana satisfies them; another great tirtha there gives the fruit of a thousand cows. Bathing at Panikhata and offering to the ancestors gives a Rajasuya and both Sankhya and Yoga. At Mishraka, Vyasa mixed together the holy places for Dadhichi's sake; bathing there equals bathing in all. Then Vyasavana: bathing at Manojava and seeing Shiva as Devamani fulfils every wish; at Madhuvati, the goddess's tirtha, one gains success with her leave; bathing with controlled diet where the Kaushiki meets the Drishadvati frees from all sins. At Vyasasthali, where Vyasa, overcome by grief for his son, resolved to die and was raised again by the gods, one feels no grief for a son. Giving a prastha of sesame at the well Kimdatta frees one from debts and brings success. Bathing at Ahna and Sudina, rare tirthas, gives the Sun's world. At Kritajapya bathing in the Ganga and worshipping Mahadeva gives the fruit of a horse sacrifice, and Koti-tirtha with Koteshvara gives ten million sacrifices. Then Vamanaka, where Vishnu as Vamana took Bali's kingdom and gave it to Indra; bathing at Vishnupada and worshipping Vamana gives Vishnu's world. Jyeshthashrama there destroys all sins and gives liberation by sight; fasting on the eleventh of the bright half of Jyeshtha and bathing on the twelfth makes one foremost among men. Brahmins installed there by Vishnu are devoted to pleasing him, and shraddhas and gifts given to them last as long as the Manu period. Koti-tirtha there gives ten million sacrifices, and seeing Koteshvara makes one a leader of Shiva's hosts; the Sun's great tirtha there brings honour in the Sun's world. Then Kulottarana, made by Vishnu to save the classes and life stages; those seeking liberation beyond celibacy reach the highest state there; a celibate student, householder, forest-dweller or renunciant who bathes saves seven, seven and seven generations of his family; Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas and Shudras devoted to it who bathe with devotion all see the highest state. Even one who remembers Kurukshetra with Vamana from afar gains liberation, still more one who lives there.

01-037.json.summary: Lomaharshana continues. Bathing in Pavana's lake and seeing Maheshvara frees one of all stains and gives Shiva's state; there the Wind god (Pavana), grieving for his son, hid himself until the gods with Brahma pleased him and brought him out. Then go to Shiva's place Amrita, where the gods and Gandharvas brought Hanuman out (so the text reads); bathing there gives immortality. At Kulottarana a pilgrim saves all his family, mother's father's and father's lines. At the famous tirtha of the royal sage Shalihotra, bathing frees from bodily stains. At Shrikunja on the Sarasvati bathing gives the fruit of an Agnishtoma. At Naimishakunja one gains the merit of bathing at Naimisha. There is also the famous tirtha of Vedavati: when Ravana seized her by the hair, she, worn by grief, gave up her life in order to destroy him; she was then born in King Janaka's house as Sita, the faithful wife of Rama, and was carried off by Ravana to bring about his own ruin; Rama killed Ravana, crowned Vibhishana and brought Sita home like fame returning to a self-controlled man. Bathing at her tirtha gives the fruit of giving a girl in marriage, freedom from stains and the highest state. Next is a great place of Brahma where a man of lower class who bathes gains Brahminhood, and a Brahmin, purified, reaches the highest state. At Soma's tirtha, where the Moon by penance gained kingship over the Brahmins, bathing and worshipping ancestors and gods takes one, pure like the moon on Kartika full moon, to heaven. Then Saptasarasvata, where seven Sarasvatis flow as one: Suprabha, Kanchanakshi, Vishala, Manasahrada (Manorama), Sarasvatyogha, Suvenu and Vimaloda. Their origins: when Brahma sacrificed at Pushkara, the sages said the sacrifice would not give great fruit because the Sarasvati was not seen there; Brahma remembered her and she came as Suprabha, and the sages honoured her; this Pushkara Sarasvati was brought to Kurukshetra by the sage Mankanaka. At Naimisha the sages led by Shaunaka asked Lomaharshana how their sacrifice could bear fruit; he said that where the Sarasvati is, the fruit is great; they remembered her and she came to flood their sacrifice as Kanchanakshi, and Mankanaka called her to Kurukshetra. At King Gaya's great sacrifice in Gaya she was called and named Vishala, and Mankanaka brought her to Kurukshetra. In northern Koshala the sage Uddalaka meditated on her and she came, worshipped by sages in bark and deerskin, known as Manohara, and Mankanaka called her to Kurukshetra to honour the sage. The Sarasvati at Kedara, called Suvenu, was brought into Kurukshetra by that sage after worshipping Shiva, for the sages' good. At Gangadvara, Daksha, sacrificing, made her appear as Vimaloda, and Mankanaka called her there too. In Kurukshetra Kuru sacrificed to the Sarasvati, and wise Markandeya, after praising her, brought her into the middle of the lake. At Saptasarasvata the perfected sage Mankanaka lived, and when he danced, Shiva stopped him.

01-038.json.summary: The sages ask Lomaharshana who Mankanaka was and why Shiva stopped his dancing. Mankanaka was a mind-born son of Kashyapa. Once, taking his bark garment to bathe, he found the beautiful Apsaras led by Rambha bathing there with him; excited, his semen fell in the water, and he caught it in a pot. It divided into seven parts, and from it were born seven sages known as the Maruts: Vayuvega, Vayubala, Vayuha, Vayumandala, Vayujvala, Vayureta and Vayuchakra, who hold up all moving and unmoving things. Long ago, it is said, Mankanaka cut his hand on the tip of kusha grass and vegetable sap flowed from the wound instead of blood. Seeing this, he danced with joy, and everything moving and unmoving danced with him, bewildered by his power. Brahma, the gods and the sages asked Mahadeva to stop him from dancing. For the gods' good Shiva asked the overjoyed sage why an ascetic on the path of dharma was so excited. The sage said, 'Do you not see the vegetable sap flowing from my hand? Seeing it I dance with great joy.' Laughing at the sage, deluded by passion, Shiva said he himself felt no wonder at it, and struck his own thumb with a fingertip; ash, white as snow, came out of the wound. Ashamed, the sage fell at his feet and praised him: he knows no god but the trident-holder, the best in the whole world, on whom Brahma and the gods depend, the first of the gods, by whose grace the gods rejoice without fear. He asked that by Shiva's grace his penance not be lost. Pleased, Shiva said his penance would grow a thousandfold and Shiva would always live with him in this hermitage; whoever bathes at Saptasarasvata and worships Shiva will find nothing hard to get in this world or the next, will surely go to the world of Sarasvati and, by Shiva's grace, reach the highest state.

01-039.json.summary: Lomaharshana continues. Next is the Aushanasa tirtha, where Ushanas (Shukra) gained perfection and the rank of a planet; bathing there frees one from the sins of birth and leads to the supreme Brahman, from which there is no return. There the sage Rahodara was freed from a great head that had seized him. The sages ask how. Long ago, when Rama (Raghava) lived in the Dandaka forest and killed Rakshasas, he cut off the head of one wicked Rakshasa with a sharp razor-edged arrow; it fell in the great forest and by chance stuck to the shank of Rahodara as he wandered there, breaking the bone and entering it. With it stuck there, the sage could hardly move, yet in pain, with pus flowing, he went to every holy place on earth. He told the sages, and they told him to go to the Aushanasa tirtha. When he touched its water, the head let go of his leg and fell into the water; free of stain and pure, he went happily to his hermitage and told everything, and the sages named the place Kapalamochana (release from the skull). Nearby is the great tirtha of Vishvamitra, where he gained Brahminhood; bathing there surely gives Brahminhood, and a Brahmin, purified, reaches the highest state. Then go, with controlled diet, to Prithudaka. There the Brahmin sage Rushangu, who remembered his past births and always lived at Gangadvara, seeing his end near, told his sons, 'I see no good here; take me to Prithudaka.' They brought him to the Sarasvati; bathing there and remembering the virtues of the place, he said that whoever gives up his body at Prithudaka, on the northern bank of the Sarasvati, while doing japa, surely gains immortality. There too is Brahmayoni, made by Brahma: staying at Prithudaka on the Sarasvati's bank, Brahma meditated to create the four classes, and Brahmins were born from his mouth, Kshatriyas from his arms, Vaishyas from his thighs and Shudras from his feet; seeing the four classes settled in their life stages, he set up the tirtha called Brahmayoni, where one seeking liberation who bathes does not see another womb. There is also the famous Avakirna, where Baka Dalbhya offered the angry King Dhritarashtra with his vehicles into the fire, and the king then came to his senses. The sages ask how. Long ago the Naimisha sages went to seek sacrificial fees, and Baka Dalbhya asked Dhritarashtra for gifts; the king, to insult him, said something false about cattle. In great anger Baka cut flesh (from the cattle) and, at Avakirna in Prithudaka, offered Dhritarashtra's kingdom into the fire; as the sacrifice went on, the kingdom wasted away through the king's wrongdoing. The king thought about what the Brahmin had done, took jewels and, with his priest, went to Avakirna to appease him. Pleased, Baka told him: 'A wise man must never despise Brahmins; a Brahmin despised can destroy three generations of a family,' and restored him to his kingdom and fame. A self-controlled person who bathes there with faith gains whatever he wishes. There too is the famous Yayata, where a river flowed with honey for King Yayati when he sacrificed; bathing there with devotion frees from all sins and gives the fruit of a horse sacrifice. At Madhusrava one should bathe and offer honey to the ancestors. There is also the great tirtha Vasishthodvaha (Vasishtha's carrying away), where bathing with devotion leads to Vasishtha's world.

01-040.json.summary: The sages ask Lomaharshana how the river came to carry Vasishtha away. There was great enmity between the royal sage Vishvamitra and Vasishtha out of rivalry in penance. Vasishtha's hermitage was at Sthanu-tirtha, and Vishvamitra's to the west of it, where Shiva (Sthanu) had sacrificed, worshipped the Sarasvati and set her up in the form of a linga. Vasishtha practised fierce penance there and Vishvamitra fell short of him. Vishvamitra called the Sarasvati and told her to bring Vasishtha to him by her current so that he could kill him there. The river was distressed and trembled, but the angry Vishvamitra told her to bring him quickly. Weeping, she went to Vasishtha and told him Vishvamitra's words. Seeing her worn and grief-stricken, the compassionate Vasishtha told her to carry him to Vishvamitra. She moved him from his place with her flood, cutting away the bank, and as he was carried he praised her: 'You flow from Brahma's lake, Sarasvati; the whole world is filled with your waters; you move in the sky and make the water in clouds; you are all waters; from you we learn; nourishment, firmness, fame, success, beauty, patience, svadha, svaha and speech depend on you; you dwell in all beings as speech.' She carried him gently to Vishvamitra's hermitage and, unhappy, handed him over. Seeing him, Vishvamitra in anger looked for a weapon to kill him. Fearing the sin of killing a Brahmin, the river carried Vasishtha away again into the middle of her waters, keeping her word to both and tricking Vishvamitra. Red-eyed with rage, Vishvamitra cursed her: 'Since you tricked me and left, flow with blood, joined by the chief of the Rakshasas.' For a year the Sarasvati flowed with water mixed with blood. Sages, gods, Gandharvas and Apsaras were grieved; ghosts, Pishachas and Rakshasas came and drank the blood happily, dancing and laughing as if they had won heaven. After some time sages on pilgrimage came and, seeing the river drunk by fierce Rakshasas, set out to save her. They asked her why the lake was so full of blood, and she told them all Vishvamitra had done. The sages then brought the Aruna, a river of holy water that destroys all sins, into the Sarasvati. Seeing the clean water, the Rakshasas were distressed and pleaded again and again: they are hungry and without dharma for ever, not sinners by their own choice; they are Brahma-rakshasas because of the sages' disfavour and their own bad deeds; Vaishyas, Shudras and Kshatriyas who do wrong deeds and hate Brahmins become Rakshasas here; their race also grows through the fault of the wombs of sinful women; this is their eternal lot, and the sages can save all the worlds. Out of pity the sages agreed among themselves that food on which someone has sneezed, that has insects, leftover food, food with hair in it, food that has been shaken or tainted by breath, and food mixed with these shall be the Rakshasas' share; so the wise should avoid such food, for whoever eats it eats the Rakshasas' food. Having purified the tirtha, the sages made the confluence there for the Rakshasas' release. Whoever fasts three nights and bathes at the famous meeting of the Aruna and Sarasvati is freed from all sins, and in the terrible Kali age, when adharma is everywhere, bathing there gives liberation. The Rakshasas bathed, were freed of sin, wore divine garlands and clothes and went to heaven.

01-041.json.summary: Lomaharshana continues. There Darvi long ago brought the four oceans; bathing in each gives the fruit of a thousand cows, and whatever is done at that tirtha of penance becomes complete, even for an evil-doer. Bathing at both Shatasahasrika and Shatika gives the fruit of a thousand cows. Soma-tirtha on the Sarasvati gives the fruit of a Rajasuya. At Renuka's hermitage a self-controlled person gains the merit of devotion to one's mother. At Rinamochana, visited by Brahma, one is freed from the debts to gods, sages and ancestors. Kumara's (Skanda's) consecration place, called Ojasa, gives fame, and one who does a shraddha there reaches Kumara's city; a shraddha there on the sixth of the bright half of Chaitra gives the merit of a shraddha at Gaya, and equals a shraddha at Sannihati during a solar eclipse; Vayu once said a shraddha at Ojasa never ends, so it should be done with every effort, and bathing there with faith on Chaitra's sixth gives the ancestors water that never fails. At Panchavata, where Mahadeva himself stands in the form of yoga, bathing and worshipping him makes one a leader of Shiva's hosts, rejoicing with the gods. Then the famous Kuru-tirtha, where Kuru did very hard penance to plough the field. Indra, pleased, said that those who perform sacrifices to Indra in Kurukshetra would go to sinless worlds of merit, then laughed and went back to heaven; he came again and again, laughing and questioning, without tiring. When Kuru, by fierce penance, began to plough his own body, Indra kindly asked what he wished. Kuru asked that those who live at this tirtha with faith reach the home of Brahma, and that people who sinned elsewhere, even those stained with the five great sins, be freed by bathing here and reach the highest goal. Seeing Kuru-tirtha, the holiest in Kurukshetra, one is freed of sin; bathing there, one is freed and, with Kuru's leave, reaches the highest state. Then go to Svargadvara at Shivadvara, where bathing gives the highest state. Then the famous Anaraka (no hell), with Brahma to the east, Maheshvara to the south, Rudra's wife to the west and Vishnu (Padmanabha) to the north, and Anaraka in the middle, rare even in the three worlds; bathing there frees one from great and lesser sins. When the sixth lunar day of Vaishakha falls on a Tuesday, one should bathe there, first please the gods by giving four water pots (karaka) with food, then give a jar (kalasha) decorated with cakes, which destroys all sins; one who bathes by this rite is freed of all stains and goes to the highest state; when the sixth falls on a Tuesday in another month too, the rite there gives liberation. Bathing in that tirtha of all tirthas, with the leave of all the gods, one reaches the highest state. The holy Kamyaka forest destroys all sins; merely entering it frees one of sin. There the Sun is present as Pusha, whose sight gives liberation; bathing there on a Sunday purifies the body and fulfils one's wishes.

01-042.json.summary: The sages ask Lomaharshana about the origin of the holy grove (kunja) east of Kamyaka, visited by the gods. He says that the Naimisha sages once came to Kurukshetra to bathe in the Sarasvati but could not get in; they made the Yajnopavitika tirtha, but the rest of the sages still found no way in. Seeing the land from Rantuka's hermitage to Sachakraka full of Brahmins, the river Sarasvati, for the good of all Brahmins and all beings, made groves (kunjas) and went on westwards. One who bathes in her eastern flow gains the fruit of bathing in the Ganga; her southern flow is the Narmada, best of rivers; in the west she joins the Yamuna; when she flows north she becomes the Sindhu. Flowing thus in all directions, the holy Sarasvati makes one who bathes in her as if bathed in all tirthas. Next is the famous tirtha of Madana (Kama) called Vihara. There the gods came wishing to see Shiva but could not see him with the goddess; they praised Nandi, lord of the hosts, who, pleased, told them of Shiva's great play with Uma at Vihara. Hearing this, the gods called their own wives and played there too; pleased with their play, Shankara said that whoever bathes at Vihara with faith will surely have wealth, grain and loved ones. Then Durga-tirtha, served by Durga; bathing there and worshipping the ancestors one does not meet a bad end. There too is the famous well of Sarasvati, whose sight gives liberation free of all sins; offering water there to gods and ancestors with faith gives undying results, and this ancestors' tirtha is especially great. Where the Sarasvati flows east (Prachi Sarasvati), entering and leaving by the path of the gods, even a killer of mother, father or Brahmin, or one who has slept with his teacher's wife, becomes pure by bathing; she is holy even for evil-doers, and those who stay three nights there keep no sin in their bodies. Nara and Narayana, Brahma, Sthanu, the Sun and the gods with Indra always serve this eastern flow; those who do shraddha there find nothing hard to get in this world or the next; so it should always be visited, especially on the fifth lunar day, which makes one prosperous. There is also the Aushana tirtha, rare in the three worlds, where Ushanas (Shukra) gained perfection by worshipping the Lord and is worshipped among the planets; those who visit it with faith reach the highest goal, and a shraddha there with devotion surely saves one's ancestors. Chaturmukha, Brahma's tirtha, stands at the boundary of the lake; those who stay there fasting on the fourteenth day, and on the eighth of the dark half of Chaitra, see the supreme subtle one from which there is no return. Then go to Sthanu-tirtha, adorned with a thousand lingas; seeing the Sthanu banyan (vata) there frees one from sins.

01-043.json.summary: The sages ask Lomaharshana about the greatness of Sthanu-tirtha and its banyan, the origin of the Sannihati lake and why it was filled with dust, the merit of seeing and touching the lingas, and the greatness of the lake. Lomaharshana tells them the great Vamana Purana, hearing which brings liberation by Vamana's grace. Sanatkumara was seated near the banyan of Sthanu with the Valakhilyas and other mind-born sons of Brahma, when the sage Markandeya came humbly and asked him about the lake's greatness, size and position: which tirthas are visible and which hidden, the very holy lingas near Sthanu that give liberation by sight, the origin of the banyan, the merit of walking around it and bathing, how Shiva as Sthanu stands in the middle of the lake, why Indra filled the tirtha with dust, the greatness of Sthanu-, Chakra-, Surya- and Soma-tirthas, and Shiva's hidden places and Vishnu's places along the Sarasvati. Sanatkumara loosened his sitting posture, bowed to Maheshvara and told what he had heard from Brahma. In the beginning, when all moving and unmoving things were lost in the one terrible ocean, there was one huge egg, the seed of creatures. Brahma lay in it and slept for a thousand ages; waking, he saw the world empty and, moved by rajas, thought of creation. Rajas is the quality of creation, sattva of preservation and tamas works at the time of dissolution; the Lord beyond the qualities is the all-pervading Person who fills everything called living; he is Brahma, Govinda and the eternal Ishvara, and whoever knows him knows all and knows liberation. What need of tirthas or life stages have those whose boundless mind rests in the self? The self is a river whose holy fords are self-restraint, whose water is truth, joined with good conduct and meditation; one who bathes in it is purified, for the inner self is not cleaned by water. The chief work of a person is that which enters the joy of knowing the self; the good call that the thing to be known, and gaining it one leaves desires. A Brahmin has no wealth like oneness, equality, truthfulness, steady good conduct, giving up punishment, freedom from anger and rest from ritual acts. This is Brahman in brief. Then the birth of Brahma: the waters are called nara, and because he lies in them he is called Narayana. Waking in that water and knowing the world was inside, the Lord split the egg; from it came Om, then Bhuh, Bhuvah and Svah, then light, the excellent light of Savitri, which dried up the water; the rest became a jelly, then a bubble, then hard, and the hardness is the earth that holds all beings. Where the egg lay is the Sannihita lake. Because light came out first, it is called Aditya. Brahma, grandfather of the worlds, was born in the egg; its inner membrane became Meru, its outer membrane the mountains, its womb water the seas and thousands of rivers. The great pure water at Brahma's navel filled the great lake, and in its middle is the great banyan in the form of Sthanu; from it came the classes, Brahmins, Kshatriyas and Vaishyas, and Shudras were born from it to serve the twice-born. As Brahma thought of creation, the mind-born great sages Sanaka and others were born; thinking again, wanting offspring, the seven sages who became lords of creatures; thinking again under rajas, the Valakhilyas, devoted to penance and Veda study. Living as forest-dwellers in the Devadaru forest with daily fire offerings, they bathed constantly, worshipped the gods and dried up their bodies with fasts and hard vows for a thousand divine years until they were thin and their veins showed, but Shankara was not pleased. Long after, Uma, passing through the sky with Shiva, saw them and, grieved, asked Shiva to end their suffering, for what endless sin could Veda-devoted men have that they were still not purified? Laughing, Shiva said she did not know the deep way of dharma: these men do not know dharma, are not free of desire or anger and are simply deluded. When she objected and asked him to show her, he told her to wait and went to them. He appeared naked, handsome in every limb, young, crowned with a forest garland and carrying a begging bowl, and went from hermitage to hermitage saying 'Give alms.' The wives of the sages, charmed by his beauty, called one another to see the beggar, brought roots and fruits and offered them; holding out his bowl and smiling, he said, 'Give, give; may it go well with you in this forest of penance,' while the goddess watched. Struck by love, they asked what kind of vow he kept, naked, with a garland, and said that if he found them pleasing, they found him so. He said such a vow is not explained in public where many listen; they said they would go somewhere private, being very curious, and seized him, one by the neck, others by the arms, knees, hair, waist and feet. Seeing their wives so disturbed, the sages cried 'Kill him!' and with sticks and stones struck down and tore off the god's fearsome linga. When it fell, the Lord vanished and went with the goddess to Mount Kailasa. With the linga fallen, the moving and unmoving world was ruined and the sages were deeply alarmed. One wise sage said they did not know the true nature of that ascetic and should go to Brahma for refuge. Deeply ashamed, they went to Brahma's hall, bowed and stood with heads down. Brahma said: 'You fools, stained by anger, you know nothing of dharma. Hear the whole of dharma, cruel ascetics. The all-pervading eternal one who lives in the self within this body is the beginningless great Sthanu, seen as separate only by appearance; as a crystal takes the colour of what is beside it, the self takes the colour of the mind, grows through actions and so enjoys heaven and hell. The wise should purify the mind by knowledge, yoga and the like; when it is pure the inner self is calm by itself, but a person whose mind is not pure is not purified by burning bodily hardships. Rites are taught only to restrain one from sin, because the very impure body is not quickly cleaned; for this the good path was set up in the world, and the division of classes and life stages was made by some ruler of the world. You live in hermitages overcome by anger and desire; for the wise the house is a hermitage, and for those without yoga the hermitage is no hermitage. Where is the giving up of all desire, and where this delusion over women, and this terrible anger by which you do not know yourselves? Whatever an angry man sacrifices, gives, practises as penance or offers in the fire brings him no fruit in the world; the angry man's fruit is in vain.' (The chapter ends here, in the middle of Brahma's speech; the story continues in the next chapter.)

01-044.json.summary: Lomaharshana reports Sanatkumara telling Markandeya the greatness of the lake (Saromahatmya). The sages, who had lost Shiva's linga, ask Brahma what will bring good to the world. Brahma takes them to Kailasa, where Shiva sits with Uma, and praises him as the endless one, giver of boons and lord of all. Shiva tells them not to fear: they should set up the fallen linga quickly at the great lake Sannihitya. Whoever worships his linga with devotion will find nothing hard to get, and even sins done knowingly are cleansed. He will be worshipped there as Sthanu, also called Sthanvishvara, and those who remember him are freed of all faults and reach freedom by seeing him. The gods and sages cannot move the linga from the Daru forest, and Brahma says Shiva let it fall by his own will, so only he can bring it. They go to Kailasa but cannot find Shiva; Brahma learns by meditation that he is in the form of an elephant. At the great lake they still cannot see him, until the Goddess, holding a water pot, gives them nectar to drink and shows him standing in the middle of the lake. They beg him to bring the linga. In elephant form he goes to the Devadaru forest hermitage, lifts the linga easily with his trunk and sets it on the western side of the lake. The gods and sages praise him with a long hymn of names: highest self, knower of the field, lord of yoga, the syllable Om, the three-eyed, blue-throated one who wears the half moon and has Uma as half his body. Praised so, Shiva gives up the elephant form and makes his presence dwell in the linga.

01-045.json.summary: Sanatkumara goes on. Shiva tells the gods and sages that this great lake Sannihita gives freedom because he has lived there. Brahmins, Kshatriyas and Vaishyas who see the linga see the highest state; every day at noon all holy waters come to Sthanu Tirtha; and whoever praises him with this hymn will always find him near. He disappears. Soon heaven is crowded with humans, because seeing the Sthanu linga takes people to heaven. The frightened gods go to Brahma, who tells Indra to fill the lake with dust. Indra rains dust for seven days, but Shiva holds up the linga and the holy banyan tree with his hand. So the place where water remains is the holiest: bathing there equals bathing in all holy waters, and a rite for the dead (shraddha) between the banyan and the linga pleases the ancestors. The sages rub the dust on their bodies, lose their sins and go to Brahma's world. Brahma places a stone linga over the first one, and when the gods complain that people still reach the highest goal by seeing it, he sets seven lingas there, one above another. Even so, those who serve the dust reach the highest state, and even Kurukshetra dust blown by the wind saves great sinners. The sins of women and men, done knowingly or not, are destroyed there. Water with black sesame offered to the ancestors west of the linga pleases them for three ages. In the Krita age the place is called Sannihitya, in the Treta age Vayu, and between the Dvapara and Kali ages it is the well Rudrahrada. Bathing there on the dark fourteenth of Chaitra, or spending the night at the banyan meditating on Shiva, gives the highest state or whatever one wishes.

01-046.json.summary: Sanatkumara describes the holy places around Sthanu's banyan. Shukra Tirtha is to the north, Soma Tirtha to the east, Daksha Tirtha to the south and Skanda Tirtha to the west, with Sthanu in the middle. Seeing him gives the highest state, and walking around these places on the eighth and fourteenth days gives the fruit of a sacrifice at every step. He then lists many lingas nearby, each with its founder and reward. Uma stays beside Shiva in linga form. There are lingas set up by the serpent Takshaka, by Vishvakarma (where Sarasvati also stands in linga form and gives intelligence), and by Brahma (Vateshvara). Walking around Sthanu's banyan equals walking around the earth. Near Sthanu are the attendant Nakulisha, the holy place Rudrakara, and Gokarna, set up by Ravana; worship there on the dark fourteenth of Ashadha frees one from all sins. Vibhishana worshipped a linga and became free of age and death, and worship there on the bright eighth of Ashadha gives immortality. Khara, Dushana and Trishiras each worshipped there and got their wishes. Other lingas include Hastipadeshvara, the lingas of Harita and Vapita, a great linga set up by Rudra in skeleton form (seeing it gives the fruit of the Agnishtoma sacrifice), and Siddheshvara. Others were set up by Mrikanda and by the Sun. The lovers Chitrangada and Rambha set up two lingas, and seeing them brings beauty and good birth. Further lingas belong to Indra, Vayu, Himavat, Kartavirya, Mitra and Varuna. Parashara gained poetic skill there, Vyasa gained knowledge of Brahman, Hanuman gained perfection and Vishnu gained the Sudarshana discus. Sages, the Valakhilyas, gandharvas, yakshas and kinnaras set up countless more lingas, and Vayu counted three and a half crores. Brahma set up the Sthanu linga on the thirteenth of Chaitra. Anyone who enters Sthanu's temple, with or without desire, is freed from terrible sins, and those who fast and worship then reach the highest state.

01-047.json.summary: Markandeya asks who first gained perfection at Sthanu Tirtha, and Sanatkumara tells the story of Vena. The line runs from Brahma to Marichi, Kashyapa, the Sun and Manu. A son of Manu ruled justly and married Bhaya, daughter of Kala (Time). Their son was Vena, who reviled the Veda, and the father went to the forest in disgust. As king, Vena, through his mother's father's fault, forbade gifts, sacrifices and fire offerings, and declared that he alone was to be worshipped. When the sages said the world rests on sacrifice, he repeated the order, and they killed him with blades of kusha grass made holy by mantras. The world without a king suffered from robbers, so the sages churned Vena's left hand. A short man came out, told to "sit down" (nishida), and the Nishadas came from him. Churning the right hand produced a tall man with divine marks, bow and arrows. The gods made him king, and he was called raja because he pleased (ranjita) the earth. Wanting to save his sinful father, the new king asked Narada, who saw that Vena had been reborn among the Mlecchas (foreign tribes) with leprosy and wasting disease. Narada told him to purify the body at Sthanu Tirtha and Sannihita lake. The king found Vena and had him carried there in a litter, but as he was about to bathe him, Vayu warned from the sky that this sinner would destroy the holy place. The gods told the son to bathe in the holy places on his father's behalf and sprinkle him with the water. He built Vena a hut and did this daily. Meanwhile a dog, once the head of Sthanu's monastery, had been reborn as a dog for wasting the god's property. Driven off by the other dogs, he came to the lake, plunged into the Sarasvati and was freed of sin. Looking for food he entered the hut. Vena was afraid of the dog and ended up in the water of Sthanu Tirtha, and drops of water from the dog's body fell on him. So, by the holy place and through his son, Vena was saved, gained a divine body and sang a very long hymn to Shiva. In it he names Shiva as all gods, all beings, the Vedas, time, the elements and the best of every kind, beyond the knowledge even of Brahma and Vishnu, and asks to be protected as a father protects his son.

01-048.json.summary: Sanatkumara goes on. Shiva, pleased with Vena's hymn, says Vena will live near him. Later Vena will be born from Shiva's body as the demon Andhaka in Hiranyaksha's house. Because of his old sin of reviling the Veda, he will desire the Mother of the world, and Shiva will kill and purify his body with the trident. Made sinless, he will become the attendant chief Bhringiriti and reach perfection. Shiva declares this hymn the best of hymns. Those who recite or hear it gain long life, fame, wealth and learning, are freed from fear of sickness, thieves and kings, and are safe in their homes from demons and spirits. A woman who hears it with her husband's leave is honoured like a goddess in both families. Shiva offers a boon. Vena asks grace for the dog, who was born a dog for eating the god's property and who helped him: out of fear of the dog he was plunged into the lake, after the gods had stopped him from bathing. Shiva grants that the dog will go to Shiva's world. Whoever hears this hymn and the greatness of Kurukshetra, of the lake and of the linga is freed from sin. Shiva vanishes. The dog remembers its past birth and takes a divine form. Vainya (Prithu) finds the hut empty, and Vena appears and thanks his good son for saving him from hell. He sets up an image of Shiva at Sthanu Tirtha and reaches perfection, and the dog goes to Shiva's abode. Freed from his debt to his father, the king rules well, has sons, performs sacrifices and gives gifts. Then he crowns his son, does penance at Kurukshetra and leaves his body by his own will for the highest state. Hearing this story frees one from all sins.

01-049.json.summary: Markandeya asks about the four-faced (Chaturmukha) and Brahmeshvara lingas. Sanatkumara tells the story. After creating all beings, Brahma, thinking again of creation, produced a lovely dark girl, desired her, and for this sin his head split. He went to Sannihitya lake, set up a four-faced linga on the north bank of the Sarasvati at Sthanu Tirtha, and worshipped it daily with incense, offerings and hymns to Rudra. Shiva came, and Brahma praised him as the pure destroyer of faults, healer where doctors fail and lord of yoga. Shiva told him not to grieve. The head Shiva cut off in the Varaha age had become this imperishable four-faced linga, and by setting up lingas here Brahma would be freed of sin. Shiva then recalled the past. When Brahma first asked Shiva to create, Shiva sank into the water at Sannihita for long penance. Tired of waiting, Brahma made another creator in his mind, who made Daksha and the lords of creatures. The hungry new beings tried to eat their creator, so Brahma fixed their food: plants for the moving creatures, and the weak for the strong. When Shiva rose from the water and saw beings created by another, he angrily tore off his linga and threw it. It stood upright in the lake, and so it is called Sthanu (the standing one). One sight of it gives freedom from which there is no return, and staying there on the dark eighth frees one from the sin of union with forbidden women. Shiva vanished, and Brahma, cleansed, set up four lingas: the first, Brahmasaras, beside Hari; the second, Brahmasadana, in his hermitage; a third east of it; and a fourth on the Sarasvati bank. They are to be worshipped in the Krita, Treta, Dvapara and Kali ages in turn. Worship of the Chaturmukha linga, and of Shankara in Brahma's hermitage, frees one from various sins of mixing, of mixed classes and of forbidden food. In the Kali age Brahma also set up a four-faced linga at Vasishtha's hermitage. Here the section on the greatness of the lake ends.

01-050.json.summary: In Pulastya's account to Narada, the god of gods (Murari, Vishnu) tells the gods that Prithudaka is holy and removes the fear of sin. When the Moon, the Sun and Jupiter (Brihaspati) stand together in the constellation Mrigashira, that lunar day is holy and is called Akshaya (imperishable). He tells them to go where the Sarasvati flows east and worship the ancestors there with the rite for the dead (shraddha). The gods with Indra go to Prithudaka in Kurukshetra, bathe, and urge Brihaspati to enter Mrigashira and make the holy day, since the Sun and Moon are already there. Brihaspati says he will go if he becomes lord of the year. On the new-moon day of Ashadha, in Mrigashira, Indra offers rice balls (pinda) of pure food with sesame and honey to the ancestors with devotion. The pleased ancestors give their own daughter Mena, and the gods give her to the snowy mountain Himavat. Himavat is happy with her, and she bears three daughters of great beauty.

01-051.json.summary: Pulastya tells Narada that Mena had three daughters and a son, Sunabha. The daughters were the red Ragini, the fair Kutila and the dark, matchless Kali. After their sixth year the girls went to do penance. The gods took Kutila to Brahma and asked if she would bear the killer of the demon Mahisha. Brahma said she could not hold Shiva's seed. She angrily vowed to win that power by penance to Vishnu, so Brahma cursed her to become water. She flooded his world, and he bound her with the words of the four Vedas, so she flows as water over his matted hair. Ragini made the same vow and was cursed to become the red twilight (Sandhya). When Mena tried to stop the third girl, saying "U ma" ("oh, don't"), the girl got the name Uma. Uma did hard penance fixed on Shiva, and her brightness drove the gods back; Brahma said she must be Shiva's beloved and that Mahisha and Taraka were as good as dead. Himavat brought her home. Shiva, keeping a vow of having no shelter, came to Himavat and was asked to stay there for his penance. Kali came to him with her friends and bowed, but after a long look he said "this is not fitting" and vanished. Grieved, she began fierce penance, made a clay image of Shiva and worshipped it. Pleased, Shiva came to her hermitage disguised as a young Brahmin student. He listed the holy places where he had bathed, and asked why so young and rich a girl had given up ornaments for matted hair and bark clothes. Her friend Somaprabha said she wanted Hara as husband. The student laughed: how could her soft hand meet his snake-covered hand, her silk his lion skin, her sandal paste his ashes? Parvati replied that whatever Hara is, kind or terrible, rich or poor, he will be her lord, and that one who listens to blame is as sinful as the one who speaks it. She rose to leave. Shiva then showed his true form, told her to go home and promised to send great sages to ask for her. He said her clay image would be worshipped as Bhadreshvara. He bathed at Prithudaka and went to Mount Mandara, where the mountain worshipped him.

01-052.json.summary: Pulastya continues to Narada. On Mandara, Shiva calls the seven sages and Arundhati. He tells them that Sati, Daksha's daughter, who gave up her life because of Daksha's anger, is born again as Uma, and asks them to request her from Himavat. Arundhati goes too, since married women know the customs among women. At Himavat's golden city they are announced by the doorkeeper mountain Gandhamadana. Himavat honours them and offers himself and his family as their servants. The sages ask old Angiras to speak, and he says that Shankara, destroyer of Daksha's sacrifice, has sent them to ask for Kali. Blessed is the father whose daughter gets such a husband, and she will be mother of all beings. Kali lowers her face, first joyful and then shy. Himavat calls Meru, Vindhya, Kailasa and the other mountains, and Mena with her son. He says he will not give his daughter without his kin's advice. All the mountains say the groom is welcome. Mena adds that the ancestors gave her for this very purpose: her son by Shiva will kill Mahisha and Taraka. Himavat tells his daughter she is given to Sharva, and Arundhati comforts the shy girl on her lap. The sages fix the wedding for the third day, when the Moon joins Uttara Phalguni at the hour called Maitra. They return to Shiva on Mandara with the news, and he honours them with Arundhati. Brahma, Vishnu, Indra and the Sun come to see Shiva, and Nandi and the attendants gather around him.

01-053.json.summary: Pulastya tells Narada about the wedding. Shiva greets Hari, Brahma, Indra and the gods and goes to Kailasa, where Aditi and other goddesses adorn him with a crest of bones, snake earrings and bracelets, and a lion skin. He sets out on his bull with Vishnu on Garuda, Brahma on his swan, and Indra holding a white umbrella. The rivers Yamuna and Sarasvati carry fly-whisks, the six seasons bring flowers, and gandharvas, apsaras, crores of Rudras, Adityas, Vasus, attendants and sages follow him. The mountains greet him at Himavat's city. The city women rush out half-dressed and half-adorned to see him, and the palace women praise him as the one who made Kama bodiless. He climbs the wedding altar. Parvati, dressed in white silk and brought by her brother Sunabha, sits with him, and the couple play wedding games with scented water, powders, pearls and vermilion. Himavat brings the honey-mixture (madhuparka) and gives Kali's hand to Shiva. Shiva replies that he has no mother, father or kin and lives without shelter on mountain peaks, but accepts the daughter. At his touch she feels great joy. Brahma tells her to look at her husband's face and walk around the fire. Seeing it, she is cooled like scorched earth after rain. They walk three times around the fire and offer rice puffs (laja). Malini catches Shiva's foot to claim a gift and asks good fortune for her friend; Shiva grants it, saying this fortune belongs to Vishnu. Meanwhile Brahma sees Kali's face, spills his seed and hides it in the sand. Shiva tells him not to kill Brahmins, and 88,000 sages, the Valakhilyas, rise from it. After the wedding night, Shiva returns with Parvati to Mandara and sends the gods home.

01-054.json.summary: Pulastya continues. Vishvakarma builds Shiva a vast golden house on Mandara, where he lives as a householder with Parvati. Once Shiva jokingly calls her "Kali" (the dark one). Hurt, she says wounds from harsh words never heal, and leaves to do penance so that he will not call her that again. A tiger waits nearby for her to fall while she stands on one foot, staring at her face. After a hundred years Brahma comes. At her request he first makes the tiger a leader of Shiva's attendants, then gives her a golden skin. She sheds her black sheath (kosha), and from it Katyayani is born. Indra takes this goddess as his sister Kaushiki, leaves her on the Vindhya mountain as Vindhyavasini with a lion as mount, and tells her to kill the gods' enemies. Back on Mandara, Shiva and Parvati remain in love-union for a thousand years until the worlds shake. Fearing that their child will take Indra's place, Indra and the gods send Agni. Agni enters in the form of a swan past the doorkeeper Nandi and calls Shiva out. The gods ask him to stop the union. Shiva agrees but says someone must receive his stirred seed, and Agni drinks it. Learning this, Parvati curses the gods to have no sons by their own wives. In her bath, while Malini rubs fragrant paste on her, Parvati makes from the dirt of her body a four-armed, elephant-faced man and puts him on the ground. Later Shiva bathes on the same seat. His sweat and Uma's, mixed with water and ash, touch the figure, and it comes alive. Shiva shows Parvati her son and names him Vinayaka, because he was born without a husband (nayaka). He says the boy will create thousands of obstacles and be worshipped by all, and gives him the attendant Ghatodara, the Mothers and the spirits who cause obstacles. Pulastya ends: this goddess also became Katyayani, who killed Shumbha and Nishumbha.

01-055.json.summary: Pulastya tells Narada about Shumbha and Nishumbha, sons of Danu, and their brother Namuchi. Indra gave Namuchi a boon that no weapon could kill him, then hid his thunderbolt in sea foam and killed him as Namuchi rubbed the foam on his face. Indra was freed of the sin of killing a Brahmin by bathing at a holy place. The angry brothers defeated the gods, took their treasures and ruled the three worlds. Raktabija, minister of Mahisha, told them the Goddess had killed Mahisha in the Vindhya, and Chanda and Munda came out of hiding in the Narmada. Chanda said the jewel-like Goddess should go to Shumbha, the master. Shumbha's messenger Sugriva reported her reply: she has foolishly vowed to marry only the one who defeats her in battle. Shumbha sent Dhumralochana to drag her by the hair, and Kaushiki burned him and his army to ash with the sound "hum". Chanda, Munda and Ruru came next. Her lion tore the army apart, and from the Goddess's angry brow came Kali, terrible, with a skull-staff and sword, who ate elephants, chariots and men. Ruru was killed and skinned. A lock of hair the Goddess tore out became a fierce half-black, half-white goddess named Chandamari, who chased Chanda and Munda on a donkey, carrying the horn of Yama's buffalo. She took Garuda's fallen feathers and the serpent Karkotaka, bound the two demons with the serpent and brought them to Kaushiki. The demons were beheaded, a crest was made of their heads, and the goddess who wore it was named Chamunda. She then destroyed more of the enemy army, and the surviving demons fled to Shumbha.

01-056.json.summary: Pulastya continues. Shumbha sends Raktabija with a huge army. As Chandika roars, the Mothers come out of her body: Brahmani from her mouth on a swan, Maheshvari on a bull, Kaumari on a peacock, Vaishnavi on Garuda, Varahi on the serpent Shesha, Mahendri on an elephant and the clawed Narasimhi from her heart. Shiva comes and offers help, and the Goddess sends him as messenger: the demons must return heaven to Indra and go to the underworld, or fight. So she is called Shivaduti. The demons attack, and the Goddess and Mothers kill them with many weapons. When Raktabija comes, every drop of his blood that falls becomes a new demon. Kaushiki tells Chamunda to open her mouth wide from sky to earth. She throws Raktabija in, pierces him with the trident so that the new demons fall into the mouth too, and when his blood dries up she cuts him to pieces with her discus. Nishumbha attacks with a sword but freezes at the sight of her beauty. He says she is too delicate to strike and should become his wife. She laughs and says only one who defeats her in battle may marry her. She cuts his sword, shield, club and arms, and he falls. Shumbha charges on an elephant, and she cuts the elephant's legs and then his head. The gods praise her as the eighteen-armed slayer of Mahisha, Shumbha and Nishumbha, in all her forms as the Mothers. She promises that reciting their hymn ends bad dreams. At their request she promises to return: as Charchika, born from the sweat of Shiva's face, linked with the demon Andhaka; as Yashoda's daughter in Nanda's house, to kill Viprachitti and others; as Shakambhari, to feed the gods in the Kali age; in the Vindhya, to protect the sages; and as a great bee, to kill the demon Arunaksha. She then departs to the sky.

01-057.json.summary: Narada asks how Skanda split the Krauncha mountain with Mahisha. Pulastya tells the story. Agni, weakened by Shiva's seed, which he had carried for five thousand years and which turned his whole body to gold (so he is called Hiranyareta), passed it to the river goddess Kutila. She carried it for five thousand years, and Brahma told her to leave it in the great reed forest (shara-vana) on the Udaya mountain. After ten thousand years a boy bright as the rising sun was born there, and the forest turned golden. The six Krittikas found him crying and quarrelled over who would nurse him. He grew six faces to drink from all of them, and became known as Kartikeya. Agni and Kutila both claimed him. Vishnu sent them to Shiva, and Parvati proposed that the child be the son of whoever he went to. At the reed forest the child split into four: Kumara went to Shiva, Vishakha to Gauri, Shakha to Kutila and Mahasena to Agni. Shiva named him Kartikeya for the Krittikas, Kumara for Kutila, Skanda for Gauri, Guha for himself, Mahasena for Agni, Sharadvata for the reed forest, and Shanmukha (six-faced). The gods took him to the holy place Aujasa on the Sarasvati in Kurukshetra and consecrated him as their general, to kill Mahisha and Taraka, with water of the seas and rivers. Parvati held him lovingly. Shiva gave him four attendants (Ghantakarna, Lohitaksha, Nandisena and Kumudamalin), and the gods, mountains, sea, serpents, rivers, sages and holy places all gave more attendants and many Mothers (matris), listed by name. Garuda gave the peacock, Aruna a cock, Agni a spear, Parvati clothes, Brihaspati a staff, Kutila a water pot, Vishnu a garland, Shiva a banner and Indra a necklace. Surrounded by attendants and Mothers, on his peacock with spear in hand, Skanda shone like the sun.

01-058.json.summary: Pulastya continues. Skanda bows to his parents and the gods and asks leave to fight. Uma tells him to bow to Vishnu, saying Shiva had told her none is higher. Vishnu then gives Skanda a blessing for safety (svastyayana), which Pulastya recites at Narada's request. It asks the gods, planets, sages, spirits and holy places to protect him, places a guardian over each direction, and asks Varaha, Narasimha and Madhava to guard him everywhere. Skanda flies off with his attendants and the Mothers and lands with a roar that reaches the underworld. The demon Patalaketu arrives wounded, telling Andhaka that an unknown archer chased him from Galava's hermitage and that he saw strange warriors vowing to kill Mahisha and Taraka. Without telling Andhaka, Mahisha, Taraka and Bana go up to fight. Skanda's attendants and the Mothers destroy the demon army in many ways. The attendant Suchakraksha's discus nearly kills Mahisha, but Bana binds Suchakraksha with his five hundred arms until Makaraksha strikes Bana free. Taraka routs the attendants with his sword, and Skanda kills him with his spear. Mahisha flees and hides in a cave of the Krauncha mountain. Skanda will not kill Krauncha, his mother's brother's son, quoting the old rule that a cow, a Brahmin, an old man, a child, a kinsman, an innocent woman and one's teachers must never be killed. Indra replies that one may kill one for the sake of many, as he himself killed his brother Namuchi. They quarrel over who is stronger and race around the mountain. When Krauncha says Indra finished first, Skanda angrily splits the mountain with his spear, killing Mahisha with it. Vishnu stops Skanda from also killing Sunabha, Krauncha's father, and takes Skanda to heaven. Skanda regrets killing his cousin. Vishnu sends him to bathe at Prithudaka in the Oghavati and see Shiva, which restores his brightness. Suchakraksha does penance, and Shiva grants that his discus will one day cut off Bana's arms. Hearing this story removes sin and increases merit.

01-059.json.summary: Narada asks who shot the demon lord (Patalaketu) who had been struck by an arrow while the demons were holding council. Pulastya says it was Ritadhvaja, a great-souled prince of the Raghu line, brave, strong and kind alike to Brahmins, the blind, the poor and the wretched; riding a horse for the sake of the sage Galava, he struck Patalaketu in the back with a half-moon arrow.
