Galava was doing penance in his hermitage and Patalaketu kept breaking his meditation out of folly. Galava could have burnt him to ashes but did not want to spend his penance, so he looked at the sky and sighed. A fine horse fell from the sky and a voice without a body said it could cover a thousand leagues in a day. Galava gave the horse to Ritadhvaja, who took up weapons and pierced the demon with arrows. Pulastya explains that the horse was sent by Vishvavasu, king of the Gandharvas and singer of Indra. His daughter Madalasa, the most beautiful woman in the three worlds, had been carried off by Patalaketu when he saw her playing in the Nandana garden; after killing the demon the prince won her and lived with her as Indra lives with Shachi. Narada then asks what Andhaka, son of Hiranyaksha, did after Mahisha and Taraka were killed. Angry, Andhaka left the underworld with a small following and a club and roamed the earth. On Mount Mandara he saw Gauri (Parvati) among her friends and was struck with desire; he said life and beauty were worthless unless she was his, and that whoever brought her to him would be his true friend. Prahlada covered his ears, shook his head and told him she was the mother of the world and wife of Shiva, and that taking another man's wife ruins a family and sends one to the underworld. He quoted a verse sung by King Gadhi: better to give up life than enjoy slander, better to keep silent than speak a lie, better to be impotent than go to another's wife, better to beg than keep enjoying another's wealth. Blind with anger and desire, Andhaka cried "This is the mother of my enemies" and ran at her. The demons followed, but Nandi, thunderbolt in hand, stopped them; Maya, Tara and the rest were struck and fled in all directions. Andhaka knocked Nandi down with his club. In fear Gauri became a hundred forms, and Andhaka wandered among them like a rutting elephant among cow elephants, unable to tell which was the mountain's daughter, for the text says four do not see: the born-blind, the blind with passion, the drunk with pride and the greedy. Thinking they were young women he did not strike them, and the hundred goddesses beat him with fine weapons until he fell. The goddess then vanished. The demon chiefs rushed back shouting, but Nandi stood ready with his thunderbolt. Nandi came to Ambika and bowed at her feet. She told her own hundred forms to go where they wished, roam the earth worshipped by men and live in gardens, forests and trees; they bowed and went to all the quarters, praised by Kinnaras. Andhaka came to his senses, did not see the goddess, saw his army beaten and fled to the underworld, where, struck by Kama's arrows and thinking of Gauri, he neither ate by day nor slept by night.

01-060.json.summary: Narada asks where Shiva was while Ambika and Nandi fought Andhaka. Pulastya says that after Shiva had stayed for a thousand years in great delusion (of love), he looked without lustre and weak. Seeing this, he decided to do penance. He took up the great vow, comforted Ambika, left Nandi as guard and wandered the earth, with a great seal on his neck, great snakes as earrings, a belt of great conch shells round his waist, a skull in his right hand and a water pot in his left, staying only one day under any tree and roaming mountain slopes and rivers. For nine hundred years he lived on roots, then water, then air. Then he put a ball (vita) in his mouth and stopped breathing on a broad flat rock on the Himalaya. The ball split his skull and came out shining from his matted hair and fell to the earth; the mountain it struck was split and levelled, and there arose the holy place called Kedara. Shiva gave Kedara a boon: men of self-control who drink its water and for six months avoid food cooked by others will surely have his linga in their heart-lotus and never take pleasure in sin; offerings to the ancestors there will be endless; bathing, giving, penance, fire offerings and prayer there will give endless fruit, and those who die there will not be born again. Shiva then bathed in the Yamuna (Kalindi), daughter of the sun, and then went to the Sarasvati, which rises at the Plaksha tree and is surrounded by a hundred holy places. He went under the water and recited the Gayatri called Drupada; he stayed under for more than a year. Then the seven worlds and oceans shook, stars fell, the gods led by Indra were shaken from their seats and the great sages prayed for the well-being of the worlds. The gods went to Brahma, who said he did not know the cause and led them to the home of Murari, the bearer of discus and mace. Narada asks who Murari is, and then asks whose son Mura was and how Vishnu killed him. Pulastya begins the story. Mura saw the sons of Diti slain in battle by the gods. Afraid of death, he did penance for many years and pleased Brahma, and asked the boon that anyone he touched with his palm in battle, even an immortal, would die; Brahma agreed. Mura went to Mount Meru and challenged gods, Yakshas and Kinnaras, but no one would fight him. He went to Amaravati and challenged Indra, who would not fight, and when Mura raised his hand and entered the city no one could stop him. He told Indra to fight or leave heaven. Indra gave up his kingdom and lived on earth; his elephant and thunderbolt were taken, and with his wife, son and the gods he built a city on the south bank of the Yamuna, while Mura enjoyed heaven with Maya, Tara and other fierce demons. Once Mura came alone on an elephant to the Sarayu river, where King Raghu of the solar line was consecrated for a sacrifice, and demanded that Raghu fight him or stop the sacrifice. The sage Vasishtha told him there was no point in beating men; he should conquer Yama (Death), who did not obey him, and then the whole earth would be his. Mura went to conquer Yama. Yama, knowing Mura could not be killed in battle, rode his buffalo to Vishnu (Keshava) and told him; Vishnu told him to go back and send Mura to him. Mura reached Yama's city and threatened to cut off Yama's head unless he stopped restraining (taking) living beings. Yama said he would obey if Mura protected him from his own controller. Asked who that was, Yama said it was Vishnu, who lives in Shvetadvipa, and sent Mura to the Ocean of Milk. Mura said he would go, but that meanwhile Yama must not take men; Yama said that he would keep to his work and Mura should go fight his controller. Mura went to the Ocean of Milk, where Janardana in four forms lies on the couch of Shesha. Narada asks how Vishnu, one, all-pervading and unmanifest, can have four forms. Pulastya says the unmanifest supreme state called Vasudeva, beyond reasoning and description, white and calm, is known as having twelve petals. Asked what these are, Pulastya says he will tell a secret told by Brahma to Sanatkumara, who told it to him. Narada asks who Sanatkumara is. Pulastya says Dharma's wife Ahimsa bore four sons who studied yoga: Sanatkumara the eldest, Sanatana, Sanaka and Sanandana. They saw the Sankhya teacher Kapila, Asuri and the great yogi Panchashikha; though elder, they served these younger teachers without pride, but did not get the knowledge of yoga from them. Sanatkumara went to Brahma and asked for the knowledge of yoga. Brahma said he would teach it only if Sanatkumara would be his son, for it may not be told to just anyone. Sanatkumara said a pupil is the same as a son. Brahma said there is a difference: the son (putra) is so called because he saves from the hell named Put, while the pupil takes away the remaining sin, as the Veda says. Asked what this hell is and what remaining sin a pupil removes, Brahma begins to explain.

01-061.json.summary: Brahma continues to Sanatkumara. He lists the sins that make up the hell called Put in seventeen groups, for example: going to another's wife or the king's wife and keeping company with sinners; stealing fruit, vehicles, scriptures or the king's share and cutting trees; killing or binding the innocent, killing a child, treachery to friends and false curses; harming, robbing or abusing Brahmins and quarrelling with kin; falling from one's own duty, destroying good conduct and lacking the sacraments; greed, envy, impurity, lying, laziness, violence and setting houses on fire. A man stained by these sins who pleases the Lord of the world by having offspring is freed from them, and this terrible hell Put is destroyed; that is why a son is called putra. Then Brahma lists the remaining sins, such as unpaid debts to gods, sages, beings, men and ancestors, eating fish, going to forbidden women, selling ghee, accepting gifts from Chandalas, hiding one's own faults and exposing others', jealousy, foul speech and cruelty. If a man with these sins pleases Shankara through a pupil richer in knowledge, he overcomes all the remaining sin. Sins of body, speech and mind, and those done in that life by father, mother, dependants, brothers and kin, are all destroyed; this is the merit of son and pupil, and if they are bad the result is reversed. So a wise man should have both a son and a pupil; the son is better than the pupil, since the pupil saves from the remaining sin but the son saves in every way. Sanatkumara swore three times that he was Brahma's son. Brahma said that only if his parents gave him would he be Brahma's heir (dayada). Asked to explain heirs, Brahma said there are six kinds of sons who are heirs and kin: the natural son (aurasa), the son of the wife by another man (kshetraja), the son given (datta), the son made (kritrima), the son born in secret (gudhotpanna) and the son abandoned and taken in (apaviddha); these share debts, ancestor offerings and wealth, the same clan and lasting standing in the family. Six others are kin but not heirs and only carry the name, not the clan: the son of an unmarried girl (kanina), the son of a bride already pregnant at marriage (sahodha), the son bought (krita), the son of a remarried woman (paunarbhava), the son who gives himself (svayamdatta) and the son of a Brahmin by a Shudra woman, married or not (parashava). He defines each: the natural son is like one's own reflection; the kshetraja is born to an unafflicted wife on her husband's order when he is impotent, mad or ruined; the datta is given by his parents; the kritrima is a friend's son given by the friend; the gudha is born in the house of an unknown father; the apaviddha is brought in from outside; the paunarbhava is born of a girl given to one man, taken away and given to another; the svayamdatta gives himself up in famine or distress or for other reasons. So Sanatkumara could not give himself and must call his parents. He thought of them, and Dharma and Ahimsa came, bowed to Brahma and sat. Sanatkumara told his father he wished to learn yoga and Brahma wanted him as a son, so they should give him; they said he was now Brahma's son and left. Brahma then taught his son the twelve-petalled yoga. Each petal joins a syllable of the mantra "om namo bhagavate vasudevaya" with a body part, a zodiac sign and a month: om at the top-knot with Aries on the head and Vaishakha; na at the mouth with Taurus and Jyeshtha; mo at the two arms with Gemini and Ashadha; bha at the eyes with Cancer and Shravana; ga at the heart with Leo and Bhadrapada; va as armour with Virgo and Ashvina; te as the weapons with Libra and Kartika; va at the navel with Scorpio and Margashirsha; su at the hips with Sagittarius and Pausha; de at the thighs with Capricorn and Magha; va at the knees with Aquarius and Phalguna; and ya at the feet with Pisces and Chaitra. So the Lord is a twelve-spoked wheel with six naves, three arrays and one form; one who knows this twelve-petalled form does not die again. The second form is full of goodness (sattva), four-coloured, four-faced, four-armed, noble, bearing the Shrivatsa mark. The third, of darkness (tamas), is Shesha, with a thousand feet and faces, who brings the dissolution of beings. The fourth, of passion (rajas), is red, four-faced, two-armed, holds a garland and creates; from the unmanifest come these three manifest forms, and from them Marichi and thousands of others. Pulastya returns to Mura: sent by Yama's words, the wicked Mura came to the four-armed Vishnu. Vishnu asked why he had come; Mura said to fight. Vishnu said, "If you have come to fight me, why does your heart keep shaking like a man with fever? I will not fight a coward." Mura, his mind confused, put his own hand on his heart, saying "How? Where? Whose?" Then Hari lightly threw his discus and cut the enemy's heart-lotus. The gods were freed from distress and praised Padmanabha. Because he killed Mura by this clever means, the discus-bearing Lord became famous as Murari.

01-062.json.summary: Pulastya goes on with the story of chapter 60. The gods reached Murari's home, bowed and told him the world was shaken. Vishnu said they should go to Shiva's home, for he would know why. Led by Janardana they went to Mount Mandara, but saw neither Shiva, his bull, the goddess nor Nandi; the mountain seemed empty to them, covered by the darkness of ignorance. Vishnu asked why they did not see Shiva standing before them. When they said they could not, he told them they had offended the god: they were very sinful, had destroyed the embryo of Mridani (Parvati) for their own ends, and so Shiva had taken away their power of discernment. To purify their bodies and see the god they must do the hot penance (taptakrichchhra) and then bathe the god: with milk, curds, ghee, the five cow products, honey and water in set numbers of jars (all doubled), then anoint him with gorochana, saffron and sandal, worship him with bilva leaves, lotuses, datura, mandara, parijata and atimukta flowers, burn aloe wood and kaleya incense, and recite the Shatarudriya hymn. Asked about the hot penance, Vishnu said: for three days drink hot water, for three days hot milk, for three days hot ghee, and for three days live on air; daily twelve palas of water, eight of milk and six of ghee. The gods did it and were freed from sin. When they asked where Shiva was, Vishnu said he was in Vishnu's own body; they still could not see him, so Vishnu showed them the linga of Shiva lying in the lotus of his own heart. The gods bathed the linga in order with milk and the rest, anointed it, worshipped it, offered incense and herbs, recited the hundred and eight names and bowed. As they wondered how Hari and Shiva, arising from goodness and from darkness, could be joined as one, the Lord became the form of all, Hari-Shankara: three-eyed, with lotus and snake earrings, matted hair and curls, Garuda and bull on his banner, a necklace of snakes on his chest, a yellow garment and a deer skin round his waist, holding discus, sword, plough, the Sharnga and Ajagava bows, the Pinaka, trident, skull-staff, skull, bell and conch. The gods led by Brahma bowed to him, "Hail to you, all-pervading, undecaying", and fixed their minds on him as one. Then Hari took them quickly to his own hermitage at Kurukshetra, where they saw Shiva standing still like a post (sthanu) in the water; they said "Hail to Sthanu" and sat down. Indra called on him to rise, give a boon and stop the shaking of the world. Shiva heard, rose quickly, laughed and greeted all the gods, and when they asked him to give up his great vow because the three worlds were shaken by his power, he said he had given it up. The gods went happily to heaven. But the earth still shook. Shiva went round Kurukshetra and found Ushanas (Shukra) doing penance on the bank of the Oghavati. Shukra said he was doing it to please Shiva and learn the life-giving knowledge (sanjivani vidya); Shiva, pleased, granted it, and Shukra stopped. Still the earth shook. Shiva went to Saptasarasvata and found the sage Mankanaka dancing wildly like a child with his arms spread; the earth and mountains shook from the force of his dance. Shiva took his hand and asked why he danced. Mankanaka said that after many years of penance to dry his body, he had seen vegetable sap flowing from a cut on his hand, and this made him so glad that he danced. Shiva showed him very white ash flowing from his own finger when struck, and said he felt no such pride, so the sage was surely deluded. Amazed, Mankanaka stopped dancing and bowed at his feet. Shiva told him to go to the hard-to-reach world of Brahma, and declared that this holy place would equal Prithudaka in merit, would always have the presence of gods, demons, Gandharvas, Vidyadharas and Kinnaras, and would wash away sin. Seven Sarasvatis would always live there: Suprabha, Kanchanakshi, Suvenu, Vimalodaka, Manohara, Oghavati and Vishala, all giving the fruit of the Soma sacrifice. Mankanaka set up an image at Kurukshetra and went to Brahma's world, and the earth became still. Shiva returned to Mandara. Pulastya ends by saying this is why Shiva was away doing penance and returned to find the mountain empty when the goddess had fought Andhaka.

01-063.json.summary: Narada asks what Andhaka did in the underworld and what Shiva did on Mandara. Pulastya says Andhaka, burning with desire, told the demons that whoever brought him the mountain's daughter would be his friend, kin, brother and father. Prahlada answered in a voice like thunder that by dharma she was his mother and the three-eyed Shiva his father. Long ago Andhaka's father (Hiranyaksha), childless and righteous, worshipped Shiva for a son. Shiva gave him Andhaka, saying: once in play Uma covered my three eyes while I was in yoga, and blind darkness arose, and from it was born this being, dark as a cloud, with a voice like thunder; take him as a fitting son; when he does evil hated by the world, desires the mother of the three worlds, or kills a Brahmin, I myself will purify his body. So Parvati is his mother and Shiva his father. Prahlada said a man of his penance and learning should not think such a sin; Shiva cannot be conquered, and one who could swim the ocean with his arms, pull down the sun or uproot Meru might conquer him, but these things cannot be done. He then told the story of King Danda, who desired another's wife and was destroyed with his kingdom. Danda, a strong king of the Ikshvaku line, took Shukra (Bhargava) as his family priest and performed many sacrifices. Shukra had a daughter named Araja. Once Shukra went to the demon Vrishaparvan to perform a sacrifice, and Araja stayed home tending the sacred fire. Danda came, learned that Shukra was away and his daughter was in the hermitage, went in and saw her, and at once, driven by fate, burned with desire. He sent away his servants, brothers, friends and Shukra's pupils and came to her alone. She welcomed him as a brother. He asked her to cool his fire of desire with her embrace. She warned him that her angry father could burn even the gods, that he was her brother by dharma and her father's pupil, and that he should ask her father, who would surely give her; women are not free to give themselves. Danda said he could not wait. He told her the story of Chitrangada, daughter of Vishvakarma, who went with friends to bathe at Naimisha; Prince Suratha, son of Sudeva, saw her and was struck with love; her friends told her she was not free to give herself while her father lived, but she gave herself to him anyway and so saved him. Araja replied with what followed: her father cursed Chitrangada, for giving herself up by her own will, never to be married, never to have joy, sons or union with a husband. At once the river Sarasvati carried the king away thirteen leagues, and she fainted. Her friends sprinkled her with water, thought she was dead and went to fetch wood and fire; she woke, saw no one, and threw herself into the Sarasvati; the Kanchanakshi river carried her into the Gomati, and the Gomati threw her into a great forest full of lions and tigers. So Araja would not give herself, guarding her virtue. Danda laughed and told her to hear what happened next to Chitrangada, her father and Suratha. In the forest the Guhyaka Anjana, flying through the sky, comforted her, said she would surely be joined with Suratha, and told her to go to the god Shrikantha. She went to Shrikantha on the south bank of the Yamuna, bathed and stood until midday. The Pashupata teacher Ritadhvaja, a Sama Veda sage, came to bathe, saw her, asked who she was, and when she told him everything he grew angry and cursed Vishvakarma to become a monkey, because he had kept his own daughter, who was meant to be given to another, from her husband. He then bathed, did the evening worship of Shiva, and told her to go to Saptagodavara and worship Shiva as Hatakeshvara; there Devavati, daughter of the demon Kandaramalin, Nandayanti, daughter of the Guhyaka Anjana, and Vedavati, daughter of Parjanya, would come, and when the three met there she would be joined with her husband. Chitrangada went there and lived purely on fruit and roots, worshipping Shiva. The sage wrote a verse on the temple of Shrikantha: "There is no god, demon, Yaksha, man or night-walker who by his own strength can wipe away the sorrow of this fawn-eyed girl." He then went to see the Lord of Pushkara and the river Payoshni.

01-064.json.summary: King Danda goes on telling Araja the story (within Prahlada's words to Andhaka). Chitrangada lived a long time at Saptagodavara, thinking of Suratha. Vishvakarma, cursed by the sage, became a monkey, fell from the peak of Meru and lived for many years on fruit and roots on the mountain Shalveya near the Shalukini river. One day the demon Kandara came there with his daughter Devavati; the monkey seized her by the hand. Kandara ran at him with a sword, and the monkey carried her to the Himalaya, saw the god Shrikantha on the Yamuna bank, left her in an empty hermitage nearby, and plunged into the Yamuna while the demon watched. Kandara thought his daughter had died with the monkey and went back to the underworld. The Yamuna carried the monkey to a land called Shiva. Swimming back towards the mountain where he had left the girl, he saw the Guhyaka Anjana coming with his daughter Nandayanti, took her for Devavati and ran at her; in fear she jumped into the Hiranvati river. Her grieving father went to Mount Anjana and did penance in silence for many years. The Hiranvati carried Nandayanti to the holy land of Kosala. Weeping, she rested under a banyan tree and heard a voice say: "Is there no one to tell that ascetic how his son is tied up in the banyan tree?" Looking round, she saw a five-year-old boy tied by his tawny matted hair at the top of the tree. He told her a monkey had tied him and he lived by the power of penance. His father was the great ascetic Ritadhvaja, at the shrine of Shiva at Unmattapura; he was born while his father was reciting the great yoga, and was named Jabali. His father foretold: he would be a child for five thousand years, a youth for ten thousand, a young man for twenty thousand and then twice that in vigour; as a child for five hundred years he would suffer hard bondage, in youth a thousand years of bodily pain, then two thousand years of great pleasures, and in old age four thousand years of hardship, sleeping on the ground and eating poor food. Going to bathe in the Hiranvati, he met the monkey, who said "Where are you going, fool? Take this Devavati left in the great hermitage", seized him, tied him by his hair to the top of the tree, and guarded it with a net of creepers on every side, above and below, which could not be broken, and went to the mountain of the gods. Nandayanti told him she was the daughter of the Guhyaka king Anjana and the nymph Pramlocha; at her birth the sage Mudgala said she would surely be the chief queen of a king, but would face great danger while a maiden; the drums of the gods sounded and a jackal howled an ill omen. Her father was taking her to a holy place when the monkey leapt from the Hiranvati bank and she threw herself into the river. Jabali told her to go to Shrikantha on the Yamuna, where his father came at midday to worship Shiva, and to tell him her story. She went there living on roots and fruit, bowed to Shrikantha, read the verse written there, understood it, and wrote Jabali's verse and her own: "Mudgala said I would be a king's wife, yet I have come to this state; may some lord save me." Going to bathe in the Yamuna she found a fine hermitage and inside it Devavati, dry-mouthed and faded; the two embraced, told each other their stories and sat talking. Meanwhile the sage Ritadhvaja came to bathe at Shrikantha, read the writing, understood by meditation what had happened, worshipped Shiva and hurried to Ayodhya to see the Ikshvaku king. He told him that his own learned son was tied up by a monkey at the edge of the king's land and only the king's son Shakuni, a master of weapons, could free him. Danda says that his father then sent his dear son Shakuni, Danda's own strong brother, with the sage. At the tall banyan Shakuni saw the boy and the nets of creepers on all sides, strung his bow and with skill cut all the creeper nets with arrows without harming the boy; five hundred years of the boy's bondage had by then passed. The sage climbed the tree; Jabali, still bound, bowed his head to his father, who embraced him and smelt his head, but could not untie him. Shakuni put down his bow and climbed up, but could not untie the hair either, for the monkey had tied it hard. Both came down; Shakuni made a canopy of arrows, cut the branch into three with half-moon arrows, and Jabali, carrying the branch, came down by a stair of arrows. With his son saved by the prince's archery, Ritadhvaja went with Jabali, still carrying the branch, to the Yamuna.

01-065.json.summary: King Danda goes on telling Araja the story. After Ritadhvaja left, the two girls, Devavati (daughter of the demon) and Nandayanti (daughter of the Yaksha), found the god Shrikantha covered with withered flowers and old offerings, and bathed and worshipped him day and night. The sage Galava came to see Shrikantha, bathed in the Yamuna and worshipped; hearing the girls sing so sweetly he took them for Gandharva girls. They greeted him, and when he asked whose daughters they were they told him the whole truth. He stayed the night, and in the morning said he was going to the Pushkara forest for the holy full moon of Kartika; the girls said they could not stay without him and went with him. Thousands of sages, kings (Nabhaga, Ikshvaku and others) and country people came, all except Ritadhvaja, and bathed at Pushkara on the Kartika full moon. Galava went into the middle, bow-shaped Pushkara with the girls. Under water he saw a great fish being courted again and again by many female fish. The fish told them they did not know dharma, for he could not bear the terrible blame of people. They replied, "Do you not see the ascetic Galava roaming as he likes with two girls? If he does not fear people's blame, why should you, living under water?" The fish said, "That fool, blind with passion, knows no fear." Ashamed, Galava stayed under the water and did not come out, controlling his senses. The girls bathed, came out and waited for him on the bank. The pilgrimage ended and everyone went home. Chitrangada was also there, alone. Then Vedavati, a Gandharva girl, daughter of Parjanya and the nymph Ghritachi, came and bathed in the middle Pushkara and saw the three girls on the two banks. She asked Chitrangada who she was. Chitrangada told her story: daughter of Vishvakarma, she went to bathe in the Sarasvati called Kanchanakshi at Naimisha, where King Suratha of Vidarbha, overcome by love, came to her for refuge; she gave herself to him though her friends tried to stop her, was cursed by her father and parted from the king, was stopped from dying by a Guhyaka, went to Shrikantha and then to Godavara, and came here, but had not found Suratha. Vedavati said that while she was playing in a forest a monkey asked if she was Devavati and who had taken her from the hermitage to Mount Meru; she said she was Vedavati; the monkey chased her, she climbed a tall bandhujiva tree, the monkey broke it with his foot and threw it, with her in it, into the ocean. As the tree fell through the sky all beings cried out, and the Siddhas and Gandharvas said: "Alas, this is the woman Brahma himself named as queen of the great Indradyumna, son of Manu, who has done a thousand sacrifices." Hearing this she fainted; somehow the tree was cut into a thousand pieces, and the wind carried her here. The two went to the girls on the north bank, and all told their stories; the four went to Saptagodavara and stayed there worshipping Hatakeshvara. Meanwhile Shakuni, Jabali and Ritadhvaja wandered many years looking for the girls; after a thousand years Jabali, tired of carrying the branch, went with his father to Shakala. There King Indradyumna, son of Manu, came out with a guest offering and honoured them, and also honoured Shakuni, son of Ikshvaku, as his brother's son. Ritadhvaja asked him to help find the lost girl Nandayanti. The king said he too had lost a fine woman: hearing the Siddhas' words, he had cut a great tree falling from the sky into a thousand pieces with arrows, so skilfully that she was not harmed, but did not know where she went. He gave chariots to the two sages and his nephew. Searching the earth, at the Badari hermitage they found a young ascetic, thin from penance, with dirty matted hair and heavy sighs. Indradyumna asked why he did such hard penance in youth; he was Suratha, who told his story, and Indradyumna, saying "Do not give up your body; you are my brother's son; come, I am going to search for a girl", embraced him and took him in his chariot. Ritadhvaja told Suratha that it was he who had sent Chitrangada to Saptagodavara, and they all set out there. Meanwhile Ghritachi, grieving, searched for her daughter on the Eastern Mountain and asked the monkey; he said he had left Devavati in the hermitage at Shrikantha on the Yamuna; she said her daughter was Vedavati, not Devavati, and they went together along the Kaushiki river. The kings and sages also came to the Kaushiki to bathe. Jabali saw the monkey and told his father this was the one who had tied him. Angry, Shakuni asked leave to kill him with one arrow. The sage, devoted to the good of all beings, said no one is bound or killed by another; binding and killing come from one's past deeds. He asked the monkey to help them; the monkey bowed and asked for orders. Told that Jabali had carried the branch tied to his hair for a thousand years and no man could free him, the monkey gently untied the hair in a moment. Pleased, Ritadhvaja offered him a boon. The monkey said he was Vishvakarma (Tvashtri), father of Chitrangada, made a monkey by the sage's curse, and asked for the curse to end and for the many sins he had done from a monkey's fickleness to be destroyed. Ritadhvaja said the curse would end when he fathered a strong son on Ghritachi. All bathed, worshipped ancestors and gods and went on in their chariots; Ghritachi flew up to the sky, the monkey followed, they saw each other, she knew he was Vishvakarma and desired him, and they made love for a long time on Mount Kolahala and reached the Vindhya. The five men reached Saptagodavara at midday, bathed and let the horses graze; the sound of the hooves brought the girls to the roof of the Hatakeshvara temple. Chitrangada, thrilled, saw the dark, long-armed youth with matted hair and said he must be Suratha, the husband she had chosen, and the golden one with white matted hair must be Ritadhvaja; Nandayanti said the other was his son Jabali. They came down and sang before the god a long hymn of Shiva's names and deeds, ending with "Hatakeshvara, hail to you". The sages and kings came in and saw them. Suratha was thrilled to see his beloved, and Ritadhvaja recognised Chitrangada through yoga. They worshipped Hatakeshvara; Chitrangada and the girls rose and greeted them, and all sat down happily. The monkey came with Ghritachi; mother and daughter (Vedavati) embraced in tears. Ritadhvaja sent the monkey to bring the Guhyaka Anjana from Mount Anjana, the demon Kandaramalin from the underworld and the Gandharva king Parjanya from heaven, and Devavati asked him to bring Galava too. The monkey, swift as the wind, did so, finding Galava near Mahishmati. Galava bathed, came to Hatakeshvara, saw the girls, greeted the sages and was honoured by the kings. The fathers came and their daughters embraced them in tears. Chitrangada, seeing them, wept, and Ritadhvaja told her the monkey was her father. Ashamed, she thought he had become a monkey because of her, a bad daughter, and asked leave to die as one who had killed her father. The sage said what must be cannot be undone; her father would be the gods' builder again when a child was born to Ghritachi. Ghritachi told her that within ten months she would bear a son to her father. Chitrangada was happy and waited to have her father present at her wedding, and all the girls waited for her sake. After ten months Ghritachi gave birth at Godavari to a son, Nala, and Vishvakarma was freed from the monkey form, embraced his daughter and called Indra, who came with the Maruts, Rudras, Gandharvas and nymphs. Indradyumna proposed the marriages: Jabali to Kandaramalin's daughter (Devavati), Shakuni to Nandayanti, himself to Vedavati, and Suratha to Chitrangada; the sage agreed. With Galava as priest making the offerings, while Gandharvas sang and nymphs danced, the weddings were held in that order. Ritadhvaja asked the gods always to stay at Saptagodavara, especially in the month of Vaishakha (Madhava); they agreed and went to heaven, the sages went home with Ritadhvaja and his son, and the kings took their wives to their cities and lived happily. Danda ends: "This is what happened long ago to Chitrangada; so you too should accept me", praising her gently, and she began to answer the king.

01-066.json.summary: Araja tells Danda she will not give herself to him, to protect both herself and him from her father's curse. Prahlada, still speaking to Andhaka, says that while she was arguing, the foolish king, overcome by desire, raped Shukra's daughter by force, and then, blind with lust, left the hermitage and went back to his city. Araja, defiled and covered with dust, came out of the hermitage and stood outside with her face down, weeping and thinking of her father, like Rohini, the moon's beloved, troubled by a great planet. After a long time, the sacrifice finished, Shukra came back from the underworld and saw his daughter outside the hermitage, defiled, like a streak of cloud reddened by twilight. He asked who had violated her and who would go to Yama's city today for playing with an angry snake. Trembling and ashamed, she said quietly that his pupil Danda had taken her by force, though she tried again and again to stop him, while she cried with no one to protect her. Red-eyed with anger, Shukra touched water and said: because that undisciplined man, ignoring my power and respect, has made Araja fall from dharma, within seven nights he, with his kingdom, army, servants and vehicles, will be turned to ash by a rain of stones. He told his daughter to stay there doing penance to be freed from the sin, and went with his pupils to the underworld. Within seven nights Danda and his kingdom were burnt to ash by a great rain of stones. So the gods left that Dandaka forest, and Shiva made it the home of Rakshasas. Prahlada says that other men's wives bring even the virtuous to ruin, and burn ordinary men to ash; so Andhaka must give up this evil idea, for even an ordinary woman can burn a man, let alone the mountain's daughter, and Shiva cannot be conquered or even looked at by gods and demons. Pulastya says Andhaka, angry, red-eyed and hissing, replied: how can the three-eyed one, alone, without dharma, his body smeared with ash, fight me in battle? Andhaka does not fear Indra or the gods; why should he fear one who looks at a woman's face? Prahlada said this was wrong both by dharma and by sense: the gap between Andhaka and Shiva is like that between a moth and fire, a jackal and a lion, a mosquito and an elephant, a stone and gold. He had warned him again and again, and now quoted the divine sage Asita: one who is righteous, free of pride and anger, humble through learning, does not harm others, is content with his own wife and avoids others' wives, has nothing to fear in the world; one who is unrighteous, quarrelsome, harms others, has no learning, wants others' wealth and wives and mixes with lower classes finds no happiness here or hereafter. Manu, son of the sun, was righteous and Agastya was content with his own wife, and such people became full of power, able to curse and bless, and honoured by gods and Siddhas. The son of Anga was unrighteous, Vibhu was always quarrelsome, the wicked Namuchi harmed others, King Nahusha wanted another's wife, Hiranyaksha wanted others' wealth, his foolish younger brother likewise, and mighty Yadu mixed with lower classes; all were destroyed long ago by their wrong conduct. So dharma must never be given up, for it is the highest goal; those without dharma go to the great Raurava hell. Dharma saves in heaven and here, adharma causes a fall in both. Going to another's wife must always be avoided; it leads to twenty-one hells, and this is the fixed dharma of all classes; one who desires another's wealth or wife goes to the Raurava hell for many years. Asita taught this to Aruna, king of birds. Andhaka said Prahlada alone was devoted to dharma; he himself did not follow it. He told Shambara to go to Mandara and say to Shiva: "Beggar, why do you enjoy this heaven-like mountain with its caves? Who gave it to you? The gods led by Indra obey me; why do you live on Mandara without regard for me? If you want the mountain, give me your wife at once." Shambara went and told Shiva exactly this, with Parvati listening. Shiva answered that Mandara had been given to him by Indra, and he could not leave it without Indra's order; as for the demand for Parvati, she could go where she wished, he could not stop her. Parvati told Shambara to tell Andhaka: "I am the prize of battle; you and Shiva are the two players; staking your lives on the game, whoever wins will have me." Shambara told Andhaka. Burning with anger, Andhaka told Duryodhana, his general, to beat the war drum hard. At its terrible sound all the great demons came to the hall; told what had happened, they armed themselves eagerly and set out with Andhaka on elephants, camels, horses and chariots, Andhaka on a chariot five nalvas wide, determined to defeat Shiva. Among them were Jambha, Kujambha, Tuhunda, Shambara, Bali, Bana, Vrishaparvan, Kalanemi, Viprachitti and Duryodhana, and many others with various weapons. So the foolish Andhaka, bound by the noose of death, came to Mount Mandara to fight Shiva.

01-067.json.summary: Pulastya says that when Shambara left, Shiva told Nandi to call the troops (ganas) under his command. Nandi touched water and called the gana leaders to mind; thousands came flying, bowed to Shiva, and Nandi presented them one by one. They included eleven crores of Rudras with three eyes and matted hair, their monkey-faced doorkeepers, crores of six-faced Kumaras (Skandas, Shakhas, Vishakhas, Naigameyas), seven hundred crores of chief Pramathas with as many Mothers, the ash-smeared Shaivas with tridents, countless Pashupatas, the Kalamukhas, the Mahavratins with skull-staffs and red hides, and the naked, silent Nirashrayas. Others with lotus eyes, the Shrivatsa mark on their chests, riding Garuda yet with the bull banner, are the Mahapashupatas, holding discus and trident, who worship Bhairava together with Vishnu as one. The lion-faced ones with tridents, arrows and bows, led by Virabhadra, were born from Shiva's hair. Shiva comforted them all with his hand and made them sit; but when he saw the Mahapashupatas he rose and embraced their leaders. The other gana chiefs were amazed and ashamed. Nandi, smiling, asked Shiva to explain the form, knowledge and insight of these Mahapashupatas. Shiva told the ganas: you worshipped me with devotion, but deluded by pride you abused the state of Vishnu; through that ignorance you did not honour him and opposed him. I am Vishnu and Vishnu is I; there is no difference between us; one form stands in two ways. These devoted ganas know me as I truly am, but you do not, because you always abused me (in Vishnu) with foolish minds; so your knowledge was lost and I did not embrace you. The ganas asked how he, pure, calm, white and stainless, could be one with Janardana, who is dark as collyrium. Laughing in a voice like thunder, Shiva said they were not fit for the great knowledge, but to avoid blame he would reveal the secret. Bathing him with milk and ghee and worshipping him with sandal gives him no pleasure if they do not make their view one; they might as well take a saw and cut his body. Such devotees deserve hell, but he protects them for the sake of his own fame, so that people will not say that Shiva's devotees and ascetics fall into hell; that is why he does not throw them into hell now for abusing the lotus-eyed lord of the world, who is himself. That lord is Sharva, all-pervading, lord of the ganas; nothing in the world is like him; he is white, yellow, red and dark; there is no higher dharma than him; the all-worshipped Sadashiva holds the qualities of goodness, passion, darkness and their mixture. The Shaivas and other chief Pramathas asked what was special about Sadashiva. Shiva then showed them that stainless form of Sadashiva: thousands of faces, feet and arms, holding a staff, hard to look at, filling the worlds on all sides, with the weapons of the gods seen in the staff. Then they saw him again with one face, surrounded by thousands of marks of both Shiva and Vishnu: half his body Vishnu's and half Shiva's, Garuda on his banner yet riding the bull, riding Garuda yet with the bull banner. As he took each form, Mahapashupata ganas were born. Shiva became one form and many, two forms, one and formless; in a moment white, red, yellow, blue, mixed and colourless; now chief of the Rudras, now Shambhu, now the sun, in half a moment Shankara and Vishnu, in a moment Sharva and Brahma. Seeing this wonder, the Shaivas and the others understood Brahma, Vishnu, Shiva and the sun as one, and when they saw Sadashiva as undivided they were freed from sin. Shiva, Hari-Ishvara, was pleased with their knowledge and offered a boon; they asked that the sin born of seeing difference be destroyed. Shiva agreed, cleansed them and embraced all the gana leaders. So the gana chiefs, comforted by the lord who removes the pain of those who bow, spread out over Mount Mandara and stayed there; covered by the cloud-dark Pramathas and touched by Shiva's feet, the white mountain shone like Shiva's mighty bull wearing a black hide, white as an autumn cloud.

01-068.json.summary: Pulastya says that Andhaka and the demons now reached Mount Mandara, whose caves were full of Pramathas. The Pramathas shouted and beat many drums; the great noise filled heaven and earth like the end of the world. Vinayaka (Ganesha), lord of obstacles, heard it in the sky, came angrily with his troops, bowed to his father and asked why he sat still and urged him to rise for battle. Shiva told Ambika he was going to kill Andhaka and she must stay alert. Parvati embraced him again and again and said, "Go, conquer Andhaka", honoured him with sandal, gorochana and collyrium and bowed at his feet. Shiva told Malini, Jaya, Vijaya, Jayanti and Aparajita to stay alert in the well-guarded house and protect the mountain's daughter carefully. Then he mounted his bull and went out with his trident, surrounded by gana chiefs shouting "Victory". Good omens appeared: a female jackal on his left went ahead howling, flesh-eating creatures followed gladly, thirsting for blood, his right side trembled to the nails, and a silent harita bird flew away. Shiva smiling told Nandi that victory was sure; Nandi agreed and sent the troops to fight along with the Mahapashupatas. The ganas crushed the demon army like thunderbolts striking trees; the demons fought back with hammers and maces. Indra, Vishnu, Brahma, the Sun, Agni and the other gods came to watch in the sky, with drums, songs and music. Tuhunda, angry, rushed forward with a terrible iron club bound with bands and shining like Indra's banner, and struck the ganas, so that those from the Rudras to Skanda broke and fled. Vinayaka rushed at him; Tuhunda struck the club on his temple, but it broke into a hundred pieces like lightning on a peak of Meru. Rahu, protecting his maternal uncle Tuhunda, bound Vinayaka with his arms. Though struck with an axe, Rahu did not let go. The gana chief Kundodara struck Rahu with a pestle, Kalashadhvaja pierced his heart with a spear, Ghatodara hit him with a mace and the Rakshasa lord Sukeshi with a sword; struck by these four, Rahu let Vinayaka go, and at once Vinayaka split Tuhunda's head with his axe. With Tuhunda dead and Rahu turned back, the gana chiefs, like the fire of the end of time, entered the demon army. Bali, swift as wind, whirled his mace and struck Vinayaka on the head, temple and trunk, broke Kundodara's hip, smashed Mahodara's skull, crushed Kumbhadhvaja's joints and Ghatodara's thigh, and rushed to kill Skanda, Vishakha and the others. Shiva told Nandi to go and kill the demons. Nandi struck Bali on the head with his thunderbolt and he fell senseless. Kujambha, Bali's uncle, threw a pestle at Nandi; Nandi caught it and killed Kujambha with it, then killed hundreds with his thunderbolt. The demons ran to Duryodhana for refuge; he hurled a spear bright as lightning at Nandi, shouting "You are dead"; Nandi cut it with his thunderbolt as a slanderer cuts a secret, and when Duryodhana came at him with his fist, Nandi cut off his head, which fell like a palm fruit, and the demons fled in all directions. Seeing his son dead, Hastin attacked Nandi with a fierce bow and covered Nandi, Vinayaka and the ganas with arrows like rain clouds on mountains, until they turned back. Kumara (Skanda) warded off the arrows with his spear and pierced Hastin's heart; he fell dead and the enemy army turned back again. The angry gana chiefs, with Nandi in front, attacked; the demons fled but turned back under Kartasvara. The tiger-faced Nandishena turned to face them with a sharp-edged spear (pattisha), and Kartasvara came at him with a mace; Nandishena whirled his weapon and struck Kartasvara on the head, killing him. Hayagriva, Kartasvara's cousin, bound Nandishena and his weapon with a noose. Vishakha, spear in hand, came angrily, but the strong Ayahshiras, noose in hand, fought him. Shakha and Naigameya ran to help; Naigameya pierced Ayahshiras with his spear, and he was pressed hard by Shiva's three sons. The four sons of Shiva struck the noose with their spears and it was destroyed, falling like something from the sky to the earth. With the noose useless, Shambara, frightened, fled, and Kumara crushed the army. Beaten by Shiva's sons and the ganas, the demon army, in despair and shaking with fear, went to Shukra for refuge.

01-069.json.summary: Pulastya continues to Narada the war of Andhaka against Shiva. Seeing his army slain by Shiva's attendants (the pramathas), Andhaka goes to his teacher Shukra and complains that his brothers such as Kujambha are dead while the pramathas never run out, and asks him to secure victory. Shukra promises, and by the proper rite recites the life-giving spell (sanjivani vidya), and all the slain demons rise again. Nandi tells Shiva that the dead have been brought back by Shukra's spell, so all their work in battle has come to little. Shiva sends Nandi to bring Shukra to him. On the way the demon Hayagriva (Hayakandhara) blocks Nandi, who knocks him senseless with a thunderbolt; then Kujambha, Jambha, Bala, Vritra, Ayahshiras, Maya, Hlada and others attack Nandi. Brahma tells Indra and the gods to help Shiva, and they come down from the sky into Shiva's army. In the uproar Nandi snatches Shukra from his chariot like a lion seizing a small deer, kills the guards and brings him to Shiva, who throws him into his mouth and keeps him in his belly. Shukra praises Shiva with many names; pleased, Shiva offers a boon, and Shukra asks to come out of his belly. Shiva shuts his eyes and tells him to go out, but wandering inside, Shukra sees all the worlds, oceans and underworlds, all gods, sages, men, animals, insects, plants and mountains, the manifest and the unmanifest, and a divine year passes without his finding an exit. Tired, he again takes refuge in Shiva with praise. Shiva laughs and lets him out through his penis (shishna), saying, "Now you are my son; all beings will praise you by the name Shukra (semen)". Shukra bows and returns to the demons, who are glad and fight again. Paired duels follow for six hundred divine years: Andhaka with Nandi, Ayahshiras with Shankukarna, Bali with Kumbhadhvaja, Virochana with Nandishena, Ashvagriva with Vishakha, Bana with Naigameya, Ganesha (Vinayaka) with an axe against the demon Tuhunda, and others; Jambha against Indra, a demon named Shambhu against Brahma, Kujambha against Vishnu, Shalva against the Sun, Trishiras against Varuna, and so on; Kalanemi alone against all the Vishvedevas, Vidyunmali alone against the eleven Rudras, Naraka against the two Ashvins, Shambara against the Adityas, Nivatakavacha and others against the Sadhyas and Maruts. When the demons cannot win, they use magic and swallow the gods and pramathas one by one, until the mountain top, covered by the cloud-dark demons, is empty. In anger Shiva creates Yawning (jrimbhika); touched by it, the demons grow lazy, drop their weapons and yawn, and the gods and pramathas rush out of their bodies like lightning from clouds and defeat them day and night. After seven hundred years the eighteen-armed Shiva performs his evening worship (sandhya): he bathes in the Sarasvati, offers flowers on his head, bows, walks around, worships the Sun with the hymn beginning "Hiranyagarbha" and the words "Homage to Tvashtri", and dances deeply moved, whirling his arms, while the gods and attendants dance with him; then he returns to battle and the demons are beaten. Thinking Shiva cannot be conquered, Andhaka tells his brother Sunda that Shiva is strong because Parvati dwells in his heart; he will take Shiva's form and seduce her while Sunda takes the form of Nandi. Disguised so and covered with wounds, they reach Mount Mandara and enter Shiva's house. Parvati, thinking her husband has been wounded fighting for her sake, tells her friends Jaya, Vijaya, Malini and Suyasha to bring old ghee, seeds, salt and curd so she can dress his wounds, and goes to meet him; but looking carefully for Shiva's marks she sees no bulls at his sides, knows him for a demon in disguise, and moves away. Andhaka, guessing her thought, leaves Sunda and chases her through the house, breaking things, and into the garden. She does not curse him, to guard her store of austerity (tapas); out of fear she enters a pure white arka flower, and her friends hide in a thicket. With Parvati gone, Andhaka takes Sunda by the hand and returns to his army, and the great battle resumes. Vishnu, to please Shiva, kills demons with arrows from his Sharnga bow, piercing five to eight at once, and with mace, discus, sword, his gaze which burns them to ash, plough and pestle, while Garuda strikes with wings, beak and chest; Brahma whirls his lotus and sprinkles water holding all holy places, which destroys the demons with their mounts. Indra charges with his thunderbolt; the demon Bala, unbeaten by gods and demons, comes at him with his fist, and the thunderbolt thrown on Bala's head breaks into a thousand pieces, and Indra turns and flees in fear. Jambha taunts him that flight is not the duty of a king. Indra goes to Vishnu for a weapon; Vishnu tells him to drop his pride and ask Agni. Agni, pleased that Indra has given up pride and come to him for refuge, draws a spear (shakti) with a hundred bells from his own power and gives it to him. Indra charges Jambha, but Jambha's fist smashes the head of Indra's elephant, which falls like a mountain, and Indra leaps off and falls from Mandara towards the earth. The Siddhas and Charanas tell him to stop; he stands in the air and asks how he can fight without a mount. The Gandharvas led by Vishvavasu send him a pure gold chariot marked with the svastika, with a monkey banner, bay horses and nets of small bells, but it has no driver, and Indra says he cannot both fight and hold the horses. The Gandharvas say they have no driver, and Indra falls to the ground with his garland, clothes, crown, hair, weapons and armlets scattered, and the earth shakes. At that moment the wife of the sage Shamika tells her husband to put their baby outside, because, as astrologers say, whatever is put outside when the earth shakes becomes double. He does so, and when he goes back in to fetch a pair of cows she stops him, saying the moment has passed and it would be halved. Outside he finds two identical boys. Worshipping the gods and his wonderful wife, he asks what the second boy's qualities and fortune will be; she at first will not say, but when he refuses to eat she tells him that, since he asked out of fear, this boy will be a craftsman (karu). At these words the boy goes off, as if senseless, to help Indra as a charioteer, and the Gandharvas, knowing this, increase his power. The boy tells Indra he will be his driver; when Indra doubts him, he says he is born of earth and of a sage's power, filled with the Gandharvas' power and skilled with horses. This Brahmin's son becomes famous as Matali. Indra mounts the chariot, enters the enemy army on Mandara and finds a great five-coloured bow with arrows lying there; bowing in mind to the gods of the three qualities, he strings it, and fierce peacock-feathered arrows marked with the names of Brahma, Shiva and Vishnu cover sky, earth and all directions, felling elephants, horses, chariots, riders and foot soldiers. Kujambha and Jambha rush at Indra with terrible maces; Vishnu kills Kujambha with his Sudarshana discus. Enraged, Jambha charges Indra like a doomed deer charging a lion; Indra drops the bow and hurls Agni's belled spear, which burns Jambha's mace to ash and pierces his heart, and he falls lifeless. The demons flee in fear; the attendants rejoice, worship Vishnu and praise Indra's valour, and Indra goes and stands by Shiva.

01-070.json.summary: Pulastya tells Narada how Andhaka was finally overcome. With the demon army broken, Shukra urges Andhaka to go home and fight Shiva another time, but Andhaka refuses to flee and shame his family, boasting he will defeat the gods, Indra and Shiva. He tells his charioteer Shambhu to drive to Shiva; the black horses, though whipped and swift as wind, sink at the haunches and take a full year to drag the chariot to Shiva's army. Andhaka covers the gods and attendants with arrows. Vishnu tells the gods not to stand idle: kill the horses and driver, break the chariot and make him chariotless, and then Shiva will burn him, for the teacher of the gods has said an enemy must not be ignored. Vishnu crushes a thousand cloud-dark horses with his mace in a moment, Skanda pierces the charioteer's heart with his spear, and Ganesha and others with Indra smash the chariot. Andhaka takes his mace, walks eight steps and tells Shiva, "Beggar, you have an army and I am alone, yet I will defeat you." Hearing this, Shiva takes Brahma, Indra, the gods and attendants into his own body and stands alone. He leaves his bull and stands on foot; as Andhaka charges, he takes a terrible form, Bhairava, with fangs, the brightness of ten million suns, a lion skin, matted hair, snakes on his neck, ten arms and three eyes, and pierces Andhaka's chest with his trident. Even pierced, Andhaka drags Bhairava a full krosha, until Shiva steadies himself and lifts the demon and his mace on the trident; Andhaka strikes Shiva's head with the mace, and blood flows from the wound in four streams. From the east stream is born the fire-bright Bhairava Vidyaraja, with lotus garlands; from the south, the black Kalaraja, adorned with ghosts; from the west, Kamaraja, coloured like the flax flower and adorned with leaves; from the north, Somaraja, with a garland of discs; from the blood of the wound, Svacchandaraja, bright as the rainbow; and from the blood on the ground, Lalitaraja. So Bhairava has seven forms, and with Vighnaraja as the eighth they are called the eight Bhairavas. Shiva holds Andhaka up on the trident like an umbrella, and the demon's blood pours down until Shiva in his seven forms is sunk in it up to the neck. From the sweat of effort on Shiva's forehead a girl is born, covered in blood, and from a drop of sweat falling on the earth a boy like a heap of glowing coals. The thirsty boy drinks Andhaka's blood and the girl licks up the blood. Shiva tells the girl that gods, sages, ancestors, serpents, Yakshas, Vidyadharas and men will worship her with offerings and flowers, and she will be called Charchika because she is smeared (charchita) with blood; she wanders the earth wearing a lion skin and goes to the mountain Hingulata. To the boy, Kuja (Mars), Shiva gives lordship among the planets, with the good and bad fortunes of the world under his control. For a thousand divine years Shiva dries Andhaka with the sun-fire of his eye until only skin and bone remain; purified by that fire, Andhaka is freed of sin, recognises Shiva as lord of all and praises him with a hymn: he calls him Bhairava, ten-armed and three-eyed, named Shiva by the gods, Hara and Sthanu by the Siddhas and sages, Bhima by Yakshas, Maheshvara by men, Ugra by night-roamers and Bhava by the ancestors; the one of the three Vedas, three fires and three worlds; Brahma, Vishnu, Indra and Dharma; the subtle and the manifest who fills all. He confesses he is sinful by birth and deed, overcome by desire, and begs for protection. Pleased, Shiva offers any boon except Ambika. Andhaka says Ambika is his mother and Shiva his father, and asks that all his sins of body, mind and speech, and his demon nature, be destroyed and that he have firm devotion to Shiva. Shiva grants it and makes him Bhringi, a leader of his attendants (ganas), takes him off the trident and heals his wounds with his own hand. He calls Brahma and the gods out of his body, shows them that Bhringi is no longer Andhaka, embraces them and sends them home, telling Indra to go first to Mount Malaya to do his own task. The attendants go on their mounts to happy worlds with wish-giving cows, wish-fulfilling trees, rivers of nectar and lakes of milk-rice. After two thousand years Shiva returns home with Nandi and Andhaka and finds Parvati in the white arka flower; she comes out and calls Jaya and her other friends. Shiva embraces her and tells her that Andhaka is now her servant and son; Nandi and Andhaka bow at her feet, and Andhaka praises her as Bhavani, mother of Skanda and of the three worlds, sister of Govinda, Kalaratri, Mahamaya, Sarasvati and Mridani. Pleased, she offers a boon; Bhringi asks that his threefold sin be removed and that he always have devotion to Shiva. She agrees, and he stays worshipping Shiva as lord of the attendants. Pulastya says this pure tale, which increases Shiva's fame, should always be told among Brahmins by one who wants merit, long life, health and wealth.

01-071.json.summary: Narada asks what Indra did on Mount Malaya. Pulastya says that Andhaka's followers led by Maya and Tara, beaten by the gods and on their way to the underworld, saw the lovely Malaya mountain, with caves where Siddhas live, creepers, sandal trees wrapped by snakes, cool fragrant south winds and the scent of madhavi flowers, and, tired from fighting, settled there to enjoy themselves while still hating the gods. Shiva, knowing this, sent Indra there. On the way Indra walks around a mother cow (gomata), then reaches the mountain and challenges the demons. They come showering arrows, but from his chariot he covers them with arrows as a cloud covers hills with rain. He kills Paka with sharp heron-feathered arrows, and because he punished (shasana) him he gets the name Pakashasana; he tears apart Pura, son of Banasura, and so becomes Purandara. The beaten demons flee to Rasatala. Narada then asks why Indra is called Gotrabhid. Pulastya says that after Hiranyakashipu was killed, Diti, having lost her sons, asked Kashyapa for a son who would kill Indra. Kashyapa said that if she kept purity and right conduct for ten times ten divine years she would bear a son who would rule the three worlds and kill his enemy. He made her pregnant and went to the eastern mountain. Indra came to her hermitage and offered to serve her, and she, driven by fate, agreed. Humble but waiting like a snake for a weak point, he fetched firewood and other things for her. One day, at the end of a thousand years, after washing her hair, she fell asleep with her head on her knees and her loose hair touching her feet, which made her impure. Seeing this lapse, Indra entered her womb through her nostril and saw a large child facing upward with hands on its hips, and in its mouth a lump of flesh like clear crystal. In anger he squeezed it in his hands; it grew hard, extended at both ends and became the hundred-jointed thunderbolt (vajra). With it he cut the unborn child into seven pieces; the child cried, and Diti woke and understood. Indra said harshly, "Do not cry (ma ruda)", and cut each piece again into seven. They became the Maruts, Indra's servants, who because of their mother's lapse move about going before him. Indra came out with the thunderbolt and, fearing her curse, told Diti with joined hands that the fault was hers, not his. Diti said she did not blame him; it was fate, since she had become impure even when the time was almost complete. She comforted the children and sent them off with the king of the gods. So, because he split his own brothers (gotra) in the womb out of fear, Indra is called Gotrabhid.

01-072.json.summary: Narada asks who held the place of the Maruts, the wind gods, in earlier Manu-ages (manvantaras). Pulastya tells their origin in each age from Svayambhuva onward. In the Svayambhuva age, Savana, son of Priyavrata, died without a son; his wife Sudeva would not let his body be burned and wept. A voice from the sky told her that if her truth was great she would have seven sons by the king, and to enter the fire. She placed her husband on the pyre and entered the fire thinking of him; soon the king rose up alive with her and flew into the sky, free to go where he wished. While in the air, the queen began her monthly course; he stayed in the sky with her for five days, and on the sixth, thinking the fertile time should not be wasted, made love to her, and his semen fell from the sky; then the two went to Brahma's world. The wives of the seven sages (named as Sumana, Nalini, Vapushmati, Chitra, Vishala, Haritalini and others) saw the cloud-coloured semen lying in a lotus, took it for nectar that would keep them young, and with their husbands' leave drank it. They lost their Brahmin power and their husbands abandoned them as faulty. They bore seven sons who cried terribly and filled the world with noise; Brahma came, told them not to cry, named them Maruts who move in the sky, and set them in the wind's path. In the Svarochisha age, the seven sons of Kratudhvaja, son of Svarochisha, did austerity on Mount Meru to win Indra's place. The fearful Indra, then named Vipashchit, sent the apsaras Putana to break it. When the brothers came to bathe in a river and saw her bathing, their semen fell and was drunk by a female water creature, the wife of the great crocodile Mahashankha; the brothers, their austerity ruined, went back to their father's kingdom. Much later this creature, in the shape of a shell, was caught in a fisherman's net, and he told the brothers; they put her in a pool in their city, where she bore seven boys and was released from her body. The motherless boys cried for milk, and Brahma came, named them Maruts and set them in the wind's path. In the Uttama age, Jyotishman, the virtuous son of King Vapushman of Nishadha, did austerity for a son by the Mandakini river, served by his wife, a daughter of the teacher of the gods, who gathered fruit, flowers, water, firewood and grass, honoured guests and grew thin. The seven sages saw her, asked the reason, and granted that they would have seven good sons. Back home she conceived, but the king died while she was pregnant; ignoring the ministers she climbed the pyre with him, and from the fire a lump of flesh fell into water, which, cooled, split into seven and became the Maruts of that age. In the Tamasa age, Ritadhvaja, son of Manu Tamasa, wanting sons, offered his own flesh, blood, bones, hair, sinews, marrow, liver and semen into the fire; after the semen fell into the seven flames a voice cried "Do not throw!", and the king died; from the fire came seven fire-bright crying infants whom Brahma made Maruts. In the Raivata age, King Ripujit, who had no son, won by austerity to the Sun a daughter, Surati. While she lived in her father's house he died; in grief she wished to die; the seven mind-born sages, who were attached to her, tried to stop her, but she lit a fire and entered it, and as the sages watched lamenting, seven boys came out of the fire, whom Brahma made Maruts. In the Chakshusha age, the truthful sage Mankana did great austerity at the Saptasarasvata holy place; the Tushita gods sent the woman Vapu to disturb him; at the river bank she excited him and his semen fell into the water. He cursed her that a horse would destroy her at a sacrifice, and went home. From the seven Sarasvati streams seven Maruts were born. Hearing of the birth of the Maruts removes sin and greatly increases merit (dharma).

01-073.json.summary: Pulastya continues: this is why the demon Bali was made king, with Prahlada as his adviser and Shukra as his priest. Seeing Bali, son of Virochana, crowned, his kinsmen came to see him; he honoured them and asked what was good for him. They told him: his grandfather Hiranyakashipu, who had ruled the three worlds as Indra, was torn apart by Vishnu in lion form before the demon lords; Andhaka's kingdom was taken by Shiva for the gods' sake; his uncle Jambha was killed by Indra and Kujambha by Vishnu like an animal; Shambhu and Paka were killed by Indra, and his brother Sudarshana and his father Virochana were also slain. Hearing of this destruction of his family by Indra, Bali prepared for war with all the great demons, on chariots, elephants, horses and on foot: Maya, the fearful general, at the front, Bali in the centre, Kalanemi behind, Shalva on the left and Taraka on the right, with thousands, millions and hundreds of millions of demons. Indra, hearing this, mounted his chariot driven by Matali, and all the gods went out on their mounts: Adityas, Vasus, Rudras, Sadhyas, Vishvedevas, the Ashvins, Vidyadharas, Guhyakas, Yakshas, Rakshasas, serpents, royal sages and Siddhas, on elephants, chariots, horses and bright bird-drawn aerial cars. Vishnu came too, and Indra and the gods bowed to him. Kartikeya with a mace led the army, Vishnu guarded the rear, Indra was in the centre, Jayanta on the left and Varuna on the right. The armies met on a flat, treeless, birdless rock plain on the slopes of the eastern (Udaya) mountain. The clash was terrible; reddish dust rose like an evening cloud, nothing could be seen, and only cries of "Cut! Pierce!" were heard, until flowing blood settled the dust. The gods under Skanda's protection killed demons and the demons under Maya killed gods; then, because they had not yet tasted the nectar of immortality (amrita), the gods and Skanda were defeated. Vishnu, whose banner bears Garuda, struck the demons with iron-tipped arrows from his Sharnga bow, and they ran to Kalanemi for refuge. Kalanemi promised them safety and, knowing Vishnu could not be beaten, grew huge like a neglected disease. Whatever god, Yaksha or Kinnara he touched he threw into his wide mouth; even without weapons he crushed the gods, Indra, the Sun and the Moon with his hands, feet and nails, and he looked like the fire at the end of time about to burn the world. The gods, Gandharvas, Siddhas, Sadhyas and Ashvins fled in all directions, while the proud demons attacked Vishnu with many weapons. Red-eyed with anger, Vishnu covered Maya, Bali and the others, with their chariots, elephants and horses, with thunderbolt-like arrows as a cloud covers mountains; the frightened demons sent hundred-headed Kalanemi against him. Kalanemi, huge as a mountain peak, raised his mace; Vishnu put down his bow and took the discus. Kalanemi laughed and boasted, in a voice like thunder, that this enemy of the demons, killer of Madhu and of Hiranyaksha, who loves to be worshipped with flowers, would not escape, and the gods would see him crushed by his fist; then he hurled the mace at Garuda. Vishnu cut the mace with the discus, then cut off both of Kalanemi's thick arms, and then his head, which fell like a ripe palm fruit. Armless and headless, the trunk still stood unmoving like Meru, until Garuda knocked it to the ground with his chest. With their general dead, the demons, pressed by the gods, threw down their weapons, armour and clothes and fled, all except Bana.

01-074.json.summary: Pulastya continues. With Bana standing firm, the demons turned back to fight. Vishnu, knowing that Bali's son Bana could not then be beaten, told the gods to fight without fear, and then vanished. Shukra told Bali that Govinda had left the gods and he should now win. Bali charged the gods with his mace, Bana with weapons in his thousand arms killed them by thousands, Maya fought with magic, taking many forms, and Vidyujjihva, Paribhadra, Vrishaparvan, Shatekshana, Vipaka and Vikshara also attacked. With Vishnu gone the gods turned and fled, chased by Bali and Bana, and left heaven for Brahma's world. Bali, with his sons, brothers and kin, began to enjoy heaven: Bali became Indra, Bana became Yama, Maya Varuna, Rahu the Moon, Hlada Agni, Svarbhanu the Sun and Shukra Brihaspati, and demons took the other gods' offices. This terrible war of gods and demons, in which Bali became Indra, took place at the end of the Dvapara and start of the fifth Kali age. Bali ruled the seven underworlds and the three worlds Bhuh, Bhuvah and Svah, lord of ten worlds, living in heaven served by Gandharvas led by Vishvavasu, with apsaras such as Tilottama dancing and Yakshas and Vidyadharas playing music. Amid these pleasures he thought of his grandfather Prahlada, the great devotee of Vishnu, who came at once from the underworld. Bali left his throne, bowed at his feet, and Prahlada raised and embraced him. Bali said that by Prahlada's grace he had beaten the gods and taken Indra's kingdom, and asked Prahlada to rule the three worlds while he stood before him as a servant, worshipping his feet and eating his leftovers, since serving one's elders gives more contentment than ruling. Prahlada said that he had already ruled a kingdom without enemies, governed the earth, honoured friends, given freely and had sons, and now lived as one practising yoga; he formally accepted the kingdom and gave it back to Bali, telling him always to serve his elders, and seated him on Indra's jewelled throne. Bali, with joined hands, asked what he must do to protect the three worlds in line with dharma, wealth, desire and liberation, and Shukra too asked Prahlada to answer. Prahlada said: do what is good for the future and for the world, earn wealth without going against dharma, consider all beings, enjoy pleasures, and act for good here and hereafter, so that he wins praise and fame and no disgrace. The best men seek wealth so that these live happily in their house: a kinsman in trouble, a friend without money, an old relative, a virtuous Brahmin, and fame with renown. Kings prosper in a land adorned with Brahmins, with Kshatriyas, well sown, and with those devoted to service; Brahmins learned in Veda and law bring peace to the king by sacrifices and the smoke of the sacrificial fire. With his permission, let Brahmins be honoured, rich in austerity and study, and busy with performing sacrifices for others and teaching. Let Kshatriyas study, sacrifice and give, live by arms and protect the people. Let Vaishyas sacrifice, study, give, farm, keep cattle and live by trade. Let Shudras always serve Brahmins, Kshatriyas and Vaishyas and obey his commands. When the classes keep to their own duties, dharma grows, and with dharma the king rises; so Bali must keep the classes to their duties, for his growth follows theirs and his loss follows theirs. Prahlada fell silent, and Bali said he would do as he was told.

01-075.json.summary: Pulastya tells Narada that with the gods gone to Brahma's world, Bali ruled the three worlds always in line with dharma. Kali (the Kali age, also called Tishya), seeing the world as righteous as in the Krita age, went to Brahma and complained that Bali had destroyed his nature. Brahma said Bali had taken away the nature not only of Kali but of the whole world; Indra, Varuna, Vayu and even the Sun were humbled by him, and no one in the three worlds could stop him except the thousand-headed, thousand-footed Hari, who would take from Bali earth, heaven, kingdom, fortune and fame. Kali, seeing Indra and the gods humbled, went to the forest of vibhitaka trees. With Kali gone, the Krita age returned in the three worlds, and dharma stood on all four feet among the four classes: austerity, non-violence, truth, purity, self-control, compassion, giving, kindness, service and sacrifice filled the world, the classes kept to their duties, Brahmins entered the life stages (ashramas), and kings protected their people. Then the boon-giving Fortune of the three worlds (Shri, Lakshmi), with a lotus garland, came to Bali. Asked who she was, she said that Vishnu, the bearer of discus and mace, had abandoned Indra, so she had come to Bali. She explained that Vishnu made four lovely women: one white, in white clothes and garlands, riding a white elephant, full of goodness (sattva); one red, riding a red horse, of passion (rajas); one yellow, golden, in a golden chariot, said to follow darkness (tamas); and one blue, in blue clothes and garlands, riding a blue bull, said to have all three qualities. The white one went to Brahma, the Moon and those who follow him; the red one he gave to the king of the gods, to Manu and the like; the yellow one to the Prajapatis, to Shukra and to the Vaishyas; and the blue one, dark as a bee, to the demons, Nairritas, Shudras and Vidyadharas. Brahmins call the white one Sarasvati and praise her with Brahma in sacrifices with mantras; Kshatriyas call the red one Jayashri (Victory), praised by Indra and Manu; Vaishyas and protectors of people praise the yellow, golden one as Lakshmi; Shudras, with demons and Rakshasas, praise the blue one with devotion as Shri Devi. In their forms rest the undying treasures (nidhis): the white is the Mahapadma treasure, made of the histories, Puranas, Vedas with their limbs and the sixty-four arts; the red is the Padma treasure of pearls, gold, silver, chariots, horses, elephants, ornaments, weapons and clothes; the yellow is the Mahanila treasure of cows, buffaloes, donkeys, camels, gold, cloth, land, plants and animals; the blue is the Shankha treasure, which destroys the others. People under Mahapadma are truthful, pure and fond of sacrifice, giving and festivals; those under Padma sacrifice, are fortunate, proud, give large fees and enjoy common pleasures; those under Mahanila mix truth and lies, give and take, and spend rightly and wrongly; those under Shankha are unbelievers, impure, miserly, without enjoyment, given to theft and lies. She says she is Ragini, Jayashri, and her vow, approved by the good, is to dwell only with the brave, never with a coward; no one in the three worlds equals Bali, who beat Indra in battle, so she has come to him of her own will, and no wonder, since he was born in Hiranyakashipu's family and has surpassed even his great-grandfather. She entered Bali and lit him up, and then, like widows seeking shelter, modesty, fortune, intelligence, steadiness and fame came to him, along with radiance, understanding, patience, prosperity, learning, good policy, compassion, Veda, tradition, peace, nourishment, contentment, beauty and other good qualities, and rested in him. So Bali became wise, self-controlled, a sacrificer, an ascetic, gentle, truthful, generous, a supporter and protector of his people, and while he ruled heaven no one was hungry, dirty or wretched; even men became bright, devoted to dharma, self-controlled and able to enjoy their desires.

01-076.json.summary: Pulastya continues. Having lost the three worlds to the demons, Indra goes with the gods to Brahma's abode, where Brahma sits with the sages and with Kashyapa, Indra's father. Indra bows and complains that the strong Bali has taken his kingdom. Brahma says Indra is reaping the fruit of his own deed; asked what wrong he has done, Kashyapa says he killed an unborn child, cutting Diti's foetus into pieces by force. Indra says the child was cut because of the mother's fault, as she had become impure. Kashyapa answers that the mother's fault made the child a servant, and Indra killed even that servant with his thunderbolt. Indra asks for an atonement to destroy his sin. Brahma, Vasishtha and Kashyapa tell him to take refuge in Vishnu (Madhava), who holds conch, discus and mace and will bring him good. Indra asks where great results can be won in a short time, and is told: in the human world. So he goes quickly to earth, to a holy place north of Kalinjara, south of the Himalaya, east of Kushasthala and west of Vasu's city. There King Gaya once performed a horse sacrifice a hundred times with fees, a human sacrifice (manushyamedha) a hundred and a thousand times, and the royal consecration (rajasuya) a thousand times, and also the great Mahamedha sacrifice, hard even for gods and demons. There Vishnu, unseen and sky-formed, made his dwelling and became known as Gadadhara, a sharp axe for the great tree of sin. There even Brahmins without Vedic learning become equal to Brahma, and men who worship their ancestors once with single-minded devotion get the endless fruit of the Mahamedha sacrifice by the Lord's grace. There the great river, daughter of a divine sage, came from the Himalaya in the form of water and destroys the world's sin by being seen, drunk and bathed in. On the bank of this river Indra builds a hermitage to worship the god. Bathing at dawn, sleeping on the ground and eating once a day, he does austerity praising Gadadhara, with all senses mastered and free from desire and anger, for a little over a year. Pleased, Gadadhara tells him he is now free of sin and will soon regain his kingdom, and that he will work for his future good. After he bathes in the river, Indra's sins appear as men and ask for orders; he tells these doers of terrible deeds, born of his sin, to be called Pulindas and live between the Himalaya and Kalinjara. Freed of sin and honoured by gods, Siddhas and Yakshas, Indra goes to the hermitage of his mother Aditi, bows at her feet and tells of his austerity. She smells his head and embraces him in tears, and he tells her of his and the gods' defeat by Bali. Grief-stricken, she takes refuge in Vishnu. Narada asks where she worshipped him.
