Pulastya says that on the seventh day of the bright half, with the sun in Makara (Capricorn), she saw the god, the Sun called Ghritarchis, rising in the east, and, fasting, silent and pure-minded, took refuge in him with a hymn: victory to him who opens the lotus, the axe for the tree of worldly life, the fire for the fuel of sin, the stopper of darkness; homage to the Sun of divine form, the ornament of the three worlds' fortune, cause of all; through him Indra has lost his kingdom and been beaten, so she seeks his shelter. She draws his image with red sandal paste, worships him with karavira flowers and incense, offers broken grain fit for the Sun and costly food with ghee for Indra's good, and praises him while fasting. On the second day, after bowing, bathing and worship, she gives grain, sesame and ghee to Brahmins and stands before him. Pleased, the Sun, Ghritarchis, comes out of the solar disc, and he, Vasudeva, tells her that he will grant her rare wish: he will give the kingdom to her sons and destroy the demons, being born from her womb. Trembling, Aditi asks how she can carry him, in whose belly the whole world, the seven oceans and mountains dwell, and asks him to restore Indra without her suffering. Vishnu says it is true no god or demon can bear him, yet he will be born of her and by his yoga power will support himself, the worlds, the mountains, her and Kashyapa; when he is in her womb the demons will lose their power. Saying this, he enters her womb with a part of his own power for Indra's good.

01-077.json.summary: Pulastya continues. With Vishnu in the dwarf (Vamana) form inside Aditi's womb, the demons lose their power, as he said. Bali asks Prahlada why. Prahlada meditates and, seeking where Vishnu now is, surveys in his mind the seven underworlds below the navel and the worlds above it, the lotus-shaped earth with golden Meru at its centre, the eight great cities of the world guardians on it, and below it the holy hermitage of Aditi, full of animals and birds. Seeing Aditi brighter than all, he looks into her womb and sees Vishnu in dwarf form, lotus-eyed, holding conch, discus and mace, his body filled with all gods and demons, taking away the demons' power; then he comes back to himself. Bowing to Vishnu, he tells Bali that the gods, beaten by him, took refuge in Hari, who promised them safety and has entered Aditi's womb; he has taken their power, just as darkness cannot stand before the sunrise. Bali, angry and driven by what was to come, asks who this Hari is: he has hundreds of demons stronger than Vasudeva, who have beaten the gods thousands of times, such as Viprachitti, who pulled a wheel from the Sun's chariot, and Ayahshanku, Shiva, Shambhu, Asiloman, Vilomakrit, Trishiras, Makaraksha, Vrishaparvan and others, any one of whom Vishnu is not worth a sixteenth part of. Prahlada, furious, says "Shame on you", calls him sinful and foolish, and asks why his tongue did not fall off for blaming Hari; he grieves that Bali's father was born of him, since Bali despises the gods, and reminds him that Hari is dearer to him than life: Bali's father is to be honoured, Prahlada is his father's teacher, and Hari is Prahlada's teacher and teacher of the world. Then he curses him: since Bali has blamed Hari, who should be worshipped, he will lose his kingdom; as surely as nothing is dearer to Prahlada than Keshava in mind, deed and word, and nothing exists apart from him in the fourteen worlds, may Bali fall from his kingdom. Bali at once gets down from his throne, bows with joined hands and asks forgiveness: elders forgive children's faults; he is glad to be cursed by him and fears neither enemies nor losing his kingdom; his only pain is having offended him; he is a foolish, helpless child. Prahlada, his delusion gone, thinks a long time and says gently that delusion clouded his judgement, so that he cursed Bali though he knew Vishnu is everywhere; this must be what is fated for Bali. So Bali should not grieve over the kingdom, for what must happen cannot be avoided. The wise do not grieve over the coming and going of sons, friends, wives, kingdom, pleasures and wealth, but bear joy and sorrow as they come from past deeds; the steady are not upset by loss or thrilled by gain. He advises Bali to take refuge in that Supreme Person, who will save him from this danger; those who take shelter in Hari, the hand that lifts those fallen in the pit of worldly life, never suffer; Bali should fix his mind on him and be his devotee. Prahlada himself will worship the Lord and go on pilgrimage to the holy places to remove his sin, and then go where Narasimha dwells. Having comforted Bali and remembered Vishnu, he takes leave of the demon leaders and sets out on pilgrimage.

01-078.json.summary: Narada asks which holy places (tirthas) Prahlada visited. Pulastya says this account of Prahlada's pilgrimage destroys the mud of sin. Leaving Meru, Prahlada went to Manasa, where Vishnu stands in the form of the Fish; he bathed, offered water to ancestors and gods, worshipped Achyuta, fasted, and went on to see the Tortoise form on the Kaushiki river, where he bathed, worshipped, fasted, gave fees to Brahmins and bowed. Then he went to Krishna to see the horse-faced Lord (Hayashiras), bathing in the Devahrada lake; then to Gajasahvaya (Hastinapura) to worship Govinda with the discus; then to the Yamuna, where he bathed and saw Trivikrama. Narada asks how Vishnu could have been Trivikrama in the past, since his three-world stride and binding of Bali is still to come, and whom he bound then. Pulastya tells the story. Dhundhu, a mighty son of Kashyapa by Danu, won from Brahma by austerity the boon that he could not be killed by the gods and Indra. At the start of the fourth Kali age, while Hiranyakashipu was alive, he conquered the gods and became Indra, and Hiranyakashipu lived on Mount Mandara under him. The demons enjoyed heaven while the gods lived unhappily in Brahma's world. Dhundhu proposed to go and conquer them there, but the demons said they knew no way: far above lies Maharloka of the great sages, whose glance burns demons; ten million yojanas further, Janaloka, where the mother cows live, whose very dust destroys demons; sixty million yojanas further, Tapoloka, where the Sadhyas live, whose breath is unbearable; and three hundred million yojanas beyond, Satyaloka, bright as a thousand suns, Brahma's home, where the sound of the Veda makes the gods bloom and the demons shrink. They did not know how Indra got there; Shukra would. Shukra told him that Indra had once performed a hundred horse sacrifices and so reached Brahma's world. Dhundhu decided to do the same, called up the treasures and the Guhyakas, invited the sages, and was consecrated by Shukra for the horse sacrifice at the ancient, sin-destroying site on the Devika river, with Bhargava Brahmins and Shukra's pupils as priests and assistants, and demons such as Svarbhanu given shares of the offerings. The horse was released, followed by the demon Asiloman. Smoke from the fire filled earth, mountains, sky and all directions, and its sharp smell reached Brahma's world. The gods, distressed, went to Vishnu and said Dhundhu, made strong by his boon, had taken the three worlds and, since no one but Shiva could protect them, had grown like a neglected disease; now, on Shukra's advice, he was doing a hundred horse sacrifices to climb to Brahma's world and defeat them, so Vishnu should find a way to wreck the sacrifice. Vishnu gave them safety and sent them away; knowing the demon could not be beaten in battle, he resolved to bind Dhundhu, a show-off of dharma (dharmadhvaja). Taking the form of a dwarf (Vamana), he lay limp like a log in the Devika's water, sinking and rising, with loose hair. Dhundhu, the demons and the sages saw him; the Brahmins, the patron and the priests left the rite and rushed to pull him out, and asked why he had fallen and who had thrown him in. Trembling, the dwarf said: a virtuous, learned Brahmin named Prabhasa, of the Varuna clan, had two dull, unhappy sons, the elder Netrabhasa and the younger himself, Gatibhasa, so named by his father in fun. Their father had a lovely house like heaven. When he died and they had done the funeral rites, he asked his brother to divide the house; the brother said he had no share, since the hunchbacked, dwarfs, lame, impotent, those with white leprosy, the mad and the blind get no share of wealth, only a bed, seat, place to live and food as they like. When he asked by what rule he was denied half his father's wealth, his angry brother lifted him and threw him in the river, where he had floated for a year until they pulled him out. He asked who they were and who the Indra-like man consecrated for sacrifice was. The Bhargavas said they were Brahmins of the Bhrigu clan and this was the great demon Dhundhu, a giver, enjoyer and sharer, consecrated for sacrifice; and they told Dhundhu to give the dwarf a rich house with all goods, servant women and jewels. Dhundhu offered him as much wealth as he wanted: a house, gold, horses, chariots and elephants. The dwarf said: if a man's wealth can be taken even by his own brother, then whatever is given to such a weak man, will not others take it too? Give servants, house, jewels and goods to capable Brahmins; to me give three steps measured by my own size, for I cannot guard more. Laughing, Dhundhu and his priests gave him three steps, since he would take nothing else. Seeing the gift made, the Lord took the Trivikrama form of endless power, killed the demons and, bowing to the sages, with the first step took the earth with its mountains, oceans, mines and towns; with the second, the sky with the heaven of the gods, the Sun, Moon and stars. When the third step was not filled, in great anger he fell on Dhundhu's back with a body as large as Meru, and his fall made a pit in the earth thirty thousand yojanas deep. He pulled the demon up, threw him into it and filled the pit with a rain of sand. By his grace Indra got back heaven and the gods the three worlds, free from trouble. Having thrown the demon into the sea of sand, Vishnu took a form in the Kalindi (Yamuna) and vanished there. So, says Pulastya, Vishnu was once a dwarf and became Trivikrama to conquer Dhundhu, and it was to this great holy place that Prahlada, son of the demon king, came.

01-079.json.summary: Pulastya continues Prahlada's pilgrimage. After bathing in the Kalindi (Yamuna), worshipping Trivikrama and fasting one night, he went to the Lingabheda mountain, bathed, saw Bhava (Shiva) and fasted a night; then to Kedara, where he bathed and worshipped Shiva and Madhava as one and stayed seven days; then to Kubjamra, where he bathed, fasted and worshipped Hrishikesha; then to Badarika hermitage, where he worshipped Narayana and bathed in the Sarasvati; at Varaha tirtha he saw and worshipped Vishnu seated on Garuda; at Bhadrakarna he worshipped Shiva as Jayesha; then he went to the Vipasha (Beas) river, and fasting on the Iravati he saw the Supreme Lord whom Pururavas worshipped at Shakala to gain great beauty and rare power, and whom Bhrigu, struck by leprosy, worshipped to gain health and endless offspring. Narada asks how Pururavas lost his ugliness. Pulastya tells a sin-destroying story from the start of the Treta age. In Shakala, a city of the Madra country, lived Sudharma, a rich, virtuous, learned merchant. Setting out for Surashtra with a large caravan of goods, he was robbed by bandits at night in the desert and, having lost everything, wandered alone like a madman until he found a beautiful shami tree with no animals or birds near it, and lay down under it, tired, hungry and thirsty. Waking at midday, he saw a ghost (preta) chief carried by another ghost and surrounded by hundreds of rough-bodied ghosts. The chief greeted him, sat in the shade, asked about him, and on hearing his story comforted him like a kinsman: wealth comes and goes with fortune, and worrying only wastes the body. He told his followers that this guest must be honoured. At once a new clay pot full of curd-rice and a strong new water jar full of pure water appeared. The two did their daily rites with the water; the chief first gave curd-rice to the merchant, then to all the ghosts, and only then ate himself; when all were satisfied the food and water vanished. Amazed, the merchant asked where food and water came from in the empty forest, why the followers were thin while he was bright, well fed and dressed in white, and who he was and what the shami tree was. The ghost said he had been a Brahmin of Shakala named Somasharma, son of Bahula. His neighbour was the rich merchant Somashrava, a famous devotee of Vishnu. He himself was a foolish miser who, though rich, gave nothing to Brahmins and did not eat good food; if he ever ate food with curd, milk or ghee, he was beaten at night by terrible men and in the morning suffered deadly cholera with no relative near, so he lived on sour gruel, sesame cake, barley meal and greens. Once, on the Shravana Dvadashi in the month of Bhadrapada, the townspeople led by Brahmins and Kshatriyas went to bathe at the meeting of the Iravati and the Nadvala, and he went too with his neighbour; having fasted on the eleventh day with self-control, he gave a pure, learned Brahmin a strong new water jar filled with water from the confluence, wrapped in cloth, with an umbrella and sandals, and a clay pot full of sweet curd-rice. In seventy years that was his only gift. When he died he became a ghost, and since he had given that food, it now feeds him; the other ghosts, who gave nothing, live on his food. The food and water he gave appear every day at midday and do not run out until he has eaten; then they vanish. The umbrella he gave became the shami tree, and the pair of sandals became the ghost who carries him. So he has told the merit of the Shravana Dvadashi. The merchant asked what he could do for him. The ghost asked him to bathe at Gaya and offer rice balls (pinda) in his name; freed from the ghost state, he would go to the world of all givers. The bright twelfth day of Bhadrapada joined with the Shravana star and a Wednesday is most beneficial. He told the merchant his followers' names, had him carried on a ghost's shoulders out of the desert to the Shurasena country, where the merchant earned much wealth by his own work and then went to Gayashirsha. There he offered pindas in order for the ghosts, then for his own ancestors and kin, and at Mahabodhi, without sesame, for himself and for others of his clan. Freed from the ghost state, the ghosts went to Brahma's world. The merchant went home, kept the Shravana Dvadashi, and on dying enjoyed rare pleasures in the Gandharva world; reborn as a man in Shakala, devoted to his duty and to the Shravana Dvadashi, he died and lived in the world of the Guhyakas; reborn as a Kshatriya's son, generous and self-controlled, he defeated enemies in a cattle raid, died and was honoured in Indra's world. When his merit ran out he was born a Brahmin in Shakala, learned in all the scriptures but very ugly. He married a Brahmin girl of matchless beauty who despised him, though he was good-natured, because she thought him ugly. In sorrow and disgust he went to a great hermitage on the bank of the Iravati and worshipped the Lord who holds beauty, through the Nakshatra-purusha rite (worship of the Lord's body as the lunar stars), and in that same life he gained great beauty, became dear to his wife and enjoyed pleasures, and from past habit he was devoted to the Shravana Dvadashi. So this Brahmin, once ugly, became by the Lord's grace as handsome as Kama, and after death he became King Pururavas.

01-080.json.summary: Narada asks how Pururavas worshipped Vishnu, lord of Shri, through the Nakshatra-purusha rite. Pulastya explains this vow, in which Vishnu's body is made of the lunar stars (nakshatras). Mula is his feet, Rohini his shins, Ashvini his knees, the two Ashadhas his thighs, the two Phalgunis his private parts, the Krittikas his hips, the two Bhadrapadas his sides, Revati his belly, Anuradha his chest, Shravishtha his back, Vishakha his arms, Hasta his hands, Punarvasu his fingers, Ashlesha his nails, Jyeshtha his neck, Shravana his ears, Pushya his mouth, Svati his teeth, Shatabhisha his jaws, Magha his nose, Mrigashirsha his eyes, Chitra his forehead, Bharani his head and Ardra his hair. The rite: beginning on the bright eighth of Chaitra when the moon is in Mula, worship the Lord's feet by the rules and feed a Brahmin; then, as the moon reaches each star, worship the matching limb and give its favourite offering (dohada), with feeding of Brahmins: knees at Ashvini with sacrificial food; thighs at the Ashadhas with cool water; private parts at the Phalgunis with cow's milk; hips at the Krittikas, fasting, with scented flower water; sides at the Bhadrapadas with jaggery and a sweet dish; belly at Revati with mung-bean sweets; chest at Anuradha with shashtika rice; back at Shravishtha with shali rice; arms at Vishakha with fine rice; hands at Hasta with barley gruel; fingers at Punarvasu with patola gourd; nails at Ashlesha with partridge meat; neck at Jyeshtha with sesame sweets; ears at Shravana with curd-rice; mouth at Pushya with ghee and milk-rice; teeth at Svati with sesame cakes; jaws at Shatabhisha with priyangu and red shali rice; nose at Magha with honey; eyes at Mrigashirsha with deer meat; forehead at Chitra and head at Bharani with fine food; and hair at Ardra with jaggery and fresh ginger, feeding Brahmins with devotion. At the end, give the Brahmin as fee fine clothes for a man and a woman, an umbrella, a pair of white sandals, the seven grains, gold and a pot of ghee; Brahmins should be honoured at each star. This eternal Person is made of the stars, and this is the best of vows, first performed by Bhrigu, destroying all sins. Worshipping the limbs of the Lord makes one's own limbs beautiful; Keshava destroys sins of seven births, those come down in the family and those from father and mother, and gives every blessing, good health, endless joy of mind, great beauty, sweet speech, radiance and whatever else is wished. By fasting on these stars in order, Arundhati won the highest fame; the Sun, wanting a son, worshipped him and got his son Revanta; Rambha got the finest beauty, Menaka sweet speech, the Moon radiance and King Pururavas a kingdom. All who worship him so obtain their wishes. Pulastya calls this rite pure, blessed and a giver of fame and beauty, and tells Narada to hear next the holy pilgrimage (of Prahlada).

01-081.json.summary: Pulastya continues telling Narada about the pilgrimage of the demon lord Prahlada. Prahlada reaches the holy river Iravati, bathes and worships Janardana (Vishnu) on the eighth day of Chaitra, and keeps the meritorious vow called Nakshatra-purusha. He then goes to Kurukshetra, invokes the Chakra-tirtha called Sudarshana with the Airavata mantra, bathes by the Vedic rule, fasts for a night and worships Kurudhvaja. He goes on to see the Man-Lion (Narasimha): he bathes in the Devika and worships him, then visits Gokarna, where he worships Vishvakarman, and Kameshvara. He bathes and offers water to the ancestors at Pundarika in the great lake and stays three days; at Vishakhayupa he sees Ajita and stays three nights at Krishna-tirtha; at Hamsapada he worships Hamsa; on the Payoshni he worships Akhanda, lord of the world; on the Vitasta he worships Kumarila, who is served by the Valakhilya and Marichipa sages, at the place where the divine cow Surabhi created her daughter, the fine Kapila cow, for the good of gods and the world. He bathes in the Deva lake, worships Shambhu (Shiva), eats curd by the rule, then at the holy place Manimant sees Shambhu, Brahma and Prajapati, worships them and stays six nights. At the river Madhumati he sees Hara (Shiva) holding the discus and Govinda (Vishnu) holding the trident. Narada asks why Shiva held Sudarshana and Vishnu the trident. Pulastya tells an old story that Vishnu once told Manu: the great demon Jalodbhava did fierce penance and won a boon from Brahma that he could not be beaten by gods or demons in battle, could not be killed by the gods' own weapons, was safe from the curses of Brahmin sages, and could take away the powers of water and fire. He troubled gods, sages and kings everywhere and stopped all rites. The gods and kings went to Hari (Vishnu) for shelter, and he went with them to Shiva on the Himalaya. The two gods made a plan and exchanged their weapons. When the demon saw them coming to kill him, he hid in fear in the river Madhumati. The two waited hidden on its two banks; when Jalodbhava left the water and climbed the Himalaya, they ran at him, Vishnu with the trident and Shiva with the discus, cut his body apart, and he fell from the mountain like a star from the sky. That is why Vishnu held the trident and Shiva the discus. At that place the river Vitasta, which destroys sin, came forth from the mountain where Shiva's foot fell. Prahlada worshipped Hari and Shankara there, fasted, and went to the Himalaya to see Girisha, guarded by Shiva and Vishnu; after worship and gifts to Brahmins he went to Bhrigutunga at the foot of the Himalaya, where Shiva gave Vishnu the finest weapon, the discus, with which Vishnu, testing its power, cut Shankara into three parts.

01-082.json.summary: Narada asks why Shiva gave the discus to Vishnu. Pulastya tells a story that adds to Shiva's glory. A learned Brahmin householder named Vitamanyu had a good, faithful wife of the Atri family named Dharmashila, and they had a son named Upamanyu. Being very poor, the mother fed the boy rice flour mixed in water and told him it was milk. One day the boy went with his father to another Brahmin's house and ate rice cooked in real milk. Having tasted it, he would no longer take the flour water and cried for milk like a chataka bird crying for rain. Weeping, his mother told him that without the favour of Shiva (Umapati, Pashupati, Virupaksha) there was no milk to eat; if he wanted milk he should worship Virupaksha, the trident holder, who can grant even the drinking of nectar. The boy asked who Virupaksha was, and she told him this story. The great demon lord Shridama conquered the world, took away all prosperity (Shri) into his power, and even wanted to steal the Shrivatsa mark from Vishnu's chest. Knowing this, Vishnu went to Shiva, who sat in yoga on a smooth slope of the Himalaya, and worshipped him for a full thousand years, standing on his big toe and praising the highest Brahman. Pleased, Shiva gave him the shining divine discus Sudarshana, which has twelve spokes, six hubs and two rims; on its spokes stand the gods, the months, the zodiac signs and the six seasons. The twelve placed there are Agni, Soma, Mitra, Varuna, Indra, Indra-Agni, the Vishvedevas, the Prajapatis, mighty Hanuman, Dhanvantari, Tapas and Tapasya, and the months from Chaitra to Phalguna. Shiva told him to kill the enemy of the gods without doubt, since the weapon never fails. Vishnu asked how he could know it never fails, and said he would test it by throwing it at Shiva himself. Shiva told him to throw it without fear. The discus cut Shiva into three parts. Seeing this, Vishnu was ashamed and fell at his feet. Shiva lovingly told him to rise: only his outer, material form was cut, not his true nature, which cannot be cut or burnt. The three parts would become holy, named Hiranyaksha, Suvarnaksha and Virupaksha, and would give merit to people. He told Vishnu to go and kill Shridama. Vishnu went to Mount Meru, saw the demon and threw the discus, crying "You are killed!"; it cut off the demon's head and he fell like a mountain peak struck by a thunderbolt. Vishnu then went home to the ocean. The mother told her son that this Virupaksha is the great god Maheshvara, and he should worship him if he wanted milk. Upamanyu worshipped Virupaksha and obtained food with milk. Pulastya ends: this is the holy story of the cutting of Shiva's body, and Prahlada came to that best of holy places for merit.

01-083.json.summary: Pulastya goes on with Prahlada's pilgrimage. After bathing at that holy place and worshipping the three-eyed Suvarnaksha, Prahlada goes to Naimisha, where thirty thousand sin-removing holy places lie between the Gomati, Kanchanakshi and Gurudaya rivers; he worships Achyuta (Vishnu), the sages of the Naimisha forest and Ishana (Shiva). At Gaya he bathes at Brahmadhvaja, walks around it, offers rice balls (pinda) to the ancestors, bathes at Udapana, worships Gadapani (Vishnu) and Gopati (Shiva), bathes at Indra-tirtha and in the Mahanadi. Then follows a long list of places, at each of which he bathes, worships the god there and often honours the ancestors: the Sarayu (Kusheshaya at Gopratara), the city Viraja, Purushottama (Ajita, the lotus-eyed), staying six nights; South Mahendra (Shiva as half-woman, Ardhanarishvara); North Mahendra (Gopala, Soma-tirtha); Mount Sahya (Vaikuntha); Mount Pariyatra (Aparajita); the Kasheru land, where Shiva showed his universal form (Vishvarupa) to his attendants; the Mankunika waters; the fragrant Malaya mountain; the Vindhya (Sadashiva); the Vipasha, with a three-night fast; and the city Avanti, where after bathing in the Shipra he sees Shiva as Mahakala in the cremation ground. There Shiva, in his dark form, destroys all beings; there he protected King Shvetaki by burning up Death (Antaka), and he lives there happily with Uma among countless attendants. Prahlada then visits the Nishadhas (Amareshvara), Mahodaya (Hayagriva, Ashva-tirtha, Shridhara), Panchala, and Prayaga, where he sees Vateshvara (Rudra) and Madhava, fasting through the month of Magha; then Varanasi, where he bathes in the Varana and other places, walks around the city and worships Avimukta, Keshava and Lola the Sun; then Madhuvana (Svayambhu), Pushkara (three holy places, Pushkaraksha and Brahma), and Koti-tirtha on the Sarasvati. There millions of Brahmins from Naimisha, Magadha, Sindhu, Dharmaranya, Pushkara, Dandaka, Champa, Bharukaccha and the Devika banks came to see Shiva, each crying "me first"; out of kindness Shiva took ten million forms, each sage worshipped him at his own spot, and so he is called Rudrakoti. Prahlada then visits Kurujangala (Sthanu sunk in the Sarasvati, Dashashvamedha, Sahasralinga, Kanya lake, greeting his teacher Shukra), Soma-tirtha, Kshirikavasa (walking round the tree, Varuna), Kurudhvaja, the city Padma (Mitra and Varuna as suns), Kumaradhara, Kapiladhara (Skanda), the Narmada (Vasudeva), Kokamukha (the Boar), Arbuda (Trisauvarna, Narihrada), Kalinjara (Nilakantha), Prabhasa at the meeting of the Sarasvati and the sea (Someshvara, who restored the waning moon cursed by Daksha), Mahalaya, the Northern Kurus (Padmanabha), Saptagodavara (Bhima), Daruvana, Brahmani, Plakshavatarana (Shrinivasa), Kundina, Shurparaka (the four-armed god), Magadharanya, Prajamukha, the Shona (Rukmavarman), Mahakoshi (Hamsa), Saindhavaranya (Sunetra), Trivishtapa (Jatadhara), Kanakhala (Bhadrakali, Virabhadra, Kubera), Girivraja (Pashupati), Kamarupa (Shashiprabha with Mridani), and Mount Trikuta, where he praises the discus-bearer, recites the holy Gajendra-moksha prayer, stays three months living on roots, fruits and water and gives gold to Brahmins. In the fearful Dandaka forest he sees the lotus-eyed god in the form of a great tree, stays three nights beneath it sleeping on the bare ground and reciting the Sarasvata hymn; at another holy place he recites the two sin-destroying hymns once spoken by Vishnu as the Boar. Finally he reaches Shalagrama, where Vishnu is present in all moving and unmoving things, and there he happily worships the Lord's feet. Pulastya says that telling, hearing or touching this account of Prahlada's pilgrimage frees people from sin.

01-084.json.summary: Pulastya tells Narada that while the demon lord Prahlada was away on his pilgrimage, Bali, son of Virochana, came to Kurukshetra. At that holy place the Brahmin Shukra, of Bhrigu's line, invited the best of the twice-born. Hearing the call, sages of the Atreya, Gautama, Kaushika and Angirasa families left Kurujangala and went north along the river Shatadru (Sutlej). They bathed in its water and went on to Vivasa, where they bathed and honoured the ancestors and gods, then to the holy Kirana river, touched by the sun's rays, then to the swift Vegavati with its holy water, then to Ishvari, and bathed in the Devika and the Payoshni. Madhava and the other ascetics then went down to bathe in the Subhanavi; when they dived under, they saw their own reflections inside the water, a great wonder, and when they came up they saw them again, amazed; after bathing all the sages came out of the river. At this point the text breaks off and the rest of the chapter repeats, without verse breaks, the end of the previous chapter's account of Prahlada's pilgrimage: from his worship of Pushkaraksha and Brahma at Pushkara, Rudrakoti on the Sarasvati (where Shiva took ten million forms for the crowding sages), Kurujangala, Prabhasa and many other places, through Trikuta and the Gajendra-moksha prayer, the Dandaka forest, the Boar's hymns and Shalagrama, ending with the same promise that telling, hearing or touching the story of Prahlada's pilgrimage frees people from sin.

01-085.json.summary: Narada asks to hear the four prayers that Prahlada recited, beginning with the Gajendra-moksha. Pulastya says that telling, hearing or remembering them destroys bad dreams; first comes the Gajendra-moksha, then the Sarasvata, then two holy prayers that remove sin. He tells the story of the Release of the Elephant King. Trikuta, a shining mountain made of all jewels, son of Meru, rises out of the Milk Ocean, its rocks washed by the waves. It is visited by gods, sages, apsarases, gandharvas, kinnaras, yakshas, siddhas, vidyadharas and ascetics, full of wild animals and many kinds of trees and birds. It has three peaks: a golden one visited by the sun, a silver one visited by the moon, and a third, the abode of Brahma, shining with diamonds, sapphires and beryl, which ungrateful, cruel, unbelieving and sinful people and those who have done no penance cannot see. On its slope lies a lake of golden lotuses, full of ducks and swans and ringed by bamboo, in which lived an evil, ugly crocodile, the enemy of elephants. One day a great elephant, leader of a herd, dark as collyrium and dripping with rut, came down thirsty to drink and play among the lotuses. The crocodile seized him while his cow elephants watched and cried out, dragged him and bound him with Varuna's nooses. The elephant struggled with all his strength and trumpeted, but grew weak and helpless. In his great distress he thought of Hari; devoted to Narayana from birth after birth, worshipping no other god, he went to him for shelter with his whole being, lifted a golden lotus with the tip of his trunk and spoke a hymn. The hymn bows to Vishnu as root nature, the unconquered, the seed, the hidden, beyond reasoning and measure, the peaceful, the ancient, the god of gods, Govinda, Padmanabha, Shiva and Hari, without qualities yet the self of qualities, Vamana, Purushottama holding bow, discus, sword and mace, the Man-Lion, the great Boar, lying on the serpent, dressed in yellow, slayer of Madhu and Kaitabha, with Brahma on the lotus from his navel; it repeatedly seeks refuge in him as the eternal, unseen, imperishable Brahman whose name frees one from the mouth of death, the highest goal of free ascetics, Trivikrama, dear to Brahmins, the thousand-headed Ananta, and ends: "Lotus-eyed one, giver of safety to devotees, protect me who have come to you." Pleased by his devotion, Vishnu came riding on Garuda, pulled both the elephant and the crocodile out of the lake, split the crocodile with his discus on dry land and freed the elephant from the nooses. The crocodile was really the gandharva Huhu, who had become a crocodile through the curse of Devala; killed by Krishna, he went to heaven. Touched by Vishnu, the elephant became a man with a divine body. Vishnu then said: people who, pure and steady, remember, tell with devotion or hear of me, you, the lake, the splitting of the crocodile, the bamboo thickets, the mountain, the ashvattha tree, the sun, the Ganga and the Naimisha forest will lose their bad dreams and have good ones; those who on rising at dawn remember the Fish, Tortoise, Boar, Vamana, Garuda, Man-Lion and the Elephant King are freed from all sins and reach a holy world. He touched the elephant and the gandharva with his hand; the elephant, now divine, took refuge in him, and Vishnu, praised by the sages, departed. Indra and the gods bowed to him, and sages and charanas praised him in wonder. Brahma said that whoever hears this daily on rising gains the highest success and loses bad dreams; telling, remembering or hearing the Gajendra-moksha frees one from sin at once, as the elephant was freed from bonds. Pulastya ends by calling this the best of prayers to Murari, which removes sin when told, heard or thought upon.

01-086.json.summary: Pulastya tells Narada the story behind the Sarasvata prayer. There was a low Kshatriya, a slanderer and enemy of Brahmins, petty, cruel by nature and fond of hurting others, who always troubled the ancestors, gods and Brahmins. When his life ended he was reborn, through his own evil deeds, as a fearful night-wandering demon (rakshasa), and for hundreds of years he lived by cruelty, seizing and eating every creature that came within reach of his arms. When he had grown old, he once saw on a river bank a great ascetic doing penance with raised arms and controlled senses, a teacher of yoga devoted to Vasudeva, who had protected himself with this protective prayer, the "cage of Vishnu" (Vishnu-panjara): Vishnu with the discus in the east, with the mace in the south, with the bow in the west, with the sword in the north, Hrishikesha in the corners, Janardana in the gaps, the Boar below and the Man-Lion above; may the sharp discus Sudarshana, the blazing mace and the twanging bow destroy all ghosts, demons, goblins (kushmanda), evil spirits, harmful beasts, snakes and men, and those who steal the mind, memory, strength, enjoyment or good marks; may there be health of mind, intellect and senses by praising Vasudeva; may Janardana be on every side; and by the truth that Hari is the highest Brahman and the form of the world, may my threefold evil be destroyed. The rakshasa rushed at him, but the protection broke his force and he stood still for four months until the Brahmin finished his meditation. Seeing the demon weak, frightened and powerless, the sage pitied him and asked why he had come. The rakshasa told him everything, said he had come to hate his own deeds, confessed that he had killed many, made many women widows and childless and destroyed small innocent creatures, and begged for teaching to remove his sin, saying that contact with the protection had filled him with disgust for his past. The sage thought long and said that turning away from sin was right, but he would not teach dharma to demons; the rakshasa should ask Brahmins devoted to teaching. Left worried, the rakshasa stopped eating creatures even when hungry and ate only one creature at every sixth meal-time. Once, hungry in a great forest, he seized a young Brahmin student who had come to gather fruit. The boy asked what he wanted; the demon said he was his food at the sixth meal-time. The boy begged leave to take the fruit to his teacher first and promised to come back; the demon said no one caught at that time is ever freed, not even a god, but he would release him on one condition: since he had done evil from childhood, by nature and because of his birth, the boy must tell him fully how to be freed from those sins; otherwise he would eat him. Unable to answer, the boy prayed to Agni: if he had served the fire and his teacher, kept his vows, held his teacher higher than mother and father, and never despised him in thought, word or deed, may Agni protect him by that truth. Sent by Agni, the goddess Sarasvati appeared, unseen by the demon, told him not to fear, and said she would sit on the tip of his tongue and speak what was good for the demon. The boy then spoke the Sarasvata prayer, to be recited at dawn, noon or evening, which gives strength and peace. It bows again and again to Hari, Krishna, Hrishikesha, Vasudeva, Janardana, Govinda lying on Shesha, the holder of conch, discus and bow, Lakshmi's lord, Damodara, Narayana, Madhava, Keshava who killed Kamsa and Keshin, with the refrain "may he remove my sin"; it takes refuge in Vasudeva whom ascetics meditate on, the all-pervading highest Brahman, who as Brahma creates the world and from whose mouths the four Vedas came, who preserves it as Vishnu, and who as Rudra destroys and dances after swallowing the world; all gods, men, trees and animals are parts of him. It asks that all sin, done by night or day, standing, walking or lying, knowingly or not, by body, mind or speech, from desire for others' wives or wealth, from slandering great souls, from food and drink, in childhood, youth, old age or past births, dissolve like a pot of salt in water by praising him. It bows to him as the future killer of Naraka, Kamsa, Arishta, Keshin and Chanura, asking who else will trick Bali, crush the pride of the Haihaya king, bridge the ocean and kill ten-headed Ravana, play in Nanda's cowherd village and kill Pralamba and Putana. Reciting it destroys sin of seven births, great sins and lesser sins; reading it equals giving sixteen pots of sesame daily for a full year; one who keeps unbroken celibacy and remembers Hari reaches Vishnu's world. The boy ended: as this is true, may the demon release me. The rakshasa released him, and the boy told him this was Vishnu's Sarasvata hymn spoken by Sarasvati, sent by Agni, from his tongue; he should worship Keshava with it day and night with firm devotion and be freed from his sin. The demon bowed, went to Shalagrama, recited the hymn day and night, did penance, worshipped Purushottama, was freed from all sin and reached Vishnu's world. Pulastya ends: whoever reads this hymn is freed from all sins.

01-087.json.summary: Pulastya gives Narada the first of the two sin-destroying hymns to Vishnu, which takes up almost the whole chapter. It bows to Vishnu under a long string of names and titles: lord of the world, Vasudeva, of many forms, the one-horned, Vrishakapi, Shrinivasa, Vishvaksena, Narayana, the one whose banner is the pole star, truth, sacrifice, dharma, the palm tree and Garuda, Vaikuntha, Purushottama, conqueror of cities and foes, womb of creation, Hiranyagarbha, lotus-eyed, lord of dharma, of creatures, of the worlds, of armies and of time, holder of mace, discus and garland, Aniruddha, Hrishikesha, both subtle and gross, Vamana, Madhusudana, thousand-headed, thousand-eyed with sun, moon and fire as eyes, thousand-footed, the sacrificial Boar, the universal form from which the universe came. He is praised as a great banyan tree whose root is the Brahmins, trunk the Kshatriyas, branches the Vaishyas and bark the Shudras; Brahmins with their fires came from his mouth, kings with weapons from his arms, Vaishyas from his sides and thighs, and Shudras from his feet. From his eye came the sun, from his feet the earth, from his ears the directions, from his navel the sky, from his mind the moon, from his breath the wind, from his desire Brahma, from his anger the three-eyed Rudra, from his head heaven, from his mouth Indra and Agni, from his dirt the animals and from his hair the plants. He is Om and the sacred ritual calls (vashat, svaha, svadha), made of all Vedas, gods, holy places and sacrifices, the lord of sacrifice who eats its share, the giver of cows, nectar and gold; he is the knower, the known and knowledge, the offerer, the offering, the fire that carries it, the ladles, the post, the fee, the priest and the patron, the goal, liberation and bliss, the wheel of time with twelve spokes, six hubs and two rims, Hayagriva, Shambhu, Indra, the wind, Mitra and Varuna, both with form and without form, who destroys great and lesser sins. The speaker ends: "I, helpless against all sins, have come to you for shelter." Pulastya says this supreme hymn, which frees from all sins, was spoken long ago by Maheshvara (Shiva) at Varanasi: Rudra went before Keshava, bathed in the holy place with white water (Sitoda) and was calmed and freed from the power of sin. A person devoted to Vishnu who reads this holy hymn spoken by the destroyer of Tripura is freed from sin, becomes calm and is honoured by the great gods.

01-088.json.summary: Pulastya tells Narada the second sin-destroying hymn, which removes sin when properly learned. It is a long series of salutations ("I bow to ...") to forms of Vishnu and Shiva, many of them the gods of the holy places that Prahlada visited on his pilgrimage: the Fish, the Tortoise, Govinda, Hayashirsha (horse-headed), Bhava, Trivikrama, Madhava and Ishana, Hrishikesha, Kumarila, Narayana, the one seated on Garuda, Urdhvakesha, the Man-Lion, Kurudhvaja, Kamapala, Akhanda, Ajita, Vishvakarman, Pundarika, Hamsa, Shambhu, Brahma with Prajapati, the trident-armed god and the discus-bearer, Suvarnaksha, Gopati, Gadapani, Kusheshaya, Ardhanarishvara, Gopala, Vaikuntha, Aparajita, Vishvarupa, Saugandhi, Panchalika, Hayagriva, Svayambhu, Amareshvara, Pushkaraksha, Avimukta, Lola, Jyeshtheshvara, Markandeya, Kartikeya, Sthanu, Langalisha, Trisauvarna, Kapardin, the moon and sun, Dhruva, Padmanabha, Hiranyaksha, Skanda, Bhima, Hatakeshvara, Pranatarpana, Rukmakavacha, Shrinivasa, Purushottama, the four-armed god, the lord of the earth, Pashupati, Shrikantha, Nilakantha, Nakulishvara, Chakrapani, Sunetra, Bhadraksha, Virabhadra, Shankukarna, Vrishadhvaja, Shashiprabha, Upendra, Kalagni-Rudra, Chhagalesha, Kokanada, Hari-Shankara, Agastya, Garuda, Kapila, Brahma and Dharmaraja. It ends by bowing to the stainless, formless, qualityless, sin-destroying refuge, and taking shelter in him. Pulastya says this holy old hymn was spoken by the great sage Agastya; it brings fortune and fame and destroys many sins when recited, remembered or heard. The closing line names it the second sin-destroying hymn, part of the account of Prahlada's pilgrimage in the story of Vamana's appearance.

01-089.json.summary: Pulastya tells Narada that while Prahlada was away on pilgrimage, Bali, son of Virochana, came to Kurukshetra to perform a sacrifice. There the Brahmin Shukra invited the Bhrigu priests. Hearing this, the sages of the Atreya, Gautama, Kaushika and Angirasa families left Kurujangala and went north along the Shatadru, then to the Vipasha, but finding no peace there went on, after bathing and honouring the ancestors and gods, to the holy Kirana, the Airavati, Ishvari, the Devika and the Payoshni. When they dived into another fair river they saw their own reflections inside the water, and again when they came up, and they went on wondering what it meant. From afar they saw a wide forest, dark as Shiva's throat, full of birdsong, with a huge tree whose top covered the sky and whose roots spread under the ground, flowering trees in five colours like stars, and lotus ponds. Delighted, they entered it like swans entering a lake, and in its middle found a holy hermitage of the four aims of life: the hermitage of Dharma facing east, surrounded by palasha trees; that of Artha (wealth) facing west, among sugarcane; that of Kama (desire) facing south, among plantain and ashoka trees; and that of Moksha (liberation) facing north, shining like clear crystal. Moksha dwells in the hermitage at the end of the Krita age, Kama at the end of the Treta, Artha at the end of the Dvapara, and Dharma at the start of the Kali age. There Vishnu, called Akhanda, the four-formed lord, had long been established by Dharma and the others, and learned yogic sages worship him with service, penance and celibacy. The sages, afraid of the demons, settled there on the Akhanda mountain. Other Brahmins, the Ashmakuttas and Marichipas, bathed in the Yamuna and went south to the Avanti land, where by Vishnu's grace the demons could not enter; the Valakhilyas and other celibates, fearing the demons, took shelter at Rudrakoti. With these gone, Shukra brought all the Bhrigus to the sacrifice and himself consecrated Bali for it. Bali sat in white clothes, garlands and paste, a deerskin on his back marked with peacock feathers, among his assembly of Hayagriva, Pralamba, Maya, Bana and others; his chief queen Vindhyavali, a sage's daughter and first of his thousand women, was consecrated with him. In the spring month Shukra released a fine white horse to roam the earth, followed by Tarakaksha. Three months later, while the fire was being fed and the demons honoured, with the sun in Gemini, Aditi, mother of the gods, gave birth to Madhava in the form of a dwarf (Vamana). Brahma came with the great sages and praised the newborn Lord as the form of goodness, eternal, of universal form, fire that burns the forest of enemies and of sins, support of the world, Narayana, Janardana, creator, sustainer and destroyer, asking him to grow and to wipe away Indra's tears. Pulastya says Hari then asked him (Pulastya) to perform his sacred-thread ceremony. Bharadvaja, grandson of Brihaspati, performed his birth rites and the thread ceremony, and the sages gave gifts: Pulaha the sacred thread, Pulastya two white garments, Agastya a deerskin, Bharadvaja the girdle, Marichi, son of Brahma, a palasha staff, Varuni a rosary, Angiras kusha-grass clothing (another reading says the Veda), an umbrella and a pair of sandals (given by Dyuraja and Bhrigu in one reading, by King Raghu and Nriga in the other), and Brihaspati a water pot. So initiated, the Lord learned the Veda with its limbs, and from Bharadvaja the Samaveda with its great tales and music; in one month, to set an example for the world, he became expert in all scriptures. Vamana then asked Bharadvaja's leave to go to Kurukshetra, where the demon king's horse sacrifice was going on, saying that the powers on earth which are his own parts showed him Bali had gone there. Bharadvaja said he did not command him and that they too would go to Bali's sacrifice, and asked in which places the Lord is always present. Vamana said that by his descents and forms he fills the earth, sky, underworld, oceans, heaven, all directions, mountains and clouds; all beings, divine and earthly, moving and unmoving, Indra, the sun, moon, Yama, the Vasus, Varuna, the fires and the world guardians, from Brahma down to plants, with form and without, came from him to fill the earth; the chief of these, honoured by gods, siddhas and demons, are present on earth, and merely seeing them or praising them destroys sin at once.

01-090.json.summary: Vamana (Vishnu) answers Bharadvaja's question by listing the places where he is always present. The first is his great Fish form in the Manasa lake, which destroys all sins when praised or touched. Then, among many others: the Tortoise on the Kaushiki, Hayashirsha at Krishnamsha, Govinda at Hastinapura, Trivikrama on the Yamuna, Bhava at Lingabheda, Madhava at Kedara, Hrishtamurdhaja at Kubjamra, Narayana at Badari, the god seated on Garuda at Varaha, Jayesha at Bhadrakarna, the friend of Brahmins on the Vipasha, the Man-Lion at Kritashaucha, Vishvakarman at Gokarna, Kamapala at Prachina, Pundarika in the great lake, Ajita at Vishakhayupa, Hamsa at Hamsapada, Akhanda on the Payoshni, Kumarila on the Vitasta, Shambhu on Mount Manimat, Prajapati at Brahmanya, the discus-holder on the Madhu river and the trident-armed one on the Himalaya, Suvarnaksha at Bhrigutunga, the yellow-clad one at Naimisha, Gopati and Gadapani at Gaya, Kusheshaya at Gopratara, Ardhanarishvara on southern Mahendra, Gopala on northern Mahendra, Vaikuntha on the Sahya, Aparajita on the Pariyatra, Vishvarupa in Kasheru, Saugandhi on the Malaya, Sadashiva at the foot of the Vindhya, Vishnu in Avanti, Amareshvara among the Nishadhas, Panchalika in Panchala, Hayagriva at Mahodaya, the god lying in yoga at Prayaga, Svayambhu at Madhuvana, Ayogandhi at Pushkara, Keshava, Avimukta and Lola at Varanasi, the mare's-mouth fire in the ocean, Kartikeya at Kumaradhara, Sthanu in Kurujangala, the garland-wearer among the people of Kishkindha, Lakshmi's lord on the Narmada, the three-eyed god and Agni at Mahishmati, Kapardin at Prabhasa, Hiranyaksha on Hemakuta, Skanda at Sharavana, Padmanabha in the Northern Kurus, Hatakeshvara at Saptagodavara, Vateshvara at Prayaga, Rukmakavacha on the Shona, Purushottama among the Madras, Shrinivasa at Plakshavatarana, the four-armed god at Shurparaka, Pashupati at Girivraja, Shrikantha on the Yamuna bank, the tree-form god in the Dandaka forest, Nilakantha at Kalinjara, the discus-bearer on Trikuta, Shashiprabha in Kamarupa, Upendra in Simhala (Lanka), and many more. He also names his forms in the seven lower worlds (for example the thousand-headed one and Kalagni-Rudra in Rasatala), in the higher worlds (Garuda in Bhuvarloka, Vishnu in Svarloka, Agastya in Maharloka, Kapila in Janaloka, Brahma in Brahmaloka), and in the seven continents (the four-armed one in Jambudvipa, Kusheshaya in Kushadvipa, and so on); and on earth he is present at Shalagrama, in all moving and unmoving beings. These ancient holy dwellings give dharma and destroy sin; by praising, remembering, seeing or touching the deity there, gods, men and sadhyas gain dharma, wealth, desire and finally liberation. Having told him this, Vamana said he would now go to the great demon's sacrifice for the good of the gods, and he went from the mountain to Kurujangala with an easy, playful gait.

01-091.json.summary: Pulastya tells Narada that as Vasudeva (Vamana) approached, the earth shook, mountains moved, the oceans were stirred, and the stars in the sky went off their courses. The Sacrifice itself became deeply troubled, fearing that Vishnu would burn it as Shiva once had, and the fires would not accept the shares offered by the Brahmins with Vedic hymns. Seeing these fearful signs, Bali bowed to Shukra and asked why the earth shook like a plantain in the wind, why the fires refused the offerings, why the seas were stirred, why the stars wandered and the directions were dark. Shukra said it was because Vasudeva was coming; the earth could not bear his steps and so it shook and the oceans overflowed. Bali asked what he should do, give or say when Vishnu came, wanting advice that was true, wholesome and kind. Shukra said that Bali had made the demons sharers in sacrifice and shut out the gods, who by the Veda are its rightful eaters, and Hari was coming for that reason; Bali should give him nothing at the sacrifice, not even the tip of a blade of grass, no land or gold, and speak only soothing but empty words, for who could give a gift to one in whose belly all the worlds live? Bali replied that he had never said "I have nothing" or refused to give; how could he do so to Janardana, lord of the world, coming as a humble beggar? Good people say that one who wants prosperity must be well disposed to Brahmins, and he had seen this to be true; people's actions in word, body and mind come from the habits of their past, even across births. He asked whether Shukra had not heard the old story of Koshakara's son in the Malaya land, and at Shukra's request told it. Koshakara, son of the sage Mudgala, a learned ascetic, had a good wife Dharmishtha, daughter of Vatsyayana. Their son was born dull, silent like the dumb and seeing nothing like the blind, so on the sixth day the mother left him at the door. A child-stealing demoness named Shurpakshi came, left her own thin baby there and carried off the Brahmin's son to eat on the Shalodara mountain. Her blind husband Ghatodara told her this was wrong, since the wise Brahmin would curse them, and sent her to bring someone else's child instead. Meanwhile the demon child, left outside, cried loudly with its thumb in its mouth; Dharmishtha called her husband, who saw a child looking just like their own, laughed and said some spirit had entered it to trick them; with mantras he bound it, drawing a line on the ground with kusha grass in his hand. Shurpakshi, invisible, threw the Brahmin's boy down at a distance from the house; Koshakara at once took his own son, and she could not take hers back, so she went away and told her husband. The Brahmin gave the demon child to his wife, and fed his own son on the curd, milk and sugarcane juice of a tawny cow with its calf. Both boys grew to seven years and were named: the demon's son Divakara (Divakirti) and their own son Nishakara (Nishakirti). After the thread ceremony Divakara learned the Veda, but Nishakara, being dull, did not. His parents, relatives, teacher and the people of Malaya blamed him, and his angry father threw him into a dry well and covered it with a great rock. After ten years his mother came by, saw the rock and asked who had put it there; from inside Nishakara said his father had. Frightened, she asked who he was; he said he was her son Nishakara, but she said she had only a son named Divakara. He told her the whole story; she lifted the rock away, he came out and bowed at her feet, and she took him to his father. Koshakara asked why he had never spoken before. Nishakara explained: in a former life he was the son of Vrishakapi, of Vrindaraka's family, born of Mala; his father taught him the scriptures on dharma, wealth, desire and liberation, history and Veda, but his great learning made him blind with pride; pride brought greed, he lost judgment and became a fool, given to sin, always wanting other men's wives and wealth. For that he died by hanging and went to the Raurava hell. After a thousand years he was born a tiger, was caught, caged and taken to a king's city, where all his knowledge came back to him. When the king went out, the queen Jita, matchless in beauty, came near, and from old habit his desire rose; he courted her in fine words, asked her to open the cage, and when she said to wait for night he refused to wait; she opened it, he broke his chains and seized her, but the king's servants surrounded him, beat him and, thinking him a demon when he cried "don't kill me", tied him to a tree and killed him. Back in hell for adultery, after a thousand years he was born a white donkey in the house of the Brahmin Agniveshya, who had many wives; again he remembered everything. One wife, Vimati, rode him to her father's house; on the way, when she got down to bathe in a river in wet clothes, he rushed at her and fell on top of her; a servant sent by the husband chased him with a stick, he fled south, his bridle caught in a bamboo thicket and he died there after six nights. After hell again he became a parrot, caught by a hunter and sold to a merchant's son, kept in the women's quarters as a learned bird and fed by the young women; one of them, the merchant's beloved Chandravali, took him out and held him to her breast, he tried to play with her, got tangled in her necklace and died. After hell he became an ox owned by a Chandala; once, yoked to a cart carrying the Chandala's woman, who sang behind him, he turned to look at her, leapt, fell, was strangled by the yoke rope and died. After a thousand years in hell he was born in Koshakara's house remembering all these births; from past habit both his learning and his bondage had come to him, so now he would never sin in thought, deed or word. Good or bad deeds, study, livelihood, bondage or death all come from past habit; when a man remembers his former births he turns from sin. He said he would go to the forest to increase merit and destroy sin, and asked his father to set Divakirti to the householder's life. He bowed to his parents and went to the Badari hermitage of Vishnu. Bali ended: in this way gifts, study and the rest come to a person from past habit, and he too had practised giving before; gift, penance and study, and also theft, great sin and arson, come from past practice. Having said this to Shukra, Bali sat meditating on Narayana, who holds discus, mace and sword.

01-092.json.summary: Pulastya tells Narada that the Lord in dwarf form (Vamana) reached the sacrifice enclosure and called out aloud: in this sacrifice the Vedas, led by Om, stand in the form of the ascetics; the horse sacrifice is the best of rites, and the demon king the chief of sacrificers. Hearing this, Bali came with the guest-water, honoured him and, with the sage Bharadvaja, led him in, worshipped him by the rule and asked what he should give. Vamana laughed, looked long at Bharadvaja and said: "My teacher's teacher keeps a sacred fire, and he will not keep it on land that belongs to another; for that I ask you, king, for three steps of land measured by my own body." Bali looked at his wife and his son Bana and said this dwarf was small not only in size but in mind, since he foolishly asked for three steps; fate does not give much wealth to the dull and unlucky. He told Vishnu to ask for elephants, horses, land, slave women, gold or whatever he wished; since Bali was the giver and lord of the world, giving only three steps would shame both giver and asker; he could give him the underworld, the earth, the sky or heaven. Vamana said elephants, horses, land and gold should go to those who want them; he wanted only three steps. Bali took the water jar and gave Vishnu the three steps. As soon as the water fell on his hand, the Lord took a divine cosmic form to stride over the three worlds. The parts of his body were the whole universe: the earth his feet, the sky his shanks, the Satya and Tapas worlds his knees, Meru and Mandara his thighs, the Vishvedevas his hips, Kama in his organ, Prajapati in his testicles, the seven seas in his sides, the worlds in his belly, rivers in the three folds of his belly, sacrifices and all pious works in his stomach, the Vasus on his back, the Rudras on his shoulders, the directions his arms, Brahma in his heart, Shri and the oceans in his chest, the moon in his mind, Aditi his neck, the Brahmins with their fires in his mouth, the scriptures on dharma, wealth, desire and liberation on his lips, Lakshmi on his forehead, the Ashvins in his ears, the wind in his breath, all hymns his teeth, Sarasvati his tongue, sun and moon his eyes, the Krittikas and other stars in his eyelashes, King Dhruva in his topknot, stars from his pores and the great sages his hairs. With one step he took the whole earth, the moon and sun at his chest; with the second he crossed the Svar, Mahar, Jana and Tapas worlds, and his great foot struck through the shell of the cosmic egg into the region beyond light. Water flowed from the broken shell and came to Vishnu's foot, and so the river was called Vishnupadi, the river of the gods, honoured by ascetics. With the third step not yet complete, the Lord came to Bali, his lip trembling a little, and said that debt leads to fearful bondage: Bali must fill the third step or accept bondage. Bali's son Bana laughed and argued: Vishnu himself made the earth small, with its six worlds, so why ask Bali for a wide earth he never made? Bali gave all the earth there is; why bind him by a trick of words? Bali cannot stretch what Vishnu himself cannot fill. Gift, worthy receiver, holy place and time are all present here: the gift is land, which grants every wish; the receiver is the god of gods; the time is when the moon is in Jyeshtha and Mula; the place is holy Kurukshetra. Who are we to teach the author of the Vedas right and wrong? It is no wonder the three worlds did not fill your three steps; this was your play. Do not bind Bali; the Lord does whatever he wishes. Vishnu as Trivikrama answered: he had asked Bali for three steps by his own measure, and Bali knowingly gave him unlimited steps; truly he could cover all the worlds with one step, but made it three for Bali's own good. Because Bali poured the water into his hand, Bali would live for a whole kalpa (cosmic age), and when the present age of Manu Shraddhadeva had passed and the Savarni age came, Bali would become Indra. Then he told Bali gently to go, by the fulfilment of his gift, to the underworld called Sutala and live there free from trouble. Bali asked where his lasting enjoyments would come from. Trivikrama said: gifts given without the proper rule, ancestor rites done without a Vedic Brahmin, and study by those who keep no vows will give their fruit to Bali; and after Indra's festival there will be a great festival for him called Dvarapratipada, when people, happy and adorned, will honour him with flowers and lamps, day and night, the chief of festivals, also called Kaumudi, just as in his own reign. Vishnu then sent Bali with his wife to Sutala, took the sacrifice to Indra's city, gave heaven back to Indra, made the gods sharers in sacrifice again, and vanished as the gods watched. After he left, Shalva with a great demon army built the famous flying city Saubha and roamed the sky at will; Maya built Tripura, of gold, copper and iron, and lived there with Tarakaksha, Vidyunmali, servants and wives; and Bana, after heaven was taken and Bali bound in the underworld, built a well-guarded city on earth called Shonita and lived there with demon lords. Pulastya ends: so Vishnu in dwarf form bound Bali to please Indra, for the gods' work and for the good of Brahmins and cows; hearing, remembering or telling this holy account of Vamana's appearance destroys sin and brings merit; and he offers to tell Narada anything else he wishes to hear.

01-093.json.summary: Narada says he has heard how Bali was bound, and asks where Vishnu went after giving heaven to Indra and vanishing, and what Bali did in Sutala. Pulastya says that Vamana, no longer a dwarf, mounted Garuda and went to Brahma's abode. Brahma rose, embraced him warmly, worshipped him and asked why he had been away so long. Vishnu said he had done a great work, binding Bali so the gods would have their share of sacrifice. Delighted, Brahma asked to be shown how. Vishnu showed him the form containing all the gods, ten thousand yojanas wide and as many high, and Brahma bowed, cried "Well done!" and praised him with a long prose hymn. The hymn bows to him as god of gods, Vasudeva, the one-horned, of many forms, Vrishakapi, Shrinivasa, Vishvaksena, Narayana, Vaikuntha, Purushottama, Aniruddha, Keshava, Govinda, Janardana, Madhusudana and Vamana, the thousand-headed, thousand-eyed, thousand-footed, thousand-armed. From him the universe arose: Brahmins from his mouth, Kshatriyas from his arms, Vaishyas from his thighs and Shudras from his lotus feet; the sky from his navel, Indra and Agni from his mouth, the sun from his eye, the moon from his mind, Brahma himself from his grace, the three-eyed Shiva from his anger, the wind from his breath, heaven from his head, the directions from his ears, the earth from his feet and the stars from his radiance. He is Om and the ritual calls, made of the Vedas, holy places, sacrifices and the patron, giver of the worlds, gold, cows and nectar, the great Fish, the Man-Lion, the offerer, the offering and the horse sacrifice, the goal of all who move, the knowledge of the wise, the yoga of yogis, the liberation of those seeking it, the prosperity of the prosperous, the soma and the sun, the consecration and the fee, the twelve months by name (Shuchi, Shukra, Nabhas, Nabhasya and the rest), time, Hayagriva, Shankara, Shambhu, Mitra and Varuna, the remover of all sins, and Trivikrama. So praised, Vishnu told Brahma to choose a boon. Brahma asked that the Lord stay in his abode in this holy form. Vishnu agreed and stayed there in the Vamana form, worshipped in Brahma's house, where apsarases dance, divine singers sing, vidyadharas play instruments, and gods, demons and siddhas praise him. Brahma, cleansed of all impurity, brought fine flowers from heaven and worshipped him. In heaven too Vamana stood, a thousand yojanas in size by Vishnu's measure, and Indra worshipped him there in the same way as Brahma. Pulastya says he has told what Trivikrama did for the good of the gods, and will now tell what the demon did in the underworld.

01-094.json.summary: Pulastya tells Narada that Bali went down to the underworld and had a city built there, adorned with precious jewels and with stairs of pure crystal; in its middle Vishvakarman built a wide palace with diamond terraces and doors hung with nets of pearls. There Bali enjoyed divine and human pleasures with his dear wife Vindhyavali, chief of his thousand women and adorned with virtue. While he lived in Sutala given to pleasure, Vishnu's discus Sudarshana, which takes away the demons' power, came into the underworld, and a great uproar like a stormy sea arose in the demon city. Bali seized his sword and asked what it was. Vindhyavali calmed him, put his sword back in its sheath, and said it was the discus of the great Vamana, which destroys the demon hosts and should be worshipped; she went out with the guest-water. When the thousand-spoked discus came, Bali bowed with joined hands, worshipped it by the rule and praised it: he bows to Hari's discus, shining like a thousand suns, with Brahma in its hub, Shiva with the trident at its edge, great mountains at the roots of its spokes, the gods with Indra, the sun and fire on its spokes, the wind, water, fire, earth and sky in its speed, clouds, lightning and stars at the spoke tips, and the Valakhilya sages outside; he asks it to burn up his sins of body, speech and mind and those of his family, father and mother, and to destroy his worries and diseases. Honoured by Bali, the discus drained the demons of their strength and left the underworld at the autumn equinox. After it had gone Bali grew distressed and, in great trouble, thought of his grandfather Prahlada, who came at once to Sutala. Bali honoured him with the guest-water and asked what is truly good: what should a man living in this world do so that he is not bound, and what is the boat that carries small-minded men across the ocean of worldly life? Prahlada praised his wish and said: for men sinking in the sea of worldly life, beaten by the winds of opposites and weighed down by children, wife and dependants, the one shelter is the boat that is Vishnu. Those who take refuge in Hari, Narayana, do not go to the court of Dharmaraja (Yama); Yama, seeing his servant with the noose in his hand, whispers in his ear, "Leave alone those who have taken refuge in Madhusudana; I am lord of other men, not of Vishnu's devotees", and King Ikshvaku also said that Vishnu's devotees are outside Yama's reach. The only tongue worth the name praises Hari, the only mind is the one given to him, the only hands are those that worship his feet; hands that cannot worship him are mere twigs, a tongue that does not speak his virtues is a growth or disease in the throat; a man who does not worship Vishnu's feet is dead while living and to be mourned by his relatives, while those devoted to Vasudeva are not to be mourned even when dead. All that is bodily, mental or spoken, with form or without, moving or still, seen or unseen, is Keshava; whoever worships Trivikrama has worshipped all worlds, gods and demons. His virtues are countless like the jewels of the sea. Those who take refuge in him do not fall back into the pit of worldly life, are not shamed, do not fear death, do not reach Yama's world or hell; Vishnu's devotees reach a goal higher than Brahmins learned in the Vedas and higher than heroes killed in battle, equal to that of the righteous and pure, and they enter Vasudeva. Those who bow to Keshava with one-pointed devotion become pure and like holy places themselves; whoever thinks of Narayana while walking, standing, sleeping, waking, drinking and eating has the greatest merit and is not born again. Those who remember Madhusudana at dawn, praise him or listen to his praise, and whose minds delight in his words, cross all difficulties. The goal of those devoted to Vishnu's service cannot be reached by penance in a thousand births; mantras, penance and the stages of life are of no use without devotion, and sacrifices, Vedas, gifts, learning, penance and fame are all wasted for one who hates Madhusudana. For a devotee of Janardana the single mantra "Namo Narayanaya" achieves everything. Every work should begin with a bow to Narayana; remembering his name destroys bad times and ill omens; billions of holy places are not worth a sixteenth part of one bow to him; repeating his name gains the merit of all holy places on earth; those who bow to Krishna reach worlds that vow-keepers and ascetics do not; even a devotee of other gods who worships Keshava falsely reaches the place of the good; constant worship of Hrishikesha gives what well-performed penance never does; remembering Padmanabha at the three junctions of the day gives the fruit of fasting. Prahlada told Bali to worship Hari always by the rites set out in the scriptures, to fix his mind on him, be his devotee, sacrifice to him and bow to him, and so gain lasting success and happiness. Those who daily remember Hari reach Vishnu's eternal state; those who meditate on him do not drink a mother's milk again (are not reborn); those who praise him go to his abode; those who listen with devotion are freed from sin and are happy as if filled with nectar. So meditation, remembrance, praise and hearing his names are equal to worship, and one who does not worship Keshava with flowers, leaves and water has surely been robbed by the thief of fate.

01-095.json.summary: Bali asks Prahlada what goal is reached by worshipping Janardana, what worship pleases him, which gifts, which lunar days for fasting and which holy acts please Vishnu, and what else should be done eagerly. Prahlada says gifts given with faith and devotion to Janardana are called imperishable by the sages; the right lunar days are those on which one worships the Lord and fasts with the mind fixed on him. When Brahmins are honoured Janardana is honoured; fools who hate them surely go to hell. Hari himself said, "Brahmins are my body", so no Brahmin, learned or unlearned, should be despised, for he too is Vishnu's divine body and should be honoured. The best flowers are those with colour, sap and scent. Good for worshipping Achyuta are jasmine (jati), shatahva, sumanas, kunda, bahuputa, bana, champaka, ashoka, karavira, yuthika, paribhadra, patala, bakula, girishalini, tilaka, japa (hibiscus), pitaka, nagara and other fragrant flowers, but not ketaki. Good leaves are those of bilva, shami, bhringa, mriganka, tamala and amalaki; the shoots and leaves of the approved flowering plants may also be used, along with tender shoots of creepers, sacred grass, water flowers such as lotuses and blue lilies, clean washed shoots of trees and the tips of durva grass. He is anointed with sandal, saffron, ushira, padmaka and kaliyaka; incense such as mahisha, kana, deodar, sihlaka with agaru, sugar, shankha and nutmeg pleases him; barley, wheat, rice, sesame, mung and urad beans prepared with ghee are dear to him. Gifts of cows, land, cloth, food and gold please him. Gifts by month: in Magha, sesame, a cow made of sesame and fuel, for Madhava; in Phalguna, rice, mung, cloth and black deerskin, for Govinda; in Chaitra, coloured cloth, beds and seats, given to Brahmins; in Vaishakha, perfumes and fragrant garlands, for Madhusudana; then (no month named, between Vaishakha and Ashadha) water jars, a water cow, a palm-leaf fan and fine sandal, for Trivikrama; in Ashadha, a pair of sandals, an umbrella, salt and amalaka, for Vamana; in Shravana, ghee, jars of milk, a ghee cow and fruits, for Shridhara; in Bhadrapada, rice pudding, honey, ghee, salt and rice with jaggery, for Hrishikesha; in Ashvina, sesame, a horse, a bull, curd, copper and iron, for Padmanabha; in Kartika, silver, gold, lamps, jewels and pearls, for Damodara; in Margashirsha, donkeys, camels, mules, elephants, carriages, goats and sheep, for Keshava; in Pausha, palaces, towns, houses and coverings, for Narayana; and at all times slave women and men, ornaments and food of six tastes, for Purushottama; indeed whatever is dearest and pure in one's house should be given to please him. One who builds a temple of Keshava wins everlasting holy worlds; one who gives gardens full of flowers and fruit enjoys pleasures at will; the temple builder saves eight generations of his family along with himself. The ancestors sang verses before the ascetic Yadu king Jyamagha: "Will someone in our family become a devotee of Vishnu and build a temple of Hari? Will a descendant plaster and sweep Vishnu's temple, and give a banner, lamps, flowers and paste to it?" Even one guilty of great or lesser sins is freed by painting a temple of Vishnu. Hearing this, Jyamagha built a temple and plastered it himself, decorated it with minerals and five-coloured paintings, gave lamps of fragrant oil and ghee, many-coloured banners, and fine gardens with great platforms where ascetics, celibates, Vedic scholars, the poor, the blind and the disabled were always honoured; and so, it is said, he reached Vishnu's abode, and those seeking Vishnu's world still follow his path. So Prahlada told Bali to build a temple of Hari, worship him, and honour learned Brahmins, especially those versed in the Puranas and of good conduct, with clothes, ornaments, jewels, cows, land and gold as far as his wealth allowed; then Murari would surely bless him. Having said this, Prahlada, honoured by Bali, attained release (vimukti), his wishes fulfilled, and left. Bali's moon-white temple shone, and he had the best of Indra's craftsmen make an image of Keshava; with his wife he himself swept and plastered the temple and made matchless offerings of barley, sugar and the like; Vindhyavali herself gave lamps in Vishnu's house, and Bali had learned Purana-reciting Brahmins sing and recite holy works. Because Bali kept to this righteous path, Janardana himself in divine form stood guard at his door to protect him, holding a pestle as bright as ten thousand suns, striking down wicked enemies and letting no one into his walled house. With Narayana guarding the door, Bali worshipped Hari inside the palace, always remembered Hari's words, which became the goad that kept him humble, and recited this story, recalling the good, true advice of his grandfather. The chapter ends in praise of heeding the words of elders: those who follow elders' words, even if harsh at first, are glad later; elders' words are the cure that removes the poison when disaster bites like a snake; they satisfy more than drinking soma; those who have no elders to guide them in trouble are like the dead, find no peace, and cannot be rescued from the flood of misfortune; so whoever hears and follows elders' words gains success at once, as Bali did.

01-096.json.summary: This last chapter closes the Purana with Pulastya's praise of it to Narada. Whoever hears this most holy Purana gains great fame and devotion and reaches Vishnu's abode. As bathing in the Ganga purifies sins, so hearing the Purana destroys wrongdoing; one who hears the Vamana suffers no diseases, poison or black magic in body or family. One who hears it daily by the rule, with devotion, worshipping and bowing to Vishnu, gains the full fruit of a horse sacrifice with its fees and of gifts of gold, land, horses, cows, elephants and chariots; a woman or man who hears even one quarter of it becomes most holy on earth. Reciting it with a single mind gives the fruit of bathing in the Ganga, at Naimisha, Pushkara, Kokamukha or at Prayaga in Magha, and of the royal consecration (Rajasuya) and the Sautramani sacrifice, and all the happiness of earth and heaven. Reading it gives the merit of giving jewels, of gifts at solar and lunar eclipses, of feeding a hungry Brahmin who keeps the sacred fire, of supporting wife and children in famine, and of serving gods, fire, Brahmins, parents and an elder brother. The Vamana is called the fourteenth and foremost Purana; hearing it destroys even great sins at once, and reading, hearing or having it read destroys all sins and pleases Vamana. This highest secret should not be told to one without devotion to Hari, one who delights in blaming Brahmins, one who gives no fee, or a sinful arguer. A Brahmin who always says "Bow, bow to Vamana, the cause" is given Vishnu's state of liberation. The reciter should be given cows, land, gold and ornaments, without stinginess, for meanness in payment destroys the merit of hearing. Read or heard at the three junctions of the day without envy, it destroys all sins and gives every kind of wealth. The colophon says the Vamana Purana is complete.
